items.stem: A 13-year-old girl is on the paediatric ward of a regional hospital, 6 hours after treatment began for severe diabetic ketoacidosis at the first presentation of type 1 diabetes. At presentation she weighed 40 kg. Her venous pH was 7.02, bicarbonate 3 mmol/L, glucose 41.0 mmol/L, sodium 130 mmol/L and urea 14.2 mmol/L. She received a 10 mL/kg 0.9% saline bolus, then fluids to replace her deficit over 48 hours with added potassium. An insulin infusion at 0.1 units/kg/hour was started after the first hour. She now has a severe headache, has vomited once, and is irritable and disorientated. Her temperature is 36.7 °C, pulse 64/min (previously 128/min), blood pressure 134/86 mm Hg (previously 106/64 mm Hg), respirations 20/min and SpO2 98% on room air. Her GCS is 13 (E3 V4 M6). Her pupils are equal and reactive. Capillary glucose is 15.8 mmol/L and serum sodium is 134 mmol/L.
items.ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Non-contrast CT brain before any further treatment
Intravenous sodium bicarbonate 1 mmol/kg over 1 hour
Increase the fluid rate to replace the deficit over 24 hours
Intravenous mannitol 0.5 to 1 g/kg over 20 minutes
items.explanation: This girl has cerebral oedema, the main cause of death in children with DKA. She has several risk factors: a first presentation, young age, severe acidosis and a high urea at presentation. It typically appears 4 to 12 hours into treatment. The warning signs are a new headache, vomiting, irritability or confusion, a falling GCS, and a falling heart rate with rising blood pressure (part of the Cushing response). The RCH DKA guideline and ISPAD 2022 say to treat on clinical grounds straight away. Give IV mannitol 0.5 to 1 g/kg over 20 minutes, or 3% hypertonic saline 2.5 to 5 mL/kg over 10 to 15 minutes. At the same time, cut the fluid rate by one third, raise the head of the bed, call senior and intensive care help, and arrange retrieval or transfer. Imaging comes only after she is stable. CT brain should not delay treatment, because a normal early scan does not rule out cerebral oedema and she could herniate while waiting for it. Bicarbonate is itself linked to cerebral oedema and has no role here. Faster fluids would make the brain swelling worse. Her glucose of 15.8 mmol/L rules out hypoglycaemia as the cause of her confusion.
why: Wrong: imaging must not delay treatment, because cerebral oedema is diagnosed clinically and an early CT may be normal; scan only once she is stable.
Wrong: bicarbonate in paediatric DKA is linked to cerebral oedema and is not indicated; her acidosis is improving with insulin and fluids.
Wrong: giving fluid faster makes cerebral oedema worse; the fluid rate should be cut by one third, not increased.
Wrong: her capillary glucose is 15.8 mmol/L, so hypoglycaemia does not explain her confusion, and the change in her heart rate and blood pressure points to raised intracranial pressure.

items.stem: A 31-year-old woman, gravida 2, para 1, at 35 weeks 4 days' gestation comes to the maternity assessment unit because her baby has moved much less than usual since the previous evening. Two years ago she had a stillbirth at 38 weeks, and that infant was small for gestational age. In this pregnancy she has diet-controlled gestational diabetes. A scan at 32 weeks showed an estimated weight on the 40th centile. She takes low-dose aspirin. Her blood pressure is 118/74 mm Hg, pulse is 86/min, respirations are 16/min and temperature is 36.7 °C. Symphysis-fundal height is 35 cm. A urine dipstick shows no protein. A 40-minute cardiotocograph (CTG) shows a baseline rate of 135 bpm, baseline variability of 10 bpm, three accelerations of at least 15 bpm lasting at least 15 seconds, and no decelerations. She feels several movements during the trace.
items.ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Same-day sonographic biometry and liquor volume assessment
Discharge with routine antenatal review at 37 weeks
Continuation of the CTG for a further 40 minutes
items.explanation: Every feature of this CTG is normal by RANZCOG criteria: the baseline is 110 to 160 bpm, variability is 6 to 25 bpm, there are accelerations and there are no decelerations. Her observations and urinalysis show no sign of pre-eclampsia or infection. A normal CTG means the fetus is not hypoxic right now. It does not rule out underlying placental insufficiency or growth restriction, so it does not exclude a later poor outcome. The Stillbirth CRE guideline on decreased fetal movements says that when a woman has risk factors for growth restriction or stillbirth, she should have an ultrasound for fetal biometry and amniotic fluid volume, ideally within 24 hours, along with obstetric review. This woman has a previous small-for-gestational-age stillbirth and gestational diabetes. The scan should be arranged today. She should then be told to come back straight away, at any hour, if movements decrease again.
why: Sending her home with routine follow-up treats the normal CTG as if it rules out compromise, which is unsafe in a woman with risk factors for stillbirth.
A single episode of reduced movements with a normal CTG and a normal assessment is not a reason for birth at 35 weeks, and preterm induction brings neonatal risks with no proven benefit.
The trace already meets every normal criterion with a good signal, so recording for longer adds no information about her placental reserve.
A Kleihauer-Betke test looks for fetomaternal haemorrhage, which would be suspected with a sinusoidal or abnormal trace, trauma or bleeding, and none of these is present here.

items.stem: A 70-year-old man sees his general practitioner with a 1-day history of a painful, swollen left knee. He cannot bear weight. Two days ago he knelt on a rusty nail while clearing soil in his garden shed and did not clean the small wound. He has type 2 diabetes treated with metformin and osteoarthritis of both knees. His record shows he completed his childhood primary immunisation course, and his last booster was given 12 years ago after a hand laceration. He has no allergies and no immunosuppressive conditions or medicines. His temperature is 38.7 °C, pulse 108/min, blood pressure 134/80 mm Hg, respiratory rate 20/min and SpO2 97% on room air. There is a 2-mm puncture wound stained with soil below the left patella. The knee is hot, with a large effusion and pain on any passive movement. Capillary glucose is 13.8 mmol/L. Same-day hospital transfer for joint aspiration has been arranged.
items.ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate additional preventive measure at this visit?
options: Serum tetanus antitoxin level before vaccinating
items.explanation: The main issue in this man is septic arthritis from direct inoculation, and he has already been referred for aspiration before antibiotics. A separate risk that is easy to miss is tetanus. A puncture wound from a rusty nail, contaminated with soil and left untreated for more than 6 hours, is tetanus-prone. Under the Australian Immunisation Handbook, a person with a documented primary course of 3 or more doses and a tetanus-prone wound needs a tetanus-containing vaccine if it has been 5 years or more since the last dose. In Australia this is usually dTpa. His last booster was 12 years ago, so he needs one injection now. Tetanus immunoglobulin is for people with fewer than 3 doses, an uncertain history, or significant immunocompromise. Well-managed type 2 diabetes on metformin does not count as significant immunocompromise for this purpose. Giving the booster now, at the first visit, means it will not be missed during the hospital admission.
why: Wrong: tetanus immunoglobulin is only added when the primary course is incomplete or uncertain, or the patient is significantly immunocompromised, and none of these applies to him.
Wrong: immunoglobulin on its own gives only short-lived passive protection and does not boost his immunity, which has waned since his last dose 12 years ago.
Wrong: a full primary course is only for people who are unvaccinated or have an uncertain history, and his record shows a completed childhood course.
Wrong: antitoxin levels are not used to guide wound management, and waiting for the result would delay a booster he clearly needs now.

items.stem:
A 57-year-old man is brought to the emergency department 1 hour after vomiting about 400 mL of bright red blood at home. He has passed black stools for 2 days. He has drunk about 10 standard drinks of beer daily for 20 years, and his last drink was last night. He takes no regular medicines. His temperature is 36.6°C, pulse is 116/min, respirations are 20/min, blood pressure is 100/62 mm Hg, and oxygen saturation is 97% on room air. He is alert and oriented. He has spider naevi on his chest and palmar erythema. The abdomen has shifting dullness, and the spleen tip is palpable. Two large-bore cannulas are inserted and a crystalloid bolus is started. Laboratory studies show:
Haemoglobin 88 g/L (130–180)
Platelets 74 x10^9/L (150–400)
INR 1.9 (0.9–1.2)
Urea 12.4 mmol/L (2.5–7.5)
Creatinine 90 µmol/L (60–110)
Albumin 26 g/L (35–50)
The gastroenterology registrar plans endoscopy within the next few hours.
items.ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Fresh frozen plasma to correct the INR
Pantoprazole infusion as the only drug therapy
Red cell transfusion to a haemoglobin above 100 g/L
items.explanation: This man has an upper GI bleed with features of decompensated alcohol-related cirrhosis and portal hypertension: ascites, splenomegaly, stigmata of chronic liver disease, low platelets, a raised INR and a low albumin. His tachycardia and borderline blood pressure point to significant blood loss. The bleed should be treated as variceal until endoscopy shows otherwise. Under Therapeutic Guidelines (eTG) and Baveno VII, a vasoactive drug (terlipressin 2 mg IV every 4 hours, or octreotide) should start as soon as a variceal bleed is suspected, before endoscopy. It lowers portal pressure, improves control of bleeding and reduces mortality. Patients with cirrhosis and GI bleeding should also get antibiotic prophylaxis (ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily). This reduces bacterial infection, rebleeding and death. Endoscopic band ligation should follow within 12 hours. Fresh frozen plasma is wrong because the INR does not reflect bleeding risk in cirrhosis, and the extra volume can raise portal pressure. A pantoprazole infusion alone is wrong because it does nothing for a variceal bleed and would delay vasoactive therapy and antibiotics. Transfusing to a haemoglobin above 100 g/L is wrong because the restrictive target is 70 to 80 g/L, and over-transfusion raises portal pressure and the risk of rebleeding. Balloon tamponade is wrong at this stage because it is a temporary bridge for bleeding that cannot be controlled after drug and endoscopic therapy.
why: Fresh frozen plasma is wrong because the INR does not predict bleeding in cirrhosis, eTG advises against routinely correcting it, and the extra volume raises portal pressure.
A pantoprazole infusion alone is wrong because it does not lower portal pressure or treat a variceal bleed, and it leaves out the vasoactive drug and antibiotics the guidelines require.
Transfusing to a haemoglobin above 100 g/L is wrong because the restrictive target is 70 to 80 g/L, and over-transfusion raises portal pressure and the risk of rebleeding.
Balloon tamponade is wrong because it is only a temporary rescue for bleeding that cannot be controlled after drug and endoscopic therapy, and endoscopy is already planned.

items.stem: A 38-year-old man presents to a general practice in Perth with a 7-week history of cough productive of yellow phlegm. For the past week the phlegm has been streaked with blood. He reports drenching night sweats and has lost 6 kg without trying. He was born in the Philippines, moved to Australia 4 years ago and works as a cleaner. He has no medical history, takes no regular medicines and has never smoked. His temperature is 37.9 °C, heart rate 96/min, respiratory rate 18/min, blood pressure 118/74 mm Hg and oxygen saturation 97% on room air. There are crackles over the left upper zone, and there is no clubbing or lymphadenopathy. White cell count is 8.4 x10^9/L (4.0–11.0), CRP is 41 mg/L (<5) and HIV serology is negative. A chest X-ray shows patchy opacification with a small cavity at the left apex. He has been given a surgical mask and moved to a separate room.
items.ask: Which of the following investigations is most likely to confirm the diagnosis?
options: Interferon-gamma release assay on peripheral blood
Tuberculin skin test read at 48 to 72 hours
Three sputum samples for acid-fast smear, culture and NAAT
Contrast-enhanced CT scan of the chest
items.explanation: This man has had a productive cough for more than 3 weeks, with haemoptysis, night sweats and weight loss. He was born in a country with high TB rates, and his chest X-ray shows a cavity in the upper lobe. This is active pulmonary tuberculosis until proven otherwise. The X-ray supports the diagnosis but cannot confirm it. Confirmation needs microbiology. The Australian guidelines (CDNA SoNG, the state TB programs and eTG Antibiotic) recommend 3 sputum samples collected at least 8 hours apart, with at least 1 taken first thing in the morning. Each sample has acid-fast bacilli smear microscopy, mycobacterial culture and a nucleic acid amplification test (NAAT, such as Xpert MTB/RIF). Smear microscopy and NAAT give a quick answer. NAAT also tells M. tuberculosis apart from non-tuberculous mycobacteria and detects rifampicin resistance. Culture is the gold standard and gives full drug-susceptibility results. A cavity usually means a high bacterial load, so expectorated sputum is very likely to be positive. The samples should be collected outdoors or in a well-ventilated room, away from other people. He also needs urgent referral to the state TB service and notification.
why: An interferon-gamma release assay shows immune sensitisation to M. tuberculosis, but it cannot tell latent infection from active disease, and a negative result does not exclude active TB.
A tuberculin skin test cannot tell latent infection from active disease, can be falsely positive after BCG vaccination (common in people born in the Philippines), and needs a second visit.
CT shows the cavity and the extent of disease in more detail, but it provides no microbiological confirmation or susceptibility results and does not change the need for sputum testing.

Bronchoscopy with lavage is invasive and carries a risk of spreading infection to staff, so it is kept for patients who cannot produce sputum or whose sputum samples are negative despite strong suspicion.

items.stem: A 72-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with 2 days of left-sided temporal headache. She has pain when brushing her hair and jaw pain that builds while chewing and settles at rest. This morning she woke with a grey shadow over the lower half of the vision in her left eye. She has hypertension treated with perindopril and has never had regular headaches. Her temperature is 37.3°C, pulse is 82/min, respirations are 16/min, blood pressure is 148/86 mm Hg, and oxygen saturation is 97% on room air. The left temporal artery is thickened, tender and pulseless. Visual acuity is 6/6 in the right eye and 6/24 in the left. There is a left relative afferent pupillary defect, and fundoscopy shows a pale, swollen left optic disc. ESR is 92 mm/h (reference <30), CRP is 64 mg/L (reference <5) and platelet count is 498 × 10^9/L (reference 150–400).
items.ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Non-contrast CT scan of the brain
Oral aspirin 300 mg as a single dose
items.explanation: This woman over 50 has a new temporal headache, scalp tenderness, jaw claudication, a thickened pulseless temporal artery, raised ESR and CRP, and thrombocytosis. This is giant cell arteritis. Her left eye shows reduced acuity, an inferior field defect, an RAPD and a pale (chalky) swollen disc, so she already has arteritic anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy. Without treatment, the other eye can lose vision within days. Therapeutic Guidelines (Rheumatology) advise that suspected GCA with any visual symptom or sign is a sight-threatening emergency. It should be treated at once with IV methylprednisolone 500 mg to 1 g daily for 3 days, then high-dose oral prednisolone, with same-day ophthalmology review. Treatment should never wait for a biopsy or imaging. Oral prednisolone 50 mg daily is the starting dose for GCA without visual involvement and is not enough once the optic nerve is ischaemic. A temporal artery biopsy confirms the diagnosis, but it stays positive for 1 to 2 weeks after steroids start, so waiting for it only risks the other eye. A CT brain is not needed: the headache came on gradually, there are no focal deficits, the picture is classic GCA, and the scan would delay treatment. Aspirin does not treat the vasculitis and cannot replace corticosteroids.
why: Oral prednisolone 40 to 60 mg is the right start for GCA without visual involvement, but she already has ischaemic optic neuropathy and needs IV pulse therapy.
A biopsy stays diagnostic for 1 to 2 weeks after steroids start, so it should be done after treatment begins, not before.
A gradual-onset headache with no focal neurological signs and classic GCA features does not need CT, and scanning first would delay sight-saving treatment.
Aspirin does not suppress the granulomatous vasculitis and cannot replace urgent high-dose corticosteroids.

items.stem: A 74-year-old woman is reviewed in the coronary care unit 3 hours after emergency coronary angiography. She came to the emergency department with central chest pain, fever and a productive cough 2 days after her sister's funeral. Her ECG showed ST elevation in V2 to V4. Angiography showed no obstructive coronary disease, and left ventriculography showed apical ballooning. Her chest X-ray shows right lower lobe pneumonia, and she is receiving ceftriaxone and azithromycin. She has had 1 L of crystalloid since arrival. Temperature is 38.2 °C, pulse 108/min, blood pressure 82/50 mmHg, respiratory rate 24/min and SpO2 95% on 2 L/min oxygen. She has a new harsh systolic murmur at the left sternal edge. Her JVP is not raised, and there are crackles at the right base only. Bedside echocardiography shows an LVEF of 35%, apical akinesis with hyperdynamic basal segments, systolic anterior motion of the mitral valve and a peak left ventricular outflow tract gradient of 70 mmHg. Serum lactate is 2.9 mmol/L (reference below 2.0).
items.ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in managing her low blood pressure?
items.explanation: This woman has Takotsubo cardiomyopathy: two stress triggers (her sister's death and pneumonia with sepsis), apical ballooning, and no culprit lesion on angiography. She now has one of its most dangerous complications, dynamic left ventricular outflow tract (LVOT) obstruction. The basal segments contract too hard, which pulls the anterior mitral leaflet into the outflow tract (systolic anterior motion, SAM). That causes the new systolic murmur, a gradient of 70 mmHg and hypotension. The obstruction gets worse with anything that empties the ventricle or makes it contract harder: low preload, low afterload, tachycardia or inotropes. Her JVP is not raised, she has no pulmonary oedema, and sepsis has left her relatively low on fluid, so the first step is a cautious crystalloid bolus to fill the LV and widen the outflow tract. Reassess after each bolus. If hypotension persists, the next options are a pure vasoconstrictor such as phenylephrine, a short-acting beta-blocker if she can tolerate it, or mechanical support that does not lower afterload. Inotropes are avoided. This is the key safety point after Takotsubo is diagnosed in a shocked patient: get an echo to look for an LVOT gradient before giving any inotrope.
why: Wrong: dobutamine is an inotrope that makes the basal segments contract harder and speeds the heart, which worsens SAM, raises the LVOT gradient and can deepen the shock.
Wrong: a nitrate dilates veins and arteries, lowering preload and afterload, which narrows the outflow tract, worsens the obstruction and would drop her blood pressure further.
Wrong: a diuretic lowers preload in a woman with no pulmonary oedema and a JVP that is not raised, so the LV cavity shrinks and the obstruction gets worse.
Wrong: a balloon pump lowers afterload, which can increase the LVOT gradient, so it is not recommended in Takotsubo with outflow obstruction.

items.stem: A 48-year-old man comes to the emergency department because of burning central chest pain that began 90 minutes after a large dinner. For 6 weeks he has had similar pain on most evenings. It is worse when he lies flat and partly eased by over-the-counter antacids, and he has acid regurgitation. For the past month, bread and steak have felt as if they stick behind his sternum. His weight has fallen from 84 kg to 79 kg over 3 months without dieting. He drinks about 4 standard drinks daily, stopped smoking 10 years ago and takes no regular medicines. Temperature is 36.8 °C, pulse 82/min, blood pressure 134/82 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min and SpO2 98% on room air. He has mild epigastric tenderness and no palpable lymph nodes. A 12-lead ECG recorded during pain is normal. High-sensitivity troponin I is 2 ng/L at 0 hours and 2 ng/L at 2 hours (99th percentile 26 ng/L). Haemoglobin is 136 g/L (reference 130 to 180 g/L).
items.ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Eight-week trial of a proton pump inhibitor
Urea breath test for Helicobacter pylori
items.explanation: The ECG taken during pain is normal, and high-sensitivity troponin is very low and unchanged at 0 and 2 hours, so acute MI is ruled out and this man is at low risk of acute coronary syndrome. His symptoms fit gastro-oesophageal reflux disease: burning retrosternal pain after meals that is worse lying flat, with acid regurgitation. He also has two alarm features. One is new dysphagia to solids. The other is unintentional loss of 5 kg, which is about 6% of his body weight. Daily alcohol and past smoking add to his risk. Under Therapeutic Guidelines (Gastrointestinal), alarm features call for an urgent gastroscopy rather than empirical treatment. The aim is to find or rule out the serious complications of reflux, such as peptic stricture, Barrett's oesophagus and oesophageal adenocarcinoma, and to take biopsies. The most important thing to prevent here is a missed or late diagnosis of cancer. A PPI can be started after the scope is booked, but it does not replace the scope.
why: An empirical PPI trial is only for reflux without alarm features, and it can ease symptoms and heal the mucosa, which delays and hides the diagnosis of cancer.
A normal ECG during pain and unchanged troponin well below the 99th percentile mean he is low risk, and his symptoms are not cardiac, so coronary imaging does not deal with the main danger.
A barium swallow can show narrowing but cannot take a biopsy, and it is not first-line for dysphagia with weight loss, so it would only delay the gastroscopy he needs.
Test-and-treat for H. pylori is for dyspepsia without alarm features, and it does not investigate dysphagia or weight loss.

items.stem: A 13-year-old girl comes to her general practitioner with her mother to discuss test results after being investigated for short stature and absent breast development. She had puffy hands and feet as a newborn and several middle ear infections in early childhood. She takes no medicines. Her height is 138 cm (well below the 3rd centile; mid-parental height 165 cm) and her BMI is 18.9 kg/m2. Pulse is 78/min, blood pressure is 114/70 mm Hg in the right arm and 118/72 mm Hg in the right leg. She has a webbed neck, a low posterior hairline, Tanner stage 1 breasts and a soft ejection systolic murmur at the right upper sternal edge. Karyotype is 45,X in all 30 cells counted, with no marker chromosome. Echocardiogram shows a bicuspid valve with fusion of the right and left coronary cusps, no stenosis or regurgitation, no coarctation, and an ascending diameter normal for body surface area. Renal ultrasound shows a horseshoe kidney without hydronephrosis. TSH is 7.8 mIU/L (0.5 to 4.5) with free T4 14 pmol/L (10 to 20).
items.ask: Which of the following life-threatening complications is she at greatest risk of over her lifetime?
items.explanation: Women with Turner syndrome have a much higher risk of aortic dissection than the general population, and it is a leading cause of early death. It often happens at a young age and at aortic diameters that would not cause concern in other people. Her risk is higher still because she has a bicuspid aortic valve. Other risk factors are coarctation, aortic dilatation, hypertension and pregnancy. Her aorta is normal now, but the 2024 international Turner syndrome guideline recommends lifelong aortic imaging (cardiac MRI or echocardiography, with diameters indexed to body size), tight blood pressure control, and a cardiology assessment before any pregnancy, including assisted conception. The mother and the girl should be told that sudden chest, back or tearing pain needs an emergency ambulance. Gonadoblastoma needs Y chromosome material, and none was seen. A horseshoe kidney carries only a small extra risk of Wilms tumour. Endocarditis can occur with a bicuspid valve, but it is much less common and less of a concern in Turner syndrome than dissection. Her thyroiditis is subclinical, so myxoedema coma is a remote risk.
why: Gonadoblastoma risk depends on Y chromosome material, and her 30-cell karyotype showed no Y chromosome or marker chromosome, with no virilisation.
A horseshoe kidney carries only a small extra risk of Wilms tumour, this tumour usually occurs in early childhood, and her ultrasound was otherwise normal.

A bicuspid valve does raise the risk of endocarditis, but it is far less common and less often fatal in Turner syndrome than dissection, and Australian guidelines do not recommend antibiotic prophylaxis for her.
Her autoimmune thyroiditis is subclinical with a normal free T4, and it will be found and treated through routine monitoring long before severe decompensation could happen.

items.stem: A 52-year-old man comes to the emergency department with 2 days of fever and constant, diffuse abdominal pain. Over the past 3 weeks his abdominal girth has increased. Alcohol-related cirrhosis was diagnosed 3 years ago. He has not attended follow-up and drinks about 10 standard drinks daily. He has never had abdominal surgery and takes no regular medicines. Temperature is 38.4°C, pulse 104/min, blood pressure 108/66 mmHg and respiratory rate 20/min. He is jaundiced. His abdomen is distended, with shifting dullness and mild diffuse tenderness but no guarding or rigidity. Serum results: albumin 24 g/L, glucose 6.1 mmol/L, LDH 190 U/L (reference less than 250 U/L) and creatinine 124 µmol/L. A diagnostic paracentesis under ultrasound guidance yields cloudy, straw-coloured fluid. Fluid results: white cell count 2100 x10^6/L with 75% neutrophils, total protein 8 g/L, albumin 5 g/L, glucose 5.6 mmol/L and LDH 105 U/L. The Gram stain shows neutrophils and no organisms.
items.ask: Which of the following is the most accurate interpretation of the paracentesis results?
options: High-gradient ascites with infection and no Runyon criteria for a surgical source
Low-gradient ascites with infection suggesting tuberculous peritonitis
High-gradient ascites with infection meeting Runyon criteria for perforation
High-gradient ascites with a polymorph count below the threshold for infection
Low-gradient ascites with infection suggesting peritoneal carcinomatosis
items.explanation: Read the fluid in three steps. First, the serum-ascites albumin gradient (SAAG) is 24 − 5 = 19 g/L. A gradient of 11 g/L or more means the ascites is due to portal hypertension, which fits his cirrhosis. Second, the absolute neutrophil count is 2100 x 0.75 = 1575 x10^6/L. Anything at or above 250 x10^6/L confirms ascitic infection, so IV antibiotics and IV albumin should start without waiting for the culture. Third, look for a surgical source using the Runyon criteria: protein above 10 g/L, glucose below 2.8 mmol/L, or LDH above the serum upper limit. His protein is 8 g/L, glucose 5.6 mmol/L and LDH 105 U/L, so he meets none of them. The Gram stain shows no organisms, and he has no peritonism. Together these point to spontaneous rather than secondary bacterial peritonitis. The low protein (below 10 g/L) is also a risk factor for SBP, and he will need long-term prophylaxis after this episode.
why: Wrong: tuberculous peritonitis gives a low gradient (below 11 g/L), lymphocyte-rich and protein-rich fluid, but his gradient is 19 g/L, the cells are mostly neutrophils and the protein is 8 g/L.
Wrong: secondary peritonitis needs at least two Runyon criteria, and his protein (8 g/L), glucose (5.6 mmol/L) and LDH (105 U/L, below the serum limit) meet none, with no organisms on Gram stain.
Wrong: the absolute neutrophil count is 1575 x10^6/L, far above the diagnostic threshold of 250 x10^6/L, so this misreads the 75% as the count or ignores the threshold.
Wrong: peritoneal carcinomatosis gives a low gradient and high protein, whereas this fluid has a gradient of 19 g/L and protein of 8 g/L, which point to portal hypertension.

items.stem: A 76-year-old man is reviewed on the surgical ward on the morning he is due to go home. Two days ago he came to the emergency department after suddenly passing a large volume of painless maroon blood with clots. He had one more small bleed in the department and none since. He has type 2 diabetes and knee osteoarthritis. He takes metformin. For the past 3 months he has also taken an over-the-counter anti-inflammatory tablet most days for knee pain. He takes no other medicines. Today his temperature is 36.8 °C, pulse is 72/min and blood pressure is 132/78 mm Hg. His abdomen is soft and not tender. Haemoglobin is 118 g/L (his baseline is 138 g/L; reference range 130 to 180 g/L). Colonoscopy after bowel preparation showed many diverticula in the sigmoid and descending colon, with no inflammation, active bleeding, polyp or tumour. He asks how he can lower the chance of this happening again.
items.ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate advice to reduce his risk of recurrent bleeding?
items.explanation: This man had a self-limiting diverticular bleed. It was sudden, painless and large, with maroon blood and clots, and colonoscopy showed diverticulosis with no other source. Diverticular bleeding often recurs, in roughly 20 to 40% of patients over the following years. Non-aspirin NSAIDs are a well-established risk factor that can be changed. They raise the risk of a first diverticular bleed and of a repeat bleed. The British Society of Gastroenterology lower GI bleeding guideline advises stopping non-aspirin NSAIDs after a diverticular bleed, and Australian guidance (eTG) also advises avoiding NSAIDs in diverticular disease. The over-the-counter anti-inflammatory he takes every day should therefore be stopped, and regular paracetamol used for his osteoarthritis pain instead. Other sensible advice is a high-fibre diet with enough fluid, and returning urgently if he bleeds again. Avoiding nuts and seeds is an old myth, and large cohort studies show no added risk of bleeding or diverticulitis. Mesalazine does not prevent diverticular bleeding or recurrent diverticulitis. A proton pump inhibitor protects the stomach and duodenum but has no effect on bleeding from colonic diverticular vessels. Surgery is kept for recurrent severe bleeding, or bleeding that endoscopy and embolisation cannot control. It is not used after a first bleed that stopped by itself.
why: Studies show nuts, seeds and popcorn do not raise the risk of diverticular bleeding or diverticulitis, so this restriction does not help.
Mesalazine has no proven role in preventing diverticular bleeding or recurrent diverticular disease.
A proton pump inhibitor protects against upper GI bleeding from NSAIDs but does nothing for bleeding from colonic diverticula.
Elective colectomy is kept for recurrent or uncontrollable bleeding and is not offered after a first bleed that stopped by itself.

items.stem: A 37-year-old woman, gravida 3, para 2, comes to the fetal medicine clinic at 17 weeks pregnant to discuss her amniocentesis result. She conceived naturally. At 10 weeks, whole-genome cell-free DNA screening (fetal fraction 11%) showed a low chance of trisomies 21, 18 and 13 and of sex chromosome conditions, and a high chance of trisomy 16. A 7-week scan had shown one gestational sac. The 12-week scan was normal, with a nuchal translucency of 1.4 mm. Amniocentesis at 16 weeks, with QF-PCR and chromosomal microarray, showed a normal female result with no trisomy 16. Both of her previous pregnancies were uncomplicated. She has no medical history, does not smoke, and takes folic acid and iodine. Her BMI is 23 kg/m2. Her blood pressure is 114/70 mm Hg and pulse is 76/min. Ultrasound today shows a single live fetus with biometry consistent with dates, no anomaly seen, normal amniotic fluid and a high posterior placenta. She is blood group O RhD positive, and her antibody screen is negative.
items.ask: This patient is at greatest risk of which of the following complications later in this pregnancy?
items.explanation: The screening result was valid (adequate fetal fraction) and showed a high chance of trisomy 16, but amniocentesis found a chromosomally normal fetus. The vanishing twin explanation is unlikely because she conceived naturally and an early scan showed one sac. The most likely explanation is therefore confined placental mosaicism (CPM): the trisomic cells are in the placenta, which supplies most of the cell-free DNA. RANZCOG/HGSA (C-Obs 59) and ISPD advise amniocentesis rather than CVS for rare autosomal trisomies for exactly this reason, because the placenta itself is likely to be abnormal. CPM involving chromosome 16 is strongly linked with placental dysfunction, which raises the risk of intrauterine growth restriction, pre-eclampsia, preterm birth and stillbirth. A normal amniocentesis result means the fetus is reassuring, but the pregnancy is still high risk. She needs continued care with a fetal medicine or obstetric team, serial growth and Doppler scans in the second half of pregnancy, blood pressure monitoring, and counselling to report reduced fetal movements. Many units also consider low-dose aspirin.
why: Her only risk factor is mild advanced maternal age, with a normal BMI and uncomplicated previous pregnancies, and placental mosaicism does not cause gestational diabetes.
After amniocentesis, leaking of fluid is uncommon and usually happens within days, so a procedure done a week ago with normal fluid today adds little later risk.
Placental dysfunction from trisomy 16 mosaicism tends to reduce amniotic fluid rather than increase it, and no fetal anomaly or diabetes is present to cause polyhydramnios.
She is RhD positive with a negative antibody screen, so the invasive procedure carries essentially no risk of clinically important sensitisation.

items.stem: A 34-year-old man comes to his general practitioner because he has had attacks of severe right-sided pain around his eye for 3 weeks. The attacks start about 1 hour after he falls asleep. He has one every night, sometimes with a second in the afternoon, and each lasts 45 to 90 minutes. During an attack, his right eye goes red and waters and his right nostril blocks. He walks around the house because he cannot settle. He had an identical 2-month bout 18 months ago that resolved completely, and an MRI of the brain with contrast at that time was normal. Home oxygen, started a week ago, stops most attacks within 15 minutes, but he is exhausted from losing sleep. He smokes 15 cigarettes a day and takes no regular medicines. Between attacks, his pulse is 68/min and his blood pressure is 124/80 mm Hg. Neurological examination is normal. A 12-lead ECG shows sinus rhythm at 68/min, PR interval 150 ms and QTc 400 ms.
items.ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment to reduce how often his attacks occur during this bout?
options: Verapamil 80 mg orally three times daily
items.explanation: This man has episodic cluster headache and is in the middle of a bout. The diagnosis rests on strictly one-sided orbital pain lasting 45 to 90 minutes, attacks at the same times each day (often soon after falling asleep), same-sided tearing, red eye and nasal blockage, restlessness, and an earlier bout that ended with full remission. An MRI from his first presentation already excluded a structural mimic. Oxygen is treating each attack, but attacks are still happening at least daily, so he needs preventive treatment for the rest of the bout. Therapeutic Guidelines (eTG) recommends verapamil as first-line prevention, starting at 80 mg orally three times daily and increasing every 1 to 2 weeks according to response. Verapamil can cause bradycardia and atrioventricular block, so record an ECG before starting and before each dose increase. His baseline PR interval of 150 ms is normal, so verapamil is safe to start. A short course of oral prednisolone can bridge him until verapamil takes effect. Amitriptyline is used to prevent tension-type headache and migraine and has no established benefit in cluster headache. Carbamazepine is first-line for trigeminal neuralgia, which causes attacks of electric-shock pain lasting seconds without marked autonomic features. Pizotifen is a migraine preventive with no proven effect in cluster headache, and it causes sedation and weight gain. Propranolol is first-line migraine prevention but does not prevent cluster attacks.
why: Amitriptyline helps prevent tension-type headache and migraine, but there is no good evidence that it reduces cluster attacks.
Carbamazepine treats trigeminal neuralgia, which causes stabbing pain lasting seconds, not 45 to 90 minute orbital attacks with autonomic features.
Pizotifen is a migraine preventive with no proven benefit in cluster headache, and it causes sedation and weight gain.
Propranolol is a first-line migraine preventive, but it is ineffective in cluster headache.

items.stem: A 77-year-old woman has been on the stroke unit for 2 days. She woke on the day of admission unable to see objects on her right. She has hypertension treated with perindopril and is otherwise well. Atorvastatin 80 mg daily was started on admission. Her temperature is 36.8°C, pulse 86/min and irregularly irregular, blood pressure 142/84 mm Hg and weight 68 kg. Each eye tested separately shows a congruous right homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing. She has no limb weakness, sensory loss or dysphasia. MRI brain shows a 30 × 20 mm acute infarct in the left medial occipital lobe with no haemorrhage on susceptibility-weighted imaging. MR angiography shows an occluded left P2 segment and no carotid stenosis. ECG shows atrial fibrillation; an ECG 3 years ago showed sinus rhythm. Echocardiography shows no valve disease. Haemoglobin is 134 g/L, platelets 241 x10^9/L, creatinine 84 micromol/L (eGFR 60 mL/min/1.73m²) and INR 1.0.
items.ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate long-term therapy to reduce her risk of recurrent stroke?
options: Aspirin 100 mg plus clopidogrel 75 mg orally daily
Enoxaparin bridging to warfarin, target INR 2 to 3
items.explanation: This woman has had a cardioembolic posterior cerebral artery infarct caused by newly found non-valvular atrial fibrillation. Her CHA2DS2-VA score is at least 5 (age 75 or over, hypertension, stroke), so her biggest risk is another embolic stroke. The Australian and New Zealand Living Clinical Guidelines for Stroke Management and eTG recommend oral anticoagulation, preferably with a DOAC rather than warfarin, for ischaemic stroke with AF. The stroke team times the start by infarct size, and with no haemorrhage on MRI an early start is reasonable. Apixaban is reduced to 2.5 mg twice daily only if two of these apply: age 80 or over, weight 60 kg or less, creatinine 133 micromol/L or more. She meets none, so she needs the full dose of 5 mg twice daily. Underdosing is a common error that leaves patients unprotected. Antiplatelet therapy, alone or in combination, does much less to prevent AF-related stroke and does not replace anticoagulation. Bridging with heparin raises the risk of bleeding, including haemorrhagic change in the infarct, and gives no extra protection.
why: Wrong: she meets none of the criteria for the reduced dose, so 2.5 mg twice daily would underdose her and leave her poorly protected from another embolic stroke.
Wrong: short-term dual antiplatelet therapy is for minor non-cardioembolic stroke or high-risk TIA, and it prevents AF-related stroke much less well than anticoagulation while still causing bleeding.
Wrong: aspirin alone gives little protection from cardioembolic stroke in AF and is not a substitute for anticoagulation in a patient without contraindications.
Wrong: DOACs are preferred to warfarin in non-valvular AF, and heparin bridging after an acute infarct raises the risk of haemorrhagic transformation without lowering early recurrence.

items.stem: A 58-year-old woman presents to a regional general practice with 8 months of gradually worsening pain in both hands and knees. The pain is worse after work and eases with rest, and morning stiffness lasts 15 minutes. Temperature is 36.7 °C, blood pressure 134/82 mm Hg and pulse 74/min. BMI is 31 kg/m2. She has hard swellings of the distal and proximal interphalangeal joints and squared thumb bases. There is no warmth or soft-tissue swelling, and no psoriasis or nail pitting. CRP is 3 mg/L (<5), ESR 14 mm/h (<30), rheumatoid factor <10 IU/mL (<20), anti-CCP 0.8 U/mL (<5) and ferritin 120 µg/L (30–300). Hand X-rays show symmetrical joint space narrowing. It is worst at the distal interphalangeal joints and is also seen at the proximal interphalangeal, first carpometacarpal and scaphotrapeziotrapezoid joints, with mild narrowing of the second and third metacarpophalangeal joints. There are marginal osteophytes and subchondral sclerosis, but no erosions, periarticular osteopenia or chondrocalcinosis.
items.ask: Which of the following is the most accurate interpretation of the hand radiographs?
options: Primary nodal osteoarthritis, as the pattern lacks erosions and periarticular osteopenia
Early rheumatoid arthritis, as the joint space narrowing is symmetrical in both hands
Psoriatic arthritis, as the distal interphalangeal joints are the most affected joints
Haemochromatosis arthropathy, as narrowing involves the second and third MCP joints
Calcium pyrophosphate arthropathy, as narrowing involves the scaphotrapeziotrapezoid joints
items.explanation: The X-ray shows the LOSS pattern of osteoarthritis: loss of joint space, osteophytes, subchondral sclerosis and (sometimes) subchondral cysts. The changes are in the typical places for nodal hand osteoarthritis: worst at the DIP joints, then the PIP joints, the thumb base (first CMC) and the scaphotrapeziotrapezoid joints. The osteophytes match her Heberden's and Bouchard's nodes. The film has none of the features of inflammatory or crystal arthritis. There are no marginal erosions, no periarticular osteopenia, no pencil-in-cup change or periostitis, and no chondrocalcinosis. Her normal CRP and ESR and negative RF and anti-CCP back this up. Mild narrowing of the MCP joints can happen in primary osteoarthritis and does not change the reading when the rest of the pattern is degenerative. Under eTG and RACGP guidance, osteoarthritis is a clinical diagnosis. These tests are used to rule out other causes, not to confirm it.
why: Wrong: rheumatoid arthritis usually spares the DIP joints and shows periarticular osteopenia and marginal erosions, and symmetry alone does not point to it.
Wrong: psoriatic arthritis shows erosions, pencil-in-cup deformity or periostitis, and she has no psoriasis or nail disease.
Wrong: haemochromatosis arthropathy mainly affects the MCP joints, with hook-like osteophytes and often chondrocalcinosis, and her ferritin is normal.
Wrong: calcium pyrophosphate arthropathy is marked by chondrocalcinosis, which is absent, and STT narrowing alongside thumb-base disease is common in primary osteoarthritis.

items.stem: A 31-year-old woman comes to her general practitioner because of headaches for 7 weeks. They began when she started working 12-hour shifts at a desk to meet the end-of-financial-year deadline at her accounting firm. Before this she had only occasional mild headaches. The headache is a bilateral, band-like tightness that builds through the afternoon. She rates it 4/10. It now comes on every afternoon. She has no nausea or photophobia, and climbing stairs does not make it worse. She takes paracetamol 1 g about five times a week and ibuprofen 400 mg once or twice a week, which takes the edge off it. She drinks four standard drinks a week and does not smoke. Her temperature is 36.7 °C, pulse is 74/min and blood pressure is 118/74 mm Hg. Her trapezius and temporalis muscles are tender. Passive neck flexion is full and painless. Fundoscopy shows sharp discs with venous pulsations, and the neurological examination is normal.
items.ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate advice to prevent progression of her headache disorder?
options: Switch to paracetamol with codeine on headache days
Take ibuprofen 400 mg regularly three times a day
Start amitriptyline 10 mg each night as prevention
Use sumatriptan 50 mg at the onset of each attack
Limit acute pain relief to fewer than 10 days per month
items.explanation: This woman has tension-type headache: it is bilateral, pressing, mild to moderate and not made worse by activity, she has no nausea or photophobia, her pericranial muscles are tender, and it started with a clear trigger (long hours at a desk under deadline stress). Her examination, including fundoscopy, is normal. The main risk for her is medication-overuse headache. She is already taking simple analgesics on about 25 to 35 days in every 4 weeks. ICHD-3 defines medication-overuse headache as headache on 15 or more days a month with regular overuse for more than 3 months. The threshold is 15 or more days a month for simple analgesics, and 10 or more days a month for triptans, opioids or combination analgesics. At 7 weeks she has not met the time criterion yet, but she is well over the frequency threshold. Following eTG, she should keep acute treatment to fewer than 10 days a month (roughly 2 to 3 days a week), keep a headache diary, and avoid codeine. Treatment should be mainly non-drug: posture and ergonomics, regular breaks, sleep, exercise, physiotherapy and stress management.
why: Codeine-containing combination products cause medication-overuse headache at a lower threshold (10 or more days a month), cause dependence, and eTG advises avoiding opioids in tension-type headache.
Taking ibuprofen regularly every day guarantees analgesic overuse, which raises her risk of medication-overuse headache as well as gastrointestinal and kidney harm.
Preventive amitriptyline is kept for established chronic tension-type headache that has not responded to non-drug measures, and it does nothing about her current analgesic overuse.
Triptans do not work for tension-type headache and cause medication-overuse headache at only 10 or more days a month, so taking one with every daily attack would make things worse.

items.stem:
A 38-year-old man comes to the emergency department with a 1-day history of worsening headache, fever, vomiting and photophobia. For 5 days before this he had right ear pain. He has no medical history, takes no medicines and has no allergies. His temperature is 39.2 °C, pulse 118/min, blood pressure 112/70 mm Hg, respirations 20/min and SpO2 97% on room air. He is alert with a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 15. He has neck stiffness, no rash, sharp optic discs and no focal neurological deficit. The right tympanic membrane is red and bulging. Blood cultures are taken and a lumbar puncture is done. Ceftriaxone 2 g and dexamethasone 10 mg are given straight after the procedure. Results:
Blood: leucocytes 19.8 x10^9/L, C-reactive protein 185 mg/L, glucose 6.0 mmol/L
CSF: turbid; opening pressure 28 cmH2O; white cells 1900 x10^6/L (90% polymorphs); red cells 6 x10^6/L; protein 2.1 g/L (0.15 to 0.45); glucose 1.2 mmol/L; Gram stain shows Gram-positive diplococci.
items.ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate change to his treatment?
items.explanation: The CSF is turbid, with many polymorphs, a high protein and a CSF:serum glucose ratio of 1.2/6.0 = 0.2 (below 0.4), so this is bacterial meningitis. Gram-positive diplococci mean Streptococcus pneumoniae, and the probable source is his right acute otitis media. Some pneumococci have reduced susceptibility to penicillin and ceftriaxone. So eTG advises adding vancomycin to ceftriaxone as soon as Gram-positive diplococci are seen, and continuing both until susceptibility results are back. Treatment is then narrowed to suit the organism. Dexamethasone should continue for 4 days, because it gives the most benefit in pneumococcal meningitis. Amoxicillin covers Listeria and is added only for patients at risk: those over 50, pregnant, immunocompromised or with alcohol dependence. He has none of these risks, and Listeria is a Gram-positive bacillus, not a diplococcus. Aciclovir is not needed: he has no confusion, seizures or focal signs, and the CSF picture is clearly bacterial with organisms seen. Changing to benzylpenicillin before susceptibility is known risks undertreating a resistant strain.
why: Amoxicillin covers Listeria, which shows as Gram-positive bacilli and is a risk only in people over 50, pregnant, immunocompromised or alcohol-dependent, and he is none of these.
Aciclovir treats HSV encephalitis, but he has no encephalitic features and the CSF is clearly bacterial, with organisms seen.
Dexamethasone should continue for 4 days in pneumococcal meningitis because this is the organism where it most reduces death and hearing loss.
Narrowing to benzylpenicillin is done only after susceptibility testing confirms a sensitive strain, so changing now could undertreat a resistant pneumococcus.

items.stem: A 61-year-old man is brought to the emergency department of a rural hospital 3 hours after central chest pressure began. The pain spreads to his left arm, and he has sweating and nausea. He has hypertension treated with perindopril. He drinks about 4 standard drinks per week and has had no falls, injections or strenuous exercise. Temperature is 36.7 °C, pulse 82/min, blood pressure 150/92 mm Hg, respiratory rate 18/min and SpO2 97% on room air. Jugular venous pressure is not raised, the chest is clear, and there is no hepatomegaly or peripheral oedema. An ECG shows ST elevation in V1 to V4. A chest X-ray shows clear lungs. Blood taken from a newly inserted cannula shows: potassium 4.1 mmol/L (3.5–5.2); bilirubin 10 µmol/L (<20); ALT 28 U/L (<45); AST 71 U/L (<35); ALP 80 U/L (30–110); GGT 30 U/L (<50); creatine kinase 590 U/L (<200); hs-troponin T 210 ng/L (<14).
items.ask: Which of the following is the most likely explanation for this patient's aspartate aminotransferase (AST) result?
options: In vitro haemolysis of the blood sample
items.explanation: The AST is raised on its own. ALT, bilirubin, ALP and GGT are all normal, and this happens alongside an anterior STEMI, a raised creatine kinase and an hs-troponin T well above the 99th percentile. AST is found in cardiac muscle as well as in liver and skeletal muscle. It leaks from infarcting myocardium, which is why it was once used as a cardiac marker. ALT is much more specific to the liver, so a normal ALT with a normal cholestatic profile points away from liver disease. Here the AST is best read as part of the myocardial infarction. It does not need liver work-up, and it must not delay reperfusion. Troponin, not AST, is the marker to follow for myocardial injury.
why: Wrong: an AST:ALT ratio above 2 can suggest alcohol, but he drinks very little, and his GGT and ALT are normal.
Wrong: congestive hepatopathy needs raised right-sided pressures, but his JVP is normal, there is no hepatomegaly or oedema, his lungs are clear, and ALT and bilirubin would usually rise too.
Wrong: in vitro haemolysis would also raise the potassium, which is normal at 4.1 mmol/L, and the sample came from a fresh cannula.
Wrong: he has had no trauma, falls, injections or exertion, and the raised troponin with ST elevation places the enzyme source in the heart, not skeletal muscle.

items.stem:
A 73-year-old man presents to his general practitioner with a dry cough that has been getting worse for 4 months. He also has breathlessness when walking uphill, a hoarse voice and a constant dull ache below his right clavicle. He has lost 5 kg without trying. He is a retired electrician who worked around asbestos lagging in the 1970s, and he has never smoked. He takes perindopril for hypertension. His temperature is 36.7 °C, pulse 82/min, blood pressure 136/80 mm Hg, respiratory rate 18/min and oxygen saturation 95% on room air. The right apex is dull to percussion. He has no clubbing, lymphadenopathy or conjunctival pallor. A chest X-ray shows a 5 cm rounded opacity at the right lung apex. Blood results are:
Haemoglobin 118 g/L (130 to 180)
MCV 87 fL (80 to 100)
White cell count 8.1 x10^9/L (4.0 to 11.0)
Platelets 438 x10^9/L (150 to 400)
Bilirubin 11 µmol/L (less than 20)
Creatinine 95 µmol/L (60 to 110); eGFR 68 mL/min/1.73 m^2
Corrected calcium 2.40 mmol/L (2.10 to 2.60)
ALP 98 U/L (30 to 110)
Albumin 32 g/L (35 to 50)
CRP 18 mg/L (less than 5)
items.ask: Which of the following best explains the abnormalities in these blood results?
options: Bone marrow infiltration by metastatic tumour
Erythropoietin deficiency from chronic kidney disease
Anaemia of inflammation due to an underlying malignancy
Haemolysis from a paraneoplastic autoimmune process
Vitamin B12 deficiency from poor dietary intake
items.explanation:
The bloods show a mild anaemia with a normal MCV (normocytic), a mildly raised platelet count, a mildly raised CRP and a low albumin. In an older man with weight loss and a 5 cm apical mass that is lung cancer until proven otherwise, this pattern fits anaemia of inflammation (anaemia of chronic disease). Tumour-driven cytokines such as IL-6 raise hepcidin, which traps iron and suppresses red cell production. The same cytokines cause a reactive thrombocytosis, a raised CRP and a low albumin. In lung cancer, thrombocytosis and hypoalbuminaemia also point to a worse prognosis.

The normal results matter too. The corrected calcium is normal, so there is no hypercalcaemia (from PTHrP or bone metastases). The normal ALP and bilirubin give no blood evidence of bone or liver spread, although normal bloods do not rule out metastases. Renal function is adequate for contrast CT. None of these results changes the plan: he still needs an urgent CT of the chest and upper abdomen and urgent referral to a lung cancer multidisciplinary team, with the aim of being seen within 2 weeks (Cancer Australia; Optimal care pathway for lung cancer).

Why the other options are wrong:
B: Marrow infiltration usually lowers the counts or gives a leucoerythroblastic film, often with a raised ALP or calcium, but here the white cell count is normal and the platelets are high.
C: An eGFR of 68 is too high to cause meaningful erythropoietin deficiency, which usually appears only when eGFR falls below about 30 to 45.
D: Haemolysis would raise the bilirubin (and LDH and reticulocytes), but his bilirubin is normal.
E: B12 deficiency causes a macrocytic anaemia, often with low platelets, but his MCV is normal and his platelets are raised.

Wrong: an eGFR of 68 mL/min/1.73 m^2 is too high to cause erythropoietin deficiency, which usually appears only when eGFR falls below about 30 to 45.
Wrong: haemolysis would raise the bilirubin (and LDH and reticulocytes), but his bilirubin is normal.
Wrong: B12 deficiency causes a macrocytic anaemia, often with low platelets, but his MCV is 87 fL and his platelets are raised.

items.stem: A 71-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with 50 minutes of heavy central chest pain that began while she was watching television. Over the past fortnight her known angina has come on with less exertion, and she now needs glyceryl trinitrate (GTN) most days. She has type 2 diabetes, hypertension and hypercholesterolaemia, and takes metformin, perindopril, atorvastatin and aspirin. In the ED she has received aspirin 300 mg, three sublingual GTN doses and intravenous morphine, and an intravenous GTN infusion has been titrated for the past 20 minutes. She still rates the pain 7/10 and is diaphoretic. Temperature is 36.7 °C, pulse 96/min, blood pressure 132/84 mmHg in both arms, respirations 18/min and SpO2 96% on room air. Two 12-lead ECGs taken 15 minutes apart show sinus rhythm with no ST-segment or T-wave changes. High-sensitivity troponin I, taken 40 minutes after onset, is 9 ng/L (99th percentile for women 16 ng/L). Chest X-ray is normal.
items.ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
items.explanation: This woman has a non-ST-elevation acute coronary syndrome. She has crescendo angina and prolonged rest pain. Her pain is still going after aspirin, repeated sublingual GTN, opioid and a titrated IV GTN infusion. The 2016 National Heart Foundation/CSANZ ACS guideline, which eTG follows, classes ongoing or recurrent ischaemic pain that does not respond to medical treatment as very high risk. This applies whatever the ECG or troponin shows. Very high-risk patients need invasive coronary angiography, with revascularisation if indicated, within 2 hours. Arrange this urgently with cardiology, including the choice of P2Y12 inhibitor and anticoagulant. A normal ECG and a normal troponin taken 40 minutes after onset do not lower her risk, because both can be normal early in a myocardial infarction. Repeat troponin, CT coronary angiography and stress testing are for patients whose pain has settled and who are at low or intermediate risk. Fibrinolysis is only for STEMI.
why: Serial troponin helps decide between unstable angina and NSTEMI, but the result would not change her management, because refractory pain already makes her very high risk.
Fibrinolysis gives no benefit and may cause harm in non-ST-elevation ACS, and her ECGs show no ST elevation.
CT coronary angiography is for stable, pain-free patients at low or intermediate risk, not for ongoing ischaemia that needs treatment in the catheter laboratory.
Stress testing is contraindicated while rest pain continues, and putting off assessment until tomorrow is unsafe in very high-risk ACS.

items.stem: A 72-year-old man is brought to the emergency department with 5 months of worsening breathlessness. Over this time he has lost 20 kg, has coughed up blood-tinged sputum and his voice has become hoarse. He has COPD, and his triple-therapy inhaler has not helped. He has smoked 20 cigarettes daily for 50 years and worked for decades as a mechanic. His temperature is 37.6 °C, pulse is 110/min, respirations are 29/min, blood pressure is 148/86 mmHg and SpO2 is 92% on room air. He has finger clubbing and a hard right supraclavicular lymph node. On the right side of the chest, expansion is reduced, percussion is stony dull and breath sounds are absent. The trachea is deviated to the left. An erect PA chest X-ray, not rotated, shows a large right effusion with a meniscus reaching the 2nd anterior rib, which obscures the right heart border and hilum. The trachea and mediastinum are displaced to the left. The left lung is clear.
items.ask: Which of the following best explains the position of the trachea and mediastinum on this film?
options: Paratracheal nodal mass displacing the airway
items.explanation: The film shows a large right effusion with the trachea and mediastinum pushed to the left, away from the fluid. Being pushed away from the fluid means the effusion has a mass effect: the fluid takes up enough space in the right hemithorax to move the mediastinum across. For this patient, it means the shift is not explained by a major right-sided collapse, so a central obstructing tumour has not pulled the mediastinum back towards the right. It also means the mediastinum is not held in place by pleural tumour. So ultrasound-guided pleural aspiration (no more than about 1.5 L at a time) is likely to ease his breathlessness, and it also gives fluid for diagnosis. A contrast CT chest should ideally be done before the effusion is fully drained. If a very large effusion had no shift, or the mediastinum had moved towards the effusion, that would suggest lobar or lung collapse from an endobronchial tumour, or a mediastinum fixed by mesothelioma or malignant nodes. In that case drainage would help less and could cause problems, and bronchoscopy should be considered. Tension pneumothorax is ruled out because the film shows a meniscus, not air.
why: Collapse causes volume loss, which pulls the trachea and mediastinum towards the affected (right) side, not away from it.
A mediastinum encased by pleural tumour, as in mesothelioma, cannot move, so a large effusion would cause little or no shift.
Hyperinflation in COPD affects both lungs and does not push the mediastinum sideways, and the left lung is described as clear.
A paratracheal nodal mass widens the mediastinum and may narrow the trachea, but it would not shift the whole mediastinum away from a large right effusion.

items.stem:
A 29-year-old woman comes back to her general practitioner to discuss blood test results. She has had four months of tiredness, cold intolerance, constipation and weight gain of 5 kg. She has had type 1 diabetes since age 11 and uses insulin glargine and insulin aspart. She drinks about 4 standard drinks a week and rarely eats fresh vegetables. Her pulse is 58/min and blood pressure 114/72 mm Hg. She has a diffuse, firm, non-tender goitre and delayed relaxation of the ankle reflexes. Vibration sense, joint position sense and gait are normal. Investigations show:
Haemoglobin 98 g/L (115–165)
MCV 116 fL (80–100)
TSH 38 mIU/L (0.4–4.0)
Free T4 5.1 pmol/L (10–20)
Anti-TPO antibodies strongly positive
Morning cortisol 430 nmol/L (normal)
Sodium 138 mmol/L, potassium 4.3 mmol/L
Serum folate 4.0 nmol/L (above 7)
Serum vitamin B12 and intrinsic factor antibodies: pending
Levothyroxine is started. A colleague suggests also starting oral folic acid 5 mg daily today.
items.ask: Starting folic acid on its own before the pending results return puts her at greatest risk of which of the following?
options: Adrenal crisis from unmasked cortisol deficiency
Secondary iron overload from rapid erythropoiesis
Subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord

An MCV of 116 fL is too high to blame on hypothyroidism alone, and her B12 result is still pending. Folic acid alone can correct the blood count in B12 deficiency, but it does nothing for the nerve damage. So the anaemia looks better while B12-related demyelination of the dorsal columns and corticospinal tracts (subacute combined degeneration) gets worse, and that damage can be permanent. Australian guidance (eTG) says folate must not be given alone until B12 deficiency has been ruled out or is being treated. A low folate with a normal neurological examination does not remove this risk, because she could be low in both. Safe options are to wait for the B12 result or to give B12 alongside folate.
why: Low potassium from rapid red cell production happens mainly when severe megaloblastic anaemia is treated with B12, and it is unlikely with her mild anaemia and normal potassium.
Adrenal crisis is the risk when levothyroxine, not folic acid, is started in untreated Addison disease, and her normal morning cortisol and electrolytes make adrenal insufficiency unlikely.
Correcting megaloblastic anaemia uses up iron and can cause iron deficiency, not iron overload.
Gastric cancer is a long-term risk of pernicious anaemia itself, and starting folic acid neither causes it nor speeds it up.

items.stem: A 61-year-old woman presents to the emergency department of a regional hospital with 2 days of lower abdominal pain and swelling. The pain began as intermittent cramps in the left lower quadrant and is now constant. She has passed no stool or flatus for 36 hours and began vomiting bile this morning. Eight years ago, two tubular adenomas were removed at colonoscopy, and she did not attend the surveillance colonoscopy she was booked for. She takes metformin for type 2 diabetes. Her temperature is 37.4 °C, pulse 112/min, blood pressure 118/72 mm Hg and respiratory rate 20/min. Her abdomen is grossly distended and tympanic, with mild generalised tenderness, no guarding and tinkling bowel sounds. The hernial orifices are normal. Digital rectal examination shows an empty rectum. Haemoglobin is 112 g/L (115–165), white cell count 12.1 x 10^9/L (4.0–11.0), creatinine 84 µmol/L (45–90), eGFR 72 mL/min/1.73 m2 and venous lactate 1.8 mmol/L (less than 2.0). Fluid resuscitation, analgesia and a nasogastric tube have been started.
items.ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate next investigation?
options: CT abdomen and pelvis with intravenous contrast
items.explanation: This woman most likely has a large bowel obstruction. She has early obstipation, gross tympanic distension, vomiting that came late, an empty rectum and tinkling bowel sounds. The most likely cause is an obstructing sigmoid cancer, given her previous adenomas, the surveillance she missed and her mild anaemia. Diverticular stricture and sigmoid volvulus are the other main causes. Her rising pulse and pain that has become constant raise concern for ischaemia or impending perforation, so she needs a definitive test now. CT of the abdomen and pelvis with intravenous contrast is the investigation of choice in Australian emergency surgical practice and in the WSES guidelines. It confirms a mechanical obstruction and shows where it is and what is causing it (tumour, stricture or volvulus). It separates true obstruction from pseudo-obstruction and detects caecal distension, ischaemia, perforation and free gas. It also stages a tumour, which guides the choice between a stent, a defunctioning stoma and resection. Her eGFR of 72 allows contrast; withhold metformin around the scan. A plain radiograph is often taken but is less sensitive and specific and seldom changes management, so it should not delay CT. A contrast enema is a second-line option when CT is unavailable or unclear. Colonoscopy is unsafe in acute obstruction. Ultrasound is limited by bowel gas.
why: A plain radiograph can suggest a dilated colon, but it cannot reliably find the level or cause, tell mechanical obstruction from pseudo-obstruction, or show ischaemia, so it does not replace CT.

A water-soluble contrast enema can confirm a distal colonic block, but it gives no information on ischaemia, staging or anything outside the bowel, so it is kept for when CT is unavailable or inconclusive.

Colonoscopy in an acutely obstructed, unprepared colon risks perforation from air insufflation and is not a first-line diagnostic test, although an endoscopist may later place a stent or take biopsies.
Gas in a grossly distended colon scatters the ultrasound beam, so ultrasound cannot reliably show the level or cause of a large bowel obstruction.

items.stem: An 81-year-old woman sees her general practitioner because her breathlessness has been getting worse for 6 weeks. She now gets breathless walking to her letterbox. She sleeps on three pillows and wakes at night gasping for air. She has had no chest pain, sweating or palpitations. She had a non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction 5 months ago and has had hypertension for 30 years. Her medicines are aspirin, atorvastatin, perindopril and metoprolol. Her pulse is 100/min and regular, blood pressure is 158/90 mm Hg, respiratory rate is 22/min and SpO2 is 94% on room air. Her jugular venous pressure is raised, her apex beat is displaced and there are crackles at both lung bases. Serum potassium is 4.3 mmol/L (reference 3.5 to 5.2). A 12-lead ECG shows sinus rhythm at 100/min and a QRS duration of 94 ms. The S wave in V1 plus the R wave in V5 measures 41 mm. There is downsloping ST depression with asymmetric T-wave inversion in leads I, aVL, V5 and V6. These changes are the same as on her ECG at hospital discharge 5 months ago.
items.ask: Which of the following is the most likely explanation for the ST-segment and T-wave changes on this ECG?
options: Subendocardial ischaemia from a new acute coronary syndrome
Delayed ventricular depolarisation from left bundle branch block
Abnormal repolarisation caused by a low serum potassium
Left ventricular hypertrophy with secondary repolarisation changes
Characteristic ST-segment scooping caused by digoxin therapy
items.explanation: The S wave in V1 plus the R wave in V5 adds up to 41 mm, which is more than the Sokolow-Lyon threshold of 35 mm. This meets the voltage criteria for left ventricular hypertrophy (LVH). With LVH, downsloping ST depression and asymmetric T-wave inversion in the lateral leads (I, aVL, V5, V6) is the classic secondary repolarisation ('strain') pattern. It fits her 30 years of hypertension and her displaced apex. The changes are the same as on her discharge ECG 5 months ago, so they are long-standing and not acute. Her new decompensated heart failure still needs hospital assessment, including a troponin and an echocardiogram. The ECG itself, though, shows chronic changes from LVH, not new ischaemia. New ischaemia is unlikely because there is no chest pain and the ST-T changes are the same as 5 months ago, although a troponin is still needed. Left bundle branch block is excluded because the QRS is 94 ms, and the diagnosis needs a QRS of 120 ms or more. Hypokalaemia is excluded because her potassium is normal at 4.3 mmol/L; it also typically causes U waves and flattened T waves. Digoxin is not one of her medicines, and its effect is a scooped (reverse-tick) ST segment, not the asymmetric T-wave inversion seen with LVH voltages.
why: There is no chest pain and the ST-T changes are the same as on the discharge ECG, so they do not point to new ischaemia, although a troponin is still needed.
A QRS duration of 94 ms rules out left bundle branch block, which needs a QRS of at least 120 ms.
Her serum potassium is normal at 4.3 mmol/L, and hypokalaemia typically causes U waves and flattened T waves, not this pattern.
She does not take digoxin, and digoxin causes a scooped ST segment, not asymmetric lateral T-wave inversion with high QRS voltages.

items.stem: A 67-year-old man comes to the emergency department with 3 days of worsening breathlessness. He now sleeps on three pillows instead of one, wakes at night gasping, and has swollen ankles. He has gained 4 kg. He has heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, atrial fibrillation and gout. His medicines are furosemide 40 mg daily, candesartan 16 mg daily (dose unchanged for 2 years), bisoprolol 5 mg daily and rivaroxaban 20 mg daily. Five days ago he started over-the-counter ibuprofen 400 mg three times daily for a painful left big toe. Temperature is 36.8 °C, pulse 108/min and irregular, blood pressure 144/86 mm Hg, respiratory rate 26/min and SpO2 91% on room air. His peripheries are warm. He has a raised JVP, bibasal crackles and pitting oedema to the shins, and no rash. Investigations show: sodium 134 mmol/L (135–145), potassium 4.9 mmol/L (3.5–5.2), urea 12.4 mmol/L (2.5–8.0), creatinine 132 µmol/L (60–110; 86 µmol/L eight months ago), eosinophils 0.2 x10^9/L (less than 0.5). Urinalysis shows no blood, protein or leucocytes.
items.ask: Which of the following is the most likely mechanism of the change in his renal function?
options: Efferent arteriolar dilation from angiotensin II receptor blockade
Afferent arteriolar constriction from loss of prostaglandin-mediated vasodilation
Acute tubular necrosis from renal hypoperfusion in cardiogenic shock
Acute interstitial nephritis from a drug hypersensitivity reaction
Intratubular crystal deposition from urate released in the gout flare
items.explanation: His creatinine has risen from a baseline of 86 to 132 µmol/L, about 1.5 times baseline, and urea is up out of proportion. This is a stage 1 acute kidney injury (KDIGO) that developed alongside his heart failure decompensation. The only new factor is 5 days of ibuprofen. In heart failure, kidney perfusion depends on prostaglandins that dilate the afferent arteriole, and an NSAID removes this. He is also on a loop diuretic, which reduces circulating volume, and an ARB, which stops angiotensin II from constricting the efferent arteriole. With all three, glomerular filtration pressure falls (the 'triple whammy'). The NSAID also causes sodium and water retention and blunts furosemide, which explains the weight gain and congestion. The urinalysis shows no blood, protein or leucocytes, which fits a haemodynamic (prerenal) cause rather than damage within the kidney. For this patient, the result means he needs admission, the ibuprofen must be stopped and not restarted, his gout flare should be treated another way (for example colchicine or prednisolone, used with care), and he needs IV diuresis with daily electrolytes and creatinine. Angiotensin II receptor blockade contributes, but his candesartan dose has not changed in 2 years and his creatinine was stable on it. Acute tubular necrosis from cardiogenic shock is unlikely: he is hypertensive with warm peripheries. Acute interstitial nephritis would usually cause a rash, fever, eosinophilia or white cells in the urine, and he has none of these. Urate crystal nephropathy happens with massive urate release, as in tumour lysis, not with a gout flare in one joint.
why: Wrong: ARB-related efferent dilation adds to the effect, but his candesartan dose has been the same for 2 years with a stable baseline creatinine, so it does not explain a new rise.
Wrong: he has no cardiogenic shock (BP 144/86 mm Hg and warm peripheries), so he has not had the poor perfusion that causes tubular necrosis.
Wrong: there is no rash, fever, eosinophilia or white cells in the urine to suggest interstitial nephritis, and the bland urinalysis fits a haemodynamic cause.
Wrong: urate crystals block the tubules only after massive urate release, as in tumour lysis, not in a gout flare of one joint.

items.stem: A 62-year-old woman comes to a rural emergency department with 3 weeks of constant burning pain in her right forefoot. The pain is worst at night when she lies flat, so she has been sleeping in a recliner with the right foot hanging over the edge. For years she has had calf pain after walking short distances. She has type 2 diabetes, hypertension, a previous myocardial infarction and an ischaemic stroke. She smokes 20 cigarettes a day. Temperature is 36.8 °C, pulse 88/min and regular, blood pressure 164/88 mmHg, respiratory rate 18/min and SpO2 96% on room air. The right great, second and third toes are black, shrivelled and hard, with a sharp line of demarcation and no discharge, swelling or erythema. The fourth toe is dusky. The right popliteal and pedal pulses are absent. The right ankle-brachial index is 0.28, and both ankle pressures are below 50 mmHg. WCC is 8.9 x10^9/L and CRP is 12 mg/L. The tertiary vascular unit has accepted her, and transfer is booked for tomorrow morning.
items.ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate measure to reduce her risk of further tissue loss while she waits for transfer?
options: Raise the limb on pillows above heart level
Warm the limb with an electric heat pad
Apply hydrogel to the blackened digits under a film
Hold the limb below heart level, padded with loose dry gauze
Apply graduated compression bandaging from toes to knee
items.explanation: She has chronic limb-threatening ischaemia: rest pain for more than 2 weeks, dry gangrene of three toes, an ABI below 0.4 and ankle pressures below 50 mmHg. She is awaiting revascularisation. Until then, the aims are to keep as much blood as possible reaching the threatened tissue (the dusky fourth toe) and to stop the dry gangrene turning into wet, infected gangrene. Letting the leg hang below heart level helps perfusion pressure by gravity, and it is also the position that eases her rest pain. A dry, loose, non-adherent dressing protects the foot from pressure and injury and keeps the dead tissue dry and mummified. Moisture would encourage bacteria and liquefaction. Debridement or amputation is left until after the vascular team has revascularised and assessed her.
why: Wrong: raising the leg lowers the perfusion pressure in a foot that is already critically ischaemic, which worsens the rest pain and puts the dusky fourth toe at further risk.
Wrong: heat raises the metabolic demand of tissue that cannot increase its blood flow, and a numb, ischaemic diabetic foot is easily burnt, so external heat can speed up tissue loss.
Wrong: hydrogel moistens the wound, which suits sloughy wounds with good blood supply, but it softens dry gangrene and can turn it into wet, infected gangrene.
Wrong: compression is contraindicated in severe arterial disease (ABI below 0.5) because it further cuts arterial inflow and can cause pressure necrosis.
