items.stem:
A 61-year-old woman comes to the emergency department with 2 days of colicky central abdominal pain and repeated bilious vomiting. She has not passed stool or flatus for 30 hours. She had an open hysterectomy 12 years ago. She takes amlodipine for hypertension. Her temperature is 37.3°C, pulse is 112/min, blood pressure is 122/74 mm Hg, respirations are 16/min, and oxygen saturation is 97% on room air. Her mucous membranes are dry. The abdomen is distended, with tinkling bowel sounds and mild generalised tenderness but no guarding. The hernial orifices are normal. She has not passed urine in 3 hours. Results are:
Na+ 132 mmol/L (135–145)
K+ 3.1 mmol/L (3.5–5.2)
Cl− 89 mmol/L (95–110)
Urea 13.6 mmol/L (2.5–7.5)
Creatinine 118 µmol/L (45–90)
Venous gas: pH 7.48, pCO2 47 mm Hg, HCO3− 33 mmol/L, lactate 1.2 mmol/L
CT shows dilated small bowel with a transition point under the scar and no features of ischaemia. A nasogastric tube is placed.
items.ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate intravenous fluid to start?
items.explanation: This woman has adhesive small bowel obstruction. Her blood results show a hypochloraemic, hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis: pH 7.48, HCO3− 33 mmol/L, Cl− 89 mmol/L and K+ 3.1 mmol/L. The anion gap is normal (132 − [89 + 33] = 10), and the pCO2 of 47 mm Hg is the expected respiratory compensation (about 0.7 × 9 ≈ 6 mm Hg above 40). She also has a prerenal acute kidney injury, with urea raised out of proportion to creatinine, a tachycardia and no urine output. This pattern comes from vomiting and nasogastric loss of gastric acid (HCl) together with fluid loss. The kidney then holds on to sodium and bicarbonate and loses potassium (contraction alkalosis with secondary hyperaldosteronism). The alkalosis is chloride-responsive: it corrects only when chloride and volume are replaced. So the right fluid is 0.9% saline (154 mmol/L chloride) with potassium chloride added, usually 20 to 40 mmol/L, for both resuscitation and replacement, with fluid balance and electrolytes monitored. Hartmann's and Plasma-Lyte contain less chloride and carry anions that the body turns into bicarbonate (lactate, acetate, gluconate), and 5% glucose and albumin do not replace what she has lost.
why: Hartmann's has less chloride (111 mmol/L) and only 5 mmol/L potassium, and its lactate is turned into bicarbonate, which makes the alkalosis worse.
Plasma-Lyte 148 has even less chloride (98 mmol/L), and its acetate and gluconate are turned into bicarbonate, so it does not correct a hypochloraemic alkalosis.
Albumin replaces neither chloride nor potassium, has no proven benefit over crystalloid for this kind of volume loss, and costs more.
5% glucose is mostly free water that does not stay in the circulation, so it will not correct her volume loss, and it will make her hyponatraemia worse.

items.stem: A 62-year-old man comes to his general practitioner to review his test results. For 18 months he has had worsening breathlessness on exertion and now has to stop after about 200 m on flat ground. He also has a daily cough with clear sputum. Last winter he had one flare-up, treated in the community with oral prednisolone, and he has never been admitted to hospital. He has a 45 pack-year smoking history. He started varenicline 2 weeks ago and has set a quit date. He has hypertension treated with perindopril. He uses salbutamol 200 micrograms via a spacer as needed, now on most days, and his technique is good. Temperature is 36.6 °C, pulse 84/min, blood pressure 132/80 mmHg, respiratory rate 18/min and SpO2 94% on room air. Air entry is reduced and there is scattered expiratory wheeze. Post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC is 0.56 and FEV1 is 55% of predicted, with no significant bronchodilator response. Blood eosinophils are 0.15 x10^9/L (reference 0.0 to 0.5). He has been referred to pulmonary rehabilitation.
items.ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate addition to his medicines?
items.explanation: This man has spirometry-confirmed COPD: post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC is below 0.7. His FEV1 of 55% predicted puts him in the moderate range in COPD-X (40 to 59%). His breathlessness persists despite a short-acting reliever, and he already has the non-drug measures under way: varenicline with a quit date, and a referral to pulmonary rehabilitation. COPD-X and eTG recommend adding a long-acting bronchodilator for persistent symptoms. A long-acting muscarinic antagonist such as tiotropium, taken once daily and kept alongside the as-needed reliever, is a standard first choice. It improves breathlessness, exercise tolerance and quality of life, and it reduces flare-ups. Inhaled corticosteroids are added only for repeated flare-ups despite long-acting bronchodilators, especially when eosinophils are raised. He has had one community-treated flare-up and his eosinophils are 0.15 x10^9/L, so a steroid is not indicated. Triple therapy, theophylline and long-term macrolides belong to later steps, if at all. Recheck his inhaler technique and review his symptoms after starting the new inhaler.
why: Wrong: guidelines do not recommend an inhaled corticosteroid alone in COPD, because it does not help breathlessness and raises the risk of pneumonia.
Wrong: triple therapy is for people who keep having flare-ups despite dual long-acting bronchodilators, and he has had one mild flare-up and his eosinophils are low.
Wrong: theophylline is a late add-on with a narrow therapeutic range, many drug interactions and less benefit than inhaled long-acting bronchodilators.
Wrong: long-term macrolide treatment is a specialist option for frequent flare-ups despite optimal inhaled therapy, and it carries risks of resistance, hearing loss and QT prolongation.

items.stem: A 27-year-old man comes to a general practice because his eyes have been yellow for 3 days. Ten days ago he developed fevers, anorexia, nausea and malaise, followed by dark urine and pale stools. Five weeks ago he returned from a 3-week backpacking trip through Vietnam, where he ate street food and had ice in his drinks. He did not have a pre-travel consultation or any travel vaccines. His travel companion became jaundiced last week. He takes no medicines or supplements and rarely drinks alcohol. His temperature is 37.6°C, pulse 88/min and blood pressure 118/74 mm Hg. He has scleral icterus and a tender, smooth liver edge 2 cm below the costal margin. He is alert, with no asterixis. Results: bilirubin 102 µmol/L (<20), ALT 1240 U/L (<40), AST 610 U/L (<40), ALP 190 U/L (30–110), GGT 85 U/L (<50), INR 1.0 (0.9–1.2), haemoglobin 141 g/L, white cell count 4.8 x10^9/L and platelets 236 x10^9/L. Abdominal ultrasound shows a mildly enlarged liver, no gallstones and a normal-calibre common bile duct.
items.ask: Which of the following investigations is most likely to confirm the diagnosis?
items.explanation: This unvaccinated traveller has a clear enteric exposure in South-East Asia. He became unwell about 4 weeks after the exposure, which fits the incubation period of hepatitis A (about 2 to 7 weeks). He had a febrile prodrome followed by jaundice, and his travel companion is also jaundiced, which suggests a shared source. His liver tests show a hepatocellular pattern: ALT about 30 times the upper limit, far more raised than ALP and GGT, with ALT above AST. His INR is normal and he is alert, so there is no sign of acute liver failure. The ultrasound excludes biliary obstruction. The most likely diagnosis is acute hepatitis A. The test that confirms it is hepatitis A IgM antibody. IgM is present when symptoms start and stays positive for about 3 to 6 months, so a positive result means recent infection. This is the first-line test for acute hepatitis in Australian guidance (eTG, CDNA SoNG). Confirmed hepatitis A must be notified to the public health unit. Close contacts who are not immune should get post-exposure prophylaxis within 2 weeks of their last exposure.
why: Thick and thin films are needed for fever in a traveller back from a malaria area, but malaria does not cause conjugated jaundice with ALT over 1000 when the haemoglobin and platelets are normal, so films will not confirm this diagnosis.

Hepatitis E is also spread enterically in Asia, but hepatitis A is more common in unvaccinated travellers and rarely spreads between people; guidelines test for hepatitis A IgM first and hepatitis E only if that is negative.
Total hepatitis A antibody is positive after past infection or vaccination as well as current infection, so on its own it cannot show that this illness is acute hepatitis A.
MRCP looks for stones or strictures in the bile ducts, and it is not indicated here because the ultrasound shows a normal-calibre duct and the liver tests point to hepatitis rather than obstruction.

items.stem: A 12-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department with 4 days of thirst, polyuria and weight loss, and 1 day of vomiting. He has no past medical history. He weighs 36 kg. His first venous blood gas shows pH 6.98, bicarbonate 4 mmol/L, glucose 34.0 mmol/L and sodium 131 mmol/L. Blood beta-hydroxybutyrate is 6.8 mmol/L and urea is 13.2 mmol/L. Fluid replacement is started, and 1 hour later an insulin infusion is started at 0.1 units/kg/h. Five hours after arrival he says he has a severe headache, vomits, and becomes irritable and confused. His pulse is 58/min (130/min on arrival), blood pressure is 142/90 mm Hg, respirations are 26/min, SpO2 is 98% on room air and temperature is 36.9 °C. GCS is 11 (E3 V3 M5). His pupils are equal and reactive. Repeat glucose is 15.2 mmol/L and sodium is 129 mmol/L. The head of the bed is raised and the fluid rate is reduced.
items.ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Non-contrast CT scan of the brain now
Sodium bicarbonate 1 mmol/kg IV over 1 hour
Dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg IV as a single dose
Cease the insulin infusion until review
items.explanation: This boy has severe DKA as his first presentation of type 1 diabetes. He has the main risk factors for cerebral oedema: young age, new diagnosis, pH below 7.1, a high urea, and a sodium that is falling instead of rising as the glucose comes down. Several hours into treatment he has a headache, vomiting, a falling GCS and a new low heart rate with high blood pressure (Cushing response). This is a clinical diagnosis of cerebral oedema. The RCH DKA guideline says to treat it straight away, without waiting for imaging. Raise the head of the bed, reduce the fluid rate, and give mannitol 0.5 to 1 g/kg (2.5 to 5 mL/kg of 20%) IV over 20 minutes. Hypertonic 3% saline 2.5 to 5 mL/kg is an alternative. Call ICU early for airway support, and do a CT only after he is stable, to look for other causes such as a clot or bleed. CT now is wrong because imaging delays treatment that can save his life, and cerebral oedema is diagnosed clinically. Sodium bicarbonate is wrong because it does not improve outcomes in DKA and is itself linked to cerebral oedema. Dexamethasone is wrong because steroids do not help this kind of brain swelling and they make hyperglycaemia worse. Stopping the insulin is wrong because the ketosis needs ongoing insulin to clear; the rate may be lowered, but the infusion should not be stopped to treat cerebral oedema.
why: Wrong: CT delays urgent treatment for a diagnosis made clinically; image only once he is stable.
Wrong: bicarbonate does not improve outcomes in DKA and is itself a risk factor for cerebral oedema.
Wrong: corticosteroids have no role in cerebral oedema from DKA and would worsen his hyperglycaemia.
Wrong: insulin is still needed to clear the ketosis, and stopping it does not treat the raised intracranial pressure.

items.stem: A 40-year-old man is brought to the emergency department 2 hours after a sudden, severe occipital headache that began while he was jogging. Two weeks ago he had a severe headache that settled within 30 minutes. He has autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease and hypertension, treated with perindopril. On arrival, his temperature is 37.3 °C, pulse 82/min, respirations 16/min, blood pressure 140/85 mm Hg and SpO2 98% on room air. His Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score is 13 (E3 V4 M6). He has neck stiffness and bilateral subhyaloid haemorrhages on fundoscopy, and no focal deficit. INR is 1.0 and platelets are 245 x10^9/L. Non-contrast CT shows diffuse blood in the basal cisterns, spreading into the ventricles, with dilated temporal horns. CT angiography shows a 7 mm anterior communicating artery aneurysm. Forty-five minutes later he vomits. His GCS is now 11 (E3 V3 M5), pulse 48/min, blood pressure 204/96 mm Hg and respirations 12/min and irregular. His pupils are still equal and reactive.
items.ask: Which of the following best explains the change in his vital signs?
items.explanation: This man has an aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhage. Blood has spread into his ventricles, and the dilated temporal horns show early hydrocephalus. Since arrival his GCS has fallen. He now has a rising systolic pressure, a slow heart rate and irregular breathing. This is Cushing's triad, a late sign that intracranial pressure is raised and the brainstem is being compressed, which means coning is imminent. Equal pupils do not rule this out, because pupil changes can come late. Do not read the rising blood pressure as something to treat on its own. It is the brain's attempt to keep up cerebral perfusion pressure, and lowering it hard could make ischaemia worse. Under eTG guidance and the Between the Flags criteria, this needs an immediate rapid response call, airway assessment, the head of the bed raised to 30 degrees, and an urgent neurosurgical review for an external ventricular drain. Delayed cerebral ischaemia usually happens on days 3 to 14, not within hours of the bleed. A hypertensive emergency does not explain the slow heart rate or the fall in GCS, and on arrival his blood pressure was only 140/85 mm Hg. A vagal response to vomiting slows the heart but lowers the blood pressure. Neurogenic stunned myocardium from a catecholamine surge typically causes a fast heart rate, low blood pressure and heart failure.
why: Wrong: delayed cerebral ischaemia from vasospasm typically happens on days 3 to 14 after the bleed, not 3 hours after the headache began.
Wrong: a hypertensive emergency would not cause a falling heart rate or irregular breathing, and his blood pressure was only 140/85 mm Hg before his GCS fell.
Wrong: a vagal response to vomiting slows the heart but lowers the blood pressure, and it would not cause a lasting fall in GCS or irregular breathing.
Wrong: neurogenic stunned myocardium from a catecholamine surge usually causes a fast heart rate, low blood pressure and pulmonary oedema, not a slow heart rate with severe hypertension.

items.stem: A 66-year-old man is on the cardiology ward of a regional hospital, waiting for transfer for coronary angiography. He was admitted 18 hours ago with a non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction and has no pain now. Overnight telemetry has shown frequent multifocal ventricular ectopic beats and two runs of non-sustained ventricular tachycardia, each 5 to 7 beats long. He has hypertension treated with indapamide. Since admission he has been given aspirin, ticagrelor, therapeutic enoxaparin, metoprolol and atorvastatin. His blood pressure is 128/76 mmHg, pulse 78/min and regular, respiratory rate 16/min and oxygen saturation 97% on room air. Heart sounds are normal and the chest is clear. A 12-lead ECG shows sinus rhythm, 1 mm ST depression in V4 to V6 and a QTc of 470 ms. Results: hs-troponin I 1960 ng/L (less than 26), K+ 3.2 mmol/L (3.5 to 5.2), Mg2+ 0.58 mmol/L (0.70 to 1.10), creatinine 90 µmol/L (60 to 110).
items.ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate measure to reduce his risk of ventricular fibrillation before angiography?
options: Intravenous amiodarone loading dose, then maintenance infusion
Intravenous magnesium sulfate, then potassium chloride infusion
Intravenous lidocaine bolus, then prophylactic infusion
Oral slow-release potassium chloride tablets alone
Oral flecainide twice daily until angiography
items.explanation: This man has an evolving NSTEMI and is waiting for angiography. Ventricular ectopy and non-sustained VT on telemetry, a borderline long QTc, and low potassium and magnesium from his thiazide-like diuretic (indapamide) put him at high risk of ventricular fibrillation. In acute coronary syndrome, Australian ACS guidance and ANZCOR advise correcting electrolytes promptly, aiming for potassium of at least 4.0 mmol/L (4.0 to 5.0) and magnesium of at least 1.0 mmol/L. Give magnesium first, for example magnesium sulfate 10 to 20 mmol IV over about an hour. Low magnesium makes low potassium hard to correct, because the kidneys keep losing potassium, and magnesium also stabilises the myocardium when the QT is long. Then give IV potassium chloride at a safe ward rate (for example 10 mmol/h through a peripheral line) with ECG monitoring, recheck the levels, and stop the indapamide. Keep him on continuous monitoring, continue the beta-blocker, and arrange early angiography to treat the ischaemic cause. Prophylactic antiarrhythmic drugs are not recommended in ACS.
why: Prophylactic amiodarone for asymptomatic non-sustained VT after myocardial infarction does not lower mortality and is not recommended; amiodarone is kept for sustained or recurrent haemodynamically important VT, or for refractory VF during cardiac arrest.
Prophylactic lidocaine in acute myocardial infarction reduces VF but increases mortality, mainly from asystole, so it is no longer used.

items.stem: A 77-year-old man sees his general practitioner to review results. For 6 months he has had increasing breathlessness on exertion and central chest tightness when climbing stairs, which settles with rest. Last week he nearly fainted while walking uphill. He has hypertension and hypercholesterolaemia and takes irbesartan 150 mg daily. His blood pressure is 132/76 mm Hg, pulse is 76/min and regular, respirations are 18/min, and oxygen saturation is 96% on room air. The carotid pulse is slow rising. There is a harsh ejection systolic murmur at the right second intercostal space that radiates to both carotids, with a soft second heart sound. Fine crackles are heard at both lung bases, and there is no peripheral oedema. A transthoracic echocardiogram shows a heavily calcified trileaflet aortic valve, peak velocity 4.5 m/s, mean gradient 50 mm Hg, valve area 0.7 cm², concentric left ventricular hypertrophy and an ejection fraction of 62%. He has been referred urgently to cardiology for heart team assessment. He asks for something to relieve his chest tightness while he waits.
items.ask: Which of the following medicines is most likely to cause a serious adverse event in this patient before his valve is replaced?
items.explanation: This man has symptomatic severe calcific aortic stenosis, with breathlessness, angina and presyncope on exertion, and heart failure with preserved ejection fraction. With a fixed outflow obstruction and a stiff, hypertrophied left ventricle, cardiac output cannot rise to make up for a fall in preload or afterload. Nitrates such as sublingual glyceryl trinitrate cause venous and arterial dilatation. That lowers preload, so the stiff ventricle underfills, and the patient can develop profound hypotension, syncope, worsening myocardial ischaemia and even cardiac arrest. eTG and the 2025 ESC/EACTS valvular guidelines advise avoiding nitrates and other potent vasodilators in severe aortic stenosis. They also advise cautious diuresis for congestion while the patient waits for TAVI or SAVR. The definitive treatment for his angina is valve replacement, not antianginal drugs. Low-dose furosemide, used carefully, is appropriate for congestion. Atorvastatin is safe and treats his hypercholesterolaemia. Paracetamol is a safe analgesic with no haemodynamic effect. Tiotropium has no meaningful effect on preload or afterload.
why: Low-dose loop diuretic, used cautiously with monitoring, is the recommended way to relieve pulmonary congestion while he waits for valve replacement.
A statin is safe in aortic stenosis and treats his hypercholesterolaemia, although it does not slow the valve disease.
Paracetamol has no vasodilator or negative inotropic effect, so it is safe in severe aortic stenosis.
A long-acting antimuscarinic inhaler does not change preload or afterload, so it carries no particular haemodynamic risk here, even if it is not indicated.

items.stem: A 52-year-old man, an electrician, sees his general practitioner because of 5 months of daytime sleepiness. He dozes off while watching television and in the afternoons, and he wakes unrefreshed despite 8 hours in bed. His wife reports loud snoring every night, with pauses in his breathing followed by gasping. He has had no sudden muscle weakness with laughter or anger, and he denies sleepiness while driving. He drinks 3 standard drinks most evenings and does not smoke. He has hypertension treated with perindopril. Blood pressure is 146/92 mm Hg, heart rate 76/min and oxygen saturation 97% on room air. BMI is 34 kg/m2, neck circumference is 44 cm and the oropharynx is crowded. His Epworth Sleepiness Scale score is 13 (normal 10 or less), STOP-Bang score 6/8 and OSA50 score 7/10. Full blood count, TSH and electrolytes are normal.
items.ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
items.explanation: This man very probably has obstructive sleep apnoea (OSA). He snores, his wife has seen him stop breathing, he is sleepy in the daytime, he has obesity with a large neck and a crowded oropharynx, he has hypertension, and he drinks alcohol in the evening. Before treatment starts, the diagnosis has to be confirmed and graded by the apnoea-hypopnoea index (AHI). His Epworth score is 8 or more and his STOP-Bang (4 or more) and OSA50 (5 or more) scores are high-risk. This meets the MBS item 12250 criteria, so a GP can refer him directly for an unattended Level 2 polysomnography done at home. Australasian Sleep Association and eTG guidance say this test is the right one for a patient with a high pre-test probability and no major other illness. Treatment then depends on the AHI: CPAP is first line for moderate to severe OSA, and everyone gets lifestyle measures (weight loss, less alcohol, side sleeping) and advice on driving. Overnight oximetry alone misses hypopnoeas that do not lower oxygen levels and cannot measure the AHI, so it is not enough to diagnose OSA. CPAP, a splint or a wake-promoting drug should not be started before the diagnosis and severity are known.
why: Oximetry alone cannot measure the AHI and misses hypopnoeas that do not lower oxygen levels, so it is not recommended for diagnosing OSA.
CPAP is first line only once a sleep study has confirmed moderate to severe OSA, and it should not be started on screening scores alone.
A mandibular advancement splint is an alternative for confirmed mild to moderate OSA or for people who cannot tolerate CPAP, so it is not a first step before diagnosis.
Modafinil is used only for sleepiness that persists despite adequate treatment of confirmed OSA, and it does nothing for the airway obstruction.

items.stem: A 10-year-old boy with moderate intellectual disability is brought to his general practitioner by his mother because he has become aggressive at home and at school over the past 4 weeks. He has hit his teacher, slaps his own belly and keeps pulling at the left side of his face. He has stopped eating toast and apples. His bowels open every 4 to 5 days with hard stools and occasional soiling. His risperidone was increased to 0.5 mg twice daily 6 weeks ago. His temperature is 36.8 °C, heart rate 94/min, blood pressure 104/66 mmHg and respiratory rate 20/min. He has a firm, mildly tender mass in the left iliac fossa. A lower left first permanent molar has a large carious cavity and is tender to percussion, and the gum next to it is red and swollen with no fluctuance. He has no facial swelling or trismus. He has a fine tremor and mild cogwheel rigidity at both wrists. A urine dipstick is negative for leucocytes and nitrites.
items.ask: In addition to starting treatment for constipation, which of the following is the most appropriate next investigation?
items.explanation: When a child with intellectual disability suddenly changes his behaviour, look for pain or illness first, because he cannot describe his symptoms. This boy has two painful causes. The first is faecal loading: hard stools every 4 to 5 days, soiling, a firm left iliac fossa mass and slapping his own belly. The RCH guideline says constipation is a clinical diagnosis, so it needs treatment, not imaging. The second is a probable periapical (dental) abscess: he pulls at the left of his face, refuses crunchy food, and has a carious molar that is tender to percussion with red, swollen gum next to it. Imaging confirms this. An orthopantomogram (or a periapical film taken by a dentist) shows the periapical lucency, the depth of the decay and how far infection has spread. It then guides urgent dental treatment, either drainage, pulp treatment or extraction, while he gets weight-based analgesia. Plain abdominal X-ray: the RCH advises against it because constipation is diagnosed clinically and the X-ray does not change management. Urine microscopy and culture: the dipstick is negative for leucocytes and nitrites, and his extra wetting fits a loaded rectum pressing on the bladder. Serum creatine kinase: he is afebrile with normal observations and only mild extrapyramidal signs, so neuroleptic malignant syndrome is unlikely; his risperidone needs a medication review instead. Thyroid function tests: thyroid disease does not explain a tender carious tooth or a faecal mass, and it would not cause a sudden 4-week change with focal pain signs.
why: Constipation is a clinical diagnosis, and the RCH advises against abdominal X-ray because it does not change management.
The dipstick is negative for leucocytes and nitrites, so a UTI is unlikely, and the mild wetting fits rectal loading.
He is afebrile with normal observations and only mild extrapyramidal signs, so neuroleptic malignant syndrome is not suspected and his risperidone needs review instead.
Thyroid disease would not explain the focal dental findings or the faecal mass, so it would not confirm a cause of this sudden change.

items.stem: A 6-week-old boy is brought to the emergency department by his father with 4 days of forceful vomiting after every feed. The vomit is milky and has never been green. He feeds eagerly straight after vomiting and has had 2 wet nappies in the past 24 hours. He was born at term and is formula fed. He weighs 4.5 kg, down from 4.9 kg 2 weeks ago. Temperature is 36.8°C, pulse 172/min, respirations 38/min, blood pressure 84/50 mm Hg and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. He is drowsy but rouses to voice. His hands and feet are cool and capillary refill time is 3 seconds. A peripheral cannula is placed. Venous gas: pH 7.53 (7.32 to 7.42), bicarbonate 37 mmol/L (20 to 28), lactate 1.1 mmol/L (under 2.0), Na 133 mmol/L (135 to 145), K 2.9 mmol/L (3.5 to 5.0), Cl 86 mmol/L (95 to 110), glucose 4.3 mmol/L. Ultrasound shows a pyloric muscle thickness of 5 mm and a channel length of 18 mm.
items.ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: 0.45% sodium chloride with 2.5% glucose at 18 mL/h intravenously
0.9% sodium chloride 45 mL intravenously over 15 minutes
Potassium chloride 2.25 mmol intravenously over 1 hour
Hydrocortisone 25 mg intravenously as a single dose
Laparoscopic pyloromyotomy on the next available list
items.explanation: This boy has hypertrophic pyloric stenosis. The ultrasound shows a muscle wall of 5 mm or more (abnormal is 3 mm or more) and a channel of 18 mm (abnormal is 15 mm or more), and he has the typical hypochloraemic, hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis. He is also in compensated shock: he is tachycardic, drowsy and cool at the hands and feet, with a capillary refill time of 3 seconds, while his blood pressure is still normal. Pyloric stenosis is a medical emergency but a surgical urgency, not a surgical emergency. The first step is to treat the shock. Keep him nil by mouth and give a 10 mL/kg bolus of 0.9% sodium chloride (45 mL for 4.5 kg), then reassess. After that, give 0.9% sodium chloride with 5% glucose for maintenance plus deficit, and add potassium once he is passing urine (RCH Pyloric stenosis, Dehydration and Intravenous fluids guidelines). Surgery waits until the bicarbonate and chloride are back to normal, because operating while he is still alkalotic risks apnoea after the anaesthetic.
why: Correct: compensated shock needs a 10 mL/kg isotonic bolus first, here 45 mL of 0.9% sodium chloride, with reassessment afterwards.
Wrong: potassium is replaced only after perfusion is restored and he is passing urine, and it does not treat the shock.
Wrong: his low potassium and alkalosis are the opposite of salt-wasting congenital adrenal hyperplasia, which causes a high potassium and an acidosis, so steroids are not needed.
Wrong: pyloromyotomy should wait until shock and the alkalosis are corrected, because operating sooner risks apnoea after the anaesthetic.

items.stem: A 41-year-old woman, a school teacher, returns to her general practitioner for review of a duodenal ulcer. Last month she presented with burning epigastric pain that woke her at night. She had been taking naproxen 500 mg twice daily for low back pain over the previous 6 months. Gastroscopy showed a 7 mm clean-based duodenal bulb ulcer with mild antral gastritis. The rapid urease (CLO) result was positive, and antral biopsies showed Helicobacter pylori with no intestinal metaplasia or dysplasia. She ceased naproxen and yesterday completed 14 days of esomeprazole, amoxicillin and clarithromycin. She is now pain-free and is taking esomeprazole 20 mg daily to complete ulcer healing. She has no melaena or weight loss. Her temperature is 36.7°C, pulse 74/min and blood pressure 124/78 mm Hg. The abdomen is soft and nontender. Haemoglobin is 136 g/L (reference 115–160 g/L).
items.ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate investigation to confirm eradication of the infection?
options: Urea breath test now, continuing the proton pump inhibitor throughout
Helicobacter pylori serology in 4 weeks, continuing the proton pump inhibitor
Faecal antigen test in 1 week, continuing the proton pump inhibitor
Repeat gastroscopy with biopsy in 8 weeks, off proton pump inhibitor
Urea breath test in 4 weeks, off proton pump inhibitor for the final 2 weeks
items.explanation: Under eTG guidance, everyone treated for Helicobacter pylori should have eradication confirmed, because clarithromycin resistance means first-line triple therapy fails in a significant minority. The preferred test of cure is the carbon-13 urea breath test. It must be done at least 4 weeks after the antibiotics finish, and the proton pump inhibitor must be stopped for at least 2 weeks before the test. Antibiotics, bismuth and PPIs all suppress the bacteria's urease activity and bacterial load, which can give a false-negative result. She can finish her PPI course for ulcer healing and then stop it 2 weeks before the test. An uncomplicated duodenal ulcer with benign biopsies does not need a repeat scope. A breath test done now while she is still on the PPI and only one day after the antibiotics could falsely reassure. Serology stays positive for months to years after successful eradication, so it cannot confirm cure. A faecal antigen test is a valid alternative only with the same timing rules, and at 1 week while she is still on the PPI it is unreliable. Repeat gastroscopy is mainly for gastric ulcers, to confirm healing and exclude cancer, or for complicated or non-healing ulcers.
why: Testing one day after the antibiotics while she is still on a PPI suppresses urease activity and is likely to give a false-negative result.
Antibodies persist long after eradication, so serology cannot tell a cured infection from an ongoing one.
Testing 1 week after the antibiotics while she is still on a PPI is too early and risks a false-negative stool antigen result.
An uncomplicated duodenal ulcer with benign histology does not need repeat endoscopy; this invasive test is reserved for gastric or complicated ulcers.

items.stem: A 79-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department of a rural hospital by her daughter. She has had 4 days of worsening headache and, since this morning, new confusion. One week ago she tripped on a rug and hit the left side of her head on a door frame. She did not lose consciousness. She has atrial fibrillation and hypertension. Her medicines are rivaroxaban 20 mg daily, last taken at 07:00 today, and amlodipine. Temperature is 36.7 °C, pulse 76/min and irregular, blood pressure 166/88 mm Hg, respiratory rate 16/min and oxygen saturation 97% on room air. Her GCS is 14 (E3 V5 M6) and falls to 13 (E3 V4 M6) over the next hour. Pupils are equal and reactive. She has a mild right pronator drift. INR is 1.2 (reference 0.9 to 1.3), APTT 32 seconds (reference 25 to 38), platelets 236 ×10^9/L and eGFR 72 mL/min/1.73 m². Non-contrast CT brain shows a crescentic, mixed-density left subdural collection 14 mm thick with 7 mm of midline shift. Neurosurgical retrieval has been requested.
items.ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management while she waits for transfer?
items.explanation: This woman has an acute-on-subacute subdural haematoma while taking a factor Xa inhibitor. Her GCS is falling, she has a focal deficit and the CT shows mass effect. The biggest immediate risk is that the haematoma keeps growing and she herniates before she reaches neurosurgery. Reversing the anticoagulant is the most important step to prevent this. A normal INR and APTT do not rule out a clinically significant rivaroxaban effect, especially when the last dose was taken only hours ago and renal function is preserved. For life-threatening bleeding on apixaban or rivaroxaban, Therapeutic Guidelines recommend andexanet alfa where it is available and local protocol allows. Otherwise, give prothrombin complex concentrate (Prothrombinex-VF 50 units/kg IV) with haematology advice. Andexanet is rarely stocked in rural Australian hospitals, so Prothrombinex-VF is the appropriate choice here. Idarucizumab is wrong because it is a specific antibody fragment against dabigatran and has no effect on factor Xa inhibitors. Phytomenadione (vitamin K) is wrong because it reverses warfarin by restoring vitamin K-dependent factor synthesis, and it does nothing to a direct factor Xa inhibitor. Fresh frozen plasma is wrong because it provides too little clotting factor to overcome factor Xa inhibition, needs a large volume and takes time to thaw. Tranexamic acid is wrong because it is an antifibrinolytic that does not reverse rivaroxaban, and its trial benefit in traumatic brain injury applies only within 3 hours of injury, not a week later.
why: Idarucizumab binds only dabigatran, a direct thrombin inhibitor, so it would not reverse rivaroxaban.
Vitamin K restores the synthesis of factors depleted by warfarin but has no effect on a direct factor Xa inhibitor.
Fresh frozen plasma gives too little factor concentration to reverse rivaroxaban, carries a large volume load and is slow to prepare.
Tranexamic acid does not reverse anticoagulation, and its benefit in head injury is limited to the first 3 hours after trauma, not a week later.

items.stem: A 49-year-old man presents to his general practitioner with three attacks of spontaneous spinning vertigo over the past 4 months. Each attack lasted 3 to 5 hours, with nausea and vomiting. Before each attack, his left ear felt blocked and he heard a roaring tinnitus. Afterwards, his hearing in that ear was muffled for several days and then improved. He feels well between attacks. He has hypertension treated with perindopril and drinks four cups of coffee a day. Today he is between attacks. Temperature is 36.7 °C, blood pressure 132/84 mm Hg and pulse 72/min, regular. Otoscopy is normal on both sides. The Weber test lateralises to the right, and the Rinne test is positive on both sides. There is no spontaneous or gaze-evoked nystagmus. The head impulse test is normal, and the Dix-Hallpike test is negative on both sides. The corneal reflexes, facial movements, gait and coordination are normal. Audiometry shows a left sensorineural loss of 40 dB at 250 and 500 Hz with normal thresholds from 2000 Hz. The right ear is normal, and tympanometry is type A on both sides.
items.ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Non-contrast CT scan of the brain and posterior fossa
Epley canalith repositioning manoeuvre on the affected side
ENT referral and gadolinium-enhanced MRI of the internal acoustic meati
Referral for intratympanic gentamicin injection into the affected ear
Duplex ultrasound of the carotid and vertebral arteries
items.explanation: This man meets the Bárány Society criteria for definite Ménière's disease of the left ear. He has had two or more spontaneous attacks of vertigo, each lasting 20 minutes to 12 hours. Audiometry documents a low-frequency sensorineural loss in that ear, and his aural symptoms fluctuate. However, the criteria also require that no other diagnosis explains the picture better. Any asymmetric sensorineural hearing loss needs a retrocochlear lesion excluded, especially a vestibular schwannoma, which can cause unilateral tinnitus, hearing loss and vertigo. The investigation of choice is a gadolinium-enhanced MRI of the internal acoustic meati, arranged through an ENT surgeon. While he waits, attacks can be treated with a short course of prochlorperazine (eTG), and he can be advised to cut down on salt, caffeine and alcohol. Prophylaxis and ablative treatments are a matter for the ENT surgeon once the diagnosis is secure. A non-contrast CT brain can miss small tumours in the internal acoustic canal or cerebellopontine angle. The Epley manoeuvre treats BPPV, but his attacks are spontaneous, last hours and come with a negative Dix-Hallpike test. Intratympanic gentamicin destroys vestibular function, so it is kept for disabling disease that has not responded to conservative treatment once the diagnosis is confirmed. Carotid and vertebral duplex is aimed at posterior circulation TIA, which is unlikely here: the attacks last hours, come with ear symptoms and leave a normal neurological examination.
why: Non-contrast CT is not sensitive enough to exclude a small vestibular schwannoma in the internal acoustic canal or cerebellopontine angle, so it would not settle the question raised by the asymmetric loss.
The Epley manoeuvre treats posterior canal BPPV, which causes brief positional vertigo with a positive Dix-Hallpike test, not spontaneous attacks lasting hours with ear symptoms.
Intratympanic gentamicin destroys vestibular function and can worsen hearing, so it is kept for disabling disease that has not responded to conservative treatment once the diagnosis is confirmed.

Posterior circulation TIA is unlikely because the attacks last hours, come with fluctuating one-sided ear symptoms and leave a normal neurological examination, and duplex ultrasound would not exclude the retrocochlear lesion that needs ruling out.

items.stem: A 22-month-old boy is brought to a general practice in regional Victoria with a 6-week history of cough. The cough is wet and happens by day and by night. It has not improved with 7 days of amoxicillin or with inhaled salbutamol through a spacer. His mother remembers that the cough started on the evening of a family barbecue. While eating popcorn there, he coughed and gagged for a short time and then settled. He has no eczema and no previous wheeze. He is fully immunised and has had no contact with tuberculosis. He is playful. His temperature is 37.3 °C, pulse 120/min, respirations 38/min, and SpO2 96% in room air. On examination there is reduced air entry and a fixed monophonic wheeze over the left lower zone only. A chest X-ray shows a hyperinflated left lung with the mediastinum shifted to the right. No radio-opaque object is seen.
items.ask: If the underlying cause is not treated, this child is most at risk of which of the following complications?
items.explanation: This toddler has an inhaled foreign body, most likely a popcorn kernel, in the left lower lobe bronchus. The clues are a choking episode at the start, a cough that has lasted weeks despite antibiotics and bronchodilators, one-sided monophonic wheeze with reduced air entry, and air trapping on the same side with the mediastinum pushed away. Organic objects are radiolucent, so a normal-looking X-ray does not rule out the diagnosis. Organic material left in the bronchus causes ongoing local inflammation, granulation tissue and infection beyond the blockage. This leads to recurrent pneumonia in the same lobe and then permanent damage to the airway: bronchiectasis. The risk goes up the longer the object stays in. This is why the RCH guideline recommends prompt rigid bronchoscopy under general anaesthesia at a paediatric centre, rather than more courses of antibiotics or inhalers. Tension pneumothorax is a rare acute event, not the expected result of an object left in place. Tracheo-oesophageal fistula is a complication of an oesophageal foreign body, especially a button battery, not a bronchial one. Pulmonary arterial hypertension needs widespread lung or vascular disease, not one blocked lobe. Asthma is not caused by a foreign body, and the poor response to salbutamol argues against it.
why: Wrong: air trapping can rarely rupture into the pleura, but this is an uncommon acute event and not the usual consequence of a retained object.
Wrong: a fistula forms when an oesophageal foreign body such as a button battery erodes into the trachea, not from an object in the bronchus.
Wrong: pulmonary arterial hypertension needs widespread lung or vascular disease, and one blocked lobe does not cause it.
Wrong: a foreign body does not cause atopic asthma, and this child has no atopy, no earlier wheeze and no response to salbutamol.

items.stem: A 36-year-old man presents to the emergency department with 4 days of yellow eyes and dark urine. Two weeks ago he developed fever, anorexia and aching wrists and knees, which have since eased. He had unprotected sex with a new partner 3 months ago. items.stem: A 63-year-old woman comes to the emergency department with 3 hours of central chest pressure that spreads to her left arm. It started while she was gardening and has not eased with rest. She is sweaty and nauseated. She has type 2 diabetes and hypertension, treated with metformin and perindopril. She has been given aspirin 300 mg, ticagrelor 180 mg, enoxaparin, sublingual and then intravenous glyceryl trinitrate, and intravenous fentanyl. Forty minutes later her pain is still 7/10. Temperature is 36.9 °C, pulse 104/min, blood pressure 106/68 mm Hg in both arms, respiratory rate 22/min and oxygen saturation 96% on room air. Her chest is clear and she has no murmurs. An ECG shows sinus tachycardia with new horizontal ST depression of 2 mm in V4 to V6, I and aVL, and no ST elevation in any lead. High-sensitivity troponin T is 88 ng/L, rising to 296 ng/L at 1 hour (99th percentile 14 ng/L). Her chest X-ray shows clear lungs and a normal mediastinum.

Stress testing is contraindicated during active, unstable ischaemia and adds nothing once the troponin and ECG have confirmed the diagnosis.

items.stem: A 74-year-old man is brought to the emergency department by ambulance after collapsing while walking to his letterbox 1 hour ago. His wife saw him fall with no warning. He was unresponsive for about 20 seconds, did not jerk, and was fully alert within a minute. A few minutes before he fell, he felt a fluttering in his chest. He has no chest pain, headache or incontinence, and he did not hit his head. He has hypertension, treated with atenolol and perindopril. His temperature is 36.7 °C, pulse 38/min and regular, blood pressure 112/60 mm Hg, respiratory rate 16/min, and oxygen saturation 97% on room air. Large waves appear intermittently in the jugular venous pulse, and the loudness of the first heart sound changes from beat to beat. The neurological examination is normal, and his tongue is not bitten. Capillary glucose is 6.1 mmol/L.
items.ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate next investigation?
items.explanation: This man had sudden syncope with no warning, palpitations just before it, and a quick, full recovery. He takes a beta blocker. At the bedside he has a slow, regular pulse, intermittent cannon a waves and a first heart sound that varies in loudness. Together these signs point to AV dissociation, most likely from complete heart block, which makes this a Stokes-Adams attack. Australian syncope guidance (eTG Cardiovascular) says every patient with transient loss of consciousness needs a 12-lead ECG straight away. Because the bradycardia is still present, a 12-lead ECG will show it now. It can confirm complete heart block (regular P waves marching through a slower, independent escape rhythm with no fixed PR interval), show whether the escape rhythm is broad (infranodal and unstable), and look for ischaemia or other conduction disease. It is fast, cheap, non-invasive and decides the next step: pacing pads, atropine or an infusion, stopping AV nodal blockers, and cardiology referral for a permanent pacemaker. A Holter monitor is for intermittent symptoms with a normal resting ECG. Echocardiography looks for structural disease but cannot identify the rhythm. CT of the head and EEG look for neurological causes that this history and examination do not support.
why: Ambulatory Holter recording is for intermittent symptoms when the resting ECG is normal, so it is the wrong first test while the arrhythmia is present now and could be recorded in minutes.
Echocardiography can assess structural heart disease once the rhythm is known, but it cannot diagnose the conduction disorder causing his syncope.

CT of the head is not indicated because he did not strike his head, has no headache and has a normal neurological examination, and an intracranial cause would not explain the slow pulse or cannon waves.
Electroencephalography is for suspected seizures, but he had no jerking, no tongue biting, no incontinence and no post-ictal confusion, and his clinical signs point to a cardiac cause.

items.stem: A 63-year-old man sees his general practitioner to discuss the result of his prostate biopsy. He was referred to a urologist after two total PSA results 4 weeks apart, 8.1 ng/mL and 8.4 ng/mL. A midstream urine culture was sterile. He has no urinary symptoms, bone pain or weight loss. He takes amlodipine for hypertension and does not take a 5-alpha reductase inhibitor. His blood pressure is 134/82 mmHg and pulse is 70/min. The urologist's letter describes a smooth, symmetrical prostate with no palpable nodule. Multiparametric MRI showed a 45 mL gland with a single 10 mm PI-RADS 4 lesion in the right peripheral zone and no extraprostatic extension. Transperineal biopsy found adenocarcinoma in 4 of 14 cores, all on the right. In each positive core, poorly formed and fused glands (pattern 4) make up about 70% of the tumour, and discrete well-formed glands (pattern 3) make up the other 30%. There is no pattern 5, cribriform growth or perineural invasion.
items.ask: Which of the following best describes this biopsy result?
items.explanation: The answer is C. On a biopsy, the Gleason score is the most common pattern plus the next most common, unless a higher pattern is present, in which case the highest pattern is counted however small it is. Here pattern 4 makes up 70% of the tumour and pattern 3 makes up 30%, with no pattern 5, so the score is 4+3=7. The 2014 ISUP grading system separates the two kinds of Gleason 7: 3+4=7 is Grade Group 2 and 4+3=7 is Grade Group 3. Grade Group 3 behaves worse than Grade Group 2 even though both scores add up to 7. With a PSA under 10 ng/mL and impalpable disease (cT1c), this is unfavourable intermediate-risk localised disease. Under Australian practice, it should be staged with PSMA PET/CT before curative treatment is planned. Option A is wrong because pattern 4 is present, and any pattern 4 rules out a score of 6. Option B is wrong because it puts the minority pattern first, when the most common pattern (4) must come first. Option D is wrong because the 30% pattern 3 counts as the second pattern, so the score is not 4+4. Option E is wrong because no pattern 5 was reported, and poorly formed and fused glands are pattern 4, not pattern 5.
why: Wrong: pattern 4 is present, so the score cannot be 3+3=6. Grade Group 1 needs pattern 3 only.
Wrong: this puts the minority pattern first. On a biopsy, the most common pattern (pattern 4, 70%) is listed first.
Wrong: pattern 3 makes up 30% of the tumour, so it is the second pattern. A score of 4+4=8 (Grade Group 4) would need pattern 4 only.
Wrong: no pattern 5 was seen. Poorly formed and fused glands are pattern 4, so a score of 9 (Grade Group 5) does not apply.

items.stem:
A 38-year-old woman comes to the emergency department with 2 days of worsening generalised headache, fever, vomiting and photophobia. She has Crohn disease and has been taking prednisolone 25 mg daily for 6 weeks for a flare. Her temperature is 39.1 °C, pulse 118/min, blood pressure 104/66 mm Hg, respiratory rate 22/min and SpO2 97% on room air. She has marked neck stiffness, a GCS of 15, no focal neurological signs and no rash. Blood cultures are drawn. She is given intravenous dexamethasone, ceftriaxone and benzylpenicillin. A non-contrast CT brain is normal. A lumbar puncture is done 1 hour after the first antibiotic doses. CSF results:

Opening pressure 28 cmH2O (10 to 20)
Appearance: turbid
White cell count 1200 ×10^6/L (below 5), 85% polymorphs
Red cell count 3 ×10^6/L
Protein 1.6 g/L (0.15 to 0.45)
Glucose 1.5 mmol/L; paired plasma glucose 8.0 mmol/L
Gram stain: no organisms seen
items.ask: Which of the following is the most accurate interpretation of the Gram stain result?
options: A bacterial cause is excluded, and the antibiotics can be stopped
A viral cause is confirmed, and aciclovir alone should be given
A fungal cause is suggested, and amphotericin should be added
The sample is probably contaminated, and the procedure should be repeated
A bacterial cause remains likely, and the present therapy should continue
items.explanation: This CSF has a bacterial pattern: it is turbid, with a raised opening pressure, a white cell count of 1200 ×10^6/L that is mostly polymorphs, protein of 1.6 g/L and a CSF:plasma glucose ratio of about 0.19 (normal is above 0.6). A negative Gram stain does not rule out bacterial meningitis. Even before antibiotics, the Gram stain finds organisms in only about 60 to 90% of cases. That rate drops after antibiotics have been given, as here, and Listeria monocytogenes shows on Gram stain in only about a third of cases. Listeria is a real concern because she has been on corticosteroids for 6 weeks. Under eTG, she should stay on empirical ceftriaxone plus benzylpenicillin (for Listeria), with dexamethasone, until the culture and bacterial PCR come back. Treatment can then be narrowed or stopped on those results, not on the Gram stain.
why: Wrong: the Gram stain is not sensitive enough to rule out bacterial meningitis, and stopping antibiotics in this neutrophilic, low-glucose CSF could be fatal.
Wrong: viral meningitis usually gives a lymphocyte-predominant CSF with a normal glucose ratio and only mildly raised protein, and a negative Gram stain cannot confirm any diagnosis.
Wrong: cryptococcal and other fungal meningitis usually cause a lymphocytic CSF with a slower onset and are diagnosed by cryptococcal antigen or India ink, not by an absent Gram stain result.
Wrong: contamination would add organisms rather than hide them, the very low red cell count rules out a traumatic tap, and repeating the lumbar puncture would add risk without changing management.

items.stem: A 61-year-old man is brought by ambulance to the emergency department of a metropolitan hospital with 50 minutes of heavy central chest pain and sweating. Paramedics gave aspirin 300 mg and two doses of sublingual glyceryl trinitrate, and afterwards he became light-headed. He has type 2 diabetes and takes metformin. His pulse is 64/min and regular, blood pressure 82/50 mm Hg (138/86 mm Hg at first paramedic contact), respiratory rate 18/min and SpO2 97% on room air. He is pale and clammy. His jugular venous pressure is raised at 6 cm above the sternal angle, his lung fields are clear and his heart sounds are normal. The 12-lead ECG shows sinus rhythm with 3 mm ST elevation in II, III and aVF, greater in III than in II, and 1 mm ST elevation in V4R. Bedside echocardiography shows a dilated, hypokinetic right ventricle, preserved left ventricular function and no pericardial effusion. The cardiac catheterisation laboratory has been activated.
items.ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate immediate treatment for his hypotension while he waits for transfer to the catheterisation laboratory?
items.explanation: This man has an inferior STEMI with right ventricular infarction, which points to a proximal right coronary artery occlusion. The evidence is ST elevation in II, III and aVF that is greater in III than II, ST elevation in V4R, a raised JVP with clear lungs, and a dilated, hypokinetic right ventricle. An infarcted right ventricle depends on preload. Nitrates dilate the veins and reduce preload, which is why his blood pressure fell after the sublingual GTN. Primary PCI has already been arranged, so the immediate priority is to restore right ventricular filling. Give cautious IV crystalloid in small boluses (such as 250 mL of 0.9% saline) and reassess blood pressure, perfusion and lung fields after each one. This follows the Australian ACS guidelines and eTG: in inferior STEMI with hypotension, avoid nitrates, record right-sided leads and give fluid first. Use inotropes or vasopressors only if hypotension persists despite adequate filling. Use atropine or pacing only for symptomatic bradycardia or AV block, which he does not have.
why: Wrong: a loop diuretic would reduce preload further and worsen hypotension, and his clear lung fields show no pulmonary oedema to treat.
Wrong: nitrates are contraindicated in hypotension and right ventricular infarction, and the GTN he has already had probably caused his fall in blood pressure.
Wrong: an IV beta blocker is contraindicated in a hypotensive patient at risk of cardiogenic shock, and inferior infarction makes bradycardia and AV block more likely.
Wrong: a vasopressor is reserved for hypotension that persists after adequate filling, and he has not yet had any fluid.

items.stem:
A 66-year-old man sees his general practitioner about 4 months of looser, more frequent stools, now three times daily. On several occasions there has been dark red blood mixed through the stool. He reports tiredness but no weight loss or abdominal pain. He had rubber band ligation of internal haemorrhoids 5 years ago. A National Bowel Cancer Screening Program kit arrived last week, and he asks whether he should complete it; his kit 2 years ago was negative. He takes no regular medicines, including no aspirin or anti-inflammatory drugs. Temperature is 36.8°C, pulse is 84/min, and blood pressure is 132/78 mm Hg. Abdominal examination is normal. Digital rectal examination and proctoscopy show small, non-bleeding internal haemorrhoids and no mass. Investigations show:
Haemoglobin 104 g/L (130–180)
MCV 74 fL (80–100)
Ferritin 6 µg/L (30–500)
TSH 2.1 mIU/L (0.4–4.0)
Tissue transglutaminase IgA negative
items.ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Complete the immunochemical faecal occult blood test kit
Oral iron and a repeat blood count in 8 weeks
Repeat rubber band ligation of the internal haemorrhoids
CT colonography as the first investigation
items.explanation: This man has a new, ongoing change in bowel habit at 66, blood mixed through the stool, and iron deficiency anaemia (Hb 104 g/L, MCV 74 fL, ferritin 6 µg/L). He takes no NSAIDs and has no other obvious source of blood loss. Colorectal cancer must be assumed until it is excluded. The Cancer Council Australia optimal care pathway says a symptomatic patient should be referred for urgent diagnostic colonoscopy. GESA guidance on iron deficiency says a man or a postmenopausal woman with iron deficiency anaemia needs both colonoscopy and gastroscopy (bidirectional endoscopy), because there can be a lesion in both the upper and lower gut. A negative coeliac test does not remove the need for gastroscopy. Small haemorrhoids that are not bleeding do not explain the change in habit or the anaemia, and a normal rectal examination does not exclude a lesion higher in the colon. An FOBT is a screening test for people without symptoms. A negative result would falsely reassure him, and the negative kit 2 years ago tells us nothing about his current symptoms.
why: An FOBT is a screening test for people without symptoms; he has red-flag symptoms and anaemia, so he needs a diagnostic test, and a negative result would falsely reassure him.
Giving iron alone without finding the source would delay the diagnosis of a likely gastrointestinal cancer, and a rise in haemoglobin would hide the problem.
Small haemorrhoids that are not bleeding do not explain blood mixed through the stool, the change in habit or the iron deficiency, so treating them misses the likely cause.
CT colonography is a second-line option when colonoscopy cannot be done; it cannot take a biopsy or examine the upper gut, which this patient's iron deficiency anaemia requires.

items.stem: A 72-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department 70 minutes after the sudden onset of right-sided weakness and difficulty speaking. She was last seen well at 08:10. She has atrial fibrillation and hypertension, treated with apixaban 5 mg twice daily and perindopril. Her last apixaban dose was at 07:30 today. Temperature is 36.7 °C, pulse 92/min and irregularly irregular, blood pressure 168/94 mm Hg, respirations 16/min and SpO2 97% on room air. She has non-fluent aphasia, a right facial droop and right arm power of 1/5 (NIHSS 15). Capillary glucose is 7.2 mmol/L, platelets 241 x10^9/L (150-400), INR 1.1 (0.9-1.2) and APTT 30 seconds (25-38). Non-contrast CT brain shows no haemorrhage. CT angiography shows a left M1 occlusion, and CT perfusion shows a 10 mL core within a 90 mL perfusion deficit. An apixaban-specific anti-Xa level is pending.
items.ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
items.explanation: This woman has an acute left middle cerebral artery stroke from a proximal (M1) large vessel occlusion. She is within 6 hours of last known well, has a disabling deficit (NIHSS 15), and has a small core with a large salvageable penumbra. The Stroke Foundation Australian and New Zealand Living Clinical Guidelines recommend endovascular thrombectomy for anterior circulation large vessel occlusion in this setting, whether or not the patient can have thrombolysis. Anticoagulation does not rule it out. She took apixaban about 2 hours ago, well within 48 hours, so IV thrombolysis is contraindicated unless a drug-specific anti-Xa level shows no meaningful anticoagulant effect. A normal INR and APTT do not exclude a clinically relevant apixaban effect. Do not wait for the pending level before the clot retrieval pathway is started, because every minute of delay costs brain tissue. Other care in the meantime: keep her nil by mouth until a swallow screen, and do not lower blood pressure routinely. The value of 168/94 mm Hg is already below the 185/110 threshold used for reperfusion therapy.
why: Wrong: she took apixaban within 48 hours, and a normal INR and APTT do not exclude a significant apixaban effect, so thrombolysis carries an unacceptable risk of haemorrhage until a drug-specific level shows no effect.
Wrong: idarucizumab reverses only dabigatran and has no effect on apixaban, a factor Xa inhibitor.
Wrong: guidelines do not support reversing a DOAC with prothrombin complex concentrate so that thrombolysis can be given, as this adds thrombotic risk and delay without proven benefit.
Wrong: aspirin gives no reperfusion for a salvageable M1 occlusion, and adding an antiplatelet in a fully anticoagulated patient before reperfusion is decided raises bleeding risk.

items.stem: A 24-year-old woman comes to the emergency department with 6 hours of worsening breathlessness, chest tightness and wheeze. She had an upper respiratory tract infection 4 days ago. She has had asthma since childhood. She uses only a reliever inhaler and has never been prescribed a preventer. On arrival she speaks in short phrases and is using her accessory muscles. Pulse is 118/min, respiratory rate 28/min, blood pressure 124/72 mm Hg, temperature 37.4 °C and SpO2 91% on room air. There is widespread expiratory wheeze. The trachea is central and air entry is equal on both sides. Over the first hour she receives oxygen by nasal prongs, salbutamol 12 puffs by spacer every 20 minutes, ipratropium 8 puffs by spacer every 20 minutes and oral prednisolone 50 mg. She is still alert but still speaks only in phrases. Pulse is 122/min, respiratory rate 27/min and SpO2 93% on 2 L/min oxygen. Wheeze persists. A chest X-ray shows hyperinflation with no pneumothorax or consolidation.
items.ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
items.explanation: This woman has acute severe asthma. She speaks only in phrases, uses her accessory muscles and has an SpO2 of 91% on room air. She has no features of life-threatening asthma: she is alert, with no cyanosis, no silent chest and no exhaustion. She has had an hour of optimal first-line treatment: repeated salbutamol by spacer, ipratropium, oral prednisolone and oxygen titrated to SpO2 92 to 96%. She is still in the severe category. The chest X-ray rules out a pneumothorax and consolidation. The Australian Asthma Handbook and eTG advise IV magnesium sulfate 10 mmol over 20 minutes for severe acute asthma that has not responded to first-line bronchodilators. She should keep having frequent salbutamol, and senior and ICU staff should be told. Aminophylline is not recommended as routine treatment because it adds little and causes arrhythmias and vomiting. IV hydrocortisone works no better than the oral prednisolone she has already had. IV salbutamol is kept for life-threatening asthma that does not respond, in a critical care setting. Nebulised adrenaline is for anaphylaxis or upper airway obstruction, not acute asthma. Before discharge she will need a preventer containing an inhaled corticosteroid and a written action plan.
why: Aminophylline is not recommended as routine treatment for acute asthma: it adds little bronchodilation to inhaled therapy and has a narrow therapeutic index, with arrhythmias, seizures and vomiting.
She has already had oral prednisolone 50 mg and can swallow, so IV hydrocortisone gives no extra benefit and repeats her corticosteroid.

An IV salbutamol infusion is kept for life-threatening asthma that does not respond to other treatment, in a critical care setting; it causes more tachycardia, lactic acidosis and hypokalaemia, and she has no life-threatening features.
Nebulised adrenaline treats anaphylaxis or upper airway obstruction such as croup, and she has no urticaria, angioedema, allergen exposure or stridor.

items.stem: A 58-year-old man comes to his general practitioner for review of heartburn. For 9 years he has had burning retrosternal pain after evening meals on most days, with sour fluid coming up into his throat when he lies down at night. He has treated it with over-the-counter antacids and has never seen a doctor about it. He has no difficulty swallowing, vomiting, black stools or weight loss. He has hypertension treated with perindopril. He smoked 20 cigarettes a day for 25 years and stopped 5 years ago. He drinks about 10 standard drinks of alcohol a week. His temperature is 36.7°C, pulse is 72/min and blood pressure is 134/84 mm Hg. His BMI is 33 kg/m2 and his waist circumference is 110 cm. Abdominal examination is normal. A resting 12-lead ECG is normal. Haemoglobin is 146 g/L (reference 130–180 g/L) and ferritin is 120 µg/L (reference 30–500 µg/L).
items.ask: Which of the following conditions is this patient at greatest risk of developing?
options: Squamous cell carcinoma of the oesophagus
items.explanation: This man has had untreated gastro-oesophageal reflux disease (GORD) for 9 years, with typical burning retrosternal pain after meals and regurgitation at night. He also has most of the recognised risk factors for Barrett's oesophagus: male sex, age over 50, reflux for many years, nocturnal symptoms, central obesity and a history of smoking. In Barrett's oesophagus, repeated acid injury replaces the squamous lining of the distal oesophagus with columnar epithelium showing intestinal metaplasia. It causes no symptoms of its own, but it can progress through dysplasia to oesophageal adenocarcinoma, so it is the key complication to look for and counsel about. Cancer Council Australia and eTG guidance support gastroscopy for a man over 50 with chronic reflux and several Barrett's risk factors, even without alarm features. Management alongside this is lifestyle change (weight loss, smaller and earlier evening meals, raising the head of the bed) and a standard-dose PPI. If Barrett's is found, he needs endoscopic surveillance. Squamous cell carcinoma is linked to smoking and heavy alcohol use, not reflux. Eosinophilic oesophagitis and achalasia are not complications of GORD. Distal gastric adenocarcinoma is driven by Helicobacter pylori, not reflux.
why: Wrong: squamous cell carcinoma is mainly caused by heavy smoking and alcohol use, not acid reflux, and his moderate drinking and past smoking make it much less likely than reflux-driven metaplasia.
Wrong: eosinophilic oesophagitis is an allergic disorder that usually affects younger atopic men with dysphagia or food bolus impaction, and it is not a complication of long-standing reflux.
Wrong: achalasia is a primary motility disorder caused by loss of myenteric neurons, and it presents with progressive dysphagia to both solids and liquids rather than developing from reflux.
Wrong: adenocarcinoma of the distal stomach is mainly linked to Helicobacter pylori and atrophic gastritis, not to acid reflux into the oesophagus.

items.stem: A 72-year-old man collapses in the emergency department waiting area 20 minutes after triage. He had come in with 4 hours of central chest heaviness and nausea. He has type 2 diabetes, hypertension and hyperlipidaemia, and takes metformin, perindopril and atorvastatin. His first rhythm is ventricular fibrillation. He receives CPR, three shocks, adrenaline 1 mg IV and amiodarone 300 mg IV. Spontaneous circulation returns after 12 minutes. He is being ventilated with a bag-valve-mask on 15 L/min oxygen. Pulse is 112/min, blood pressure is 98/60 mm Hg, temperature is 35.6 °C and SpO2 is 97%. GCS is 3. A 12-lead ECG shows ST elevation in V1 to V5. A venous blood gas taken 5 minutes after return of circulation shows: pH 7.09 (7.32 to 7.42); pCO2 62 mm Hg (41 to 51); bicarbonate 18 mmol/L (22 to 28); base excess -11 mmol/L (-2 to +2); lactate 9.2 mmol/L (below 2.0); potassium 5.6 mmol/L (3.5 to 5.2); glucose 15.1 mmol/L (4.0 to 7.8).
items.ask: Which of the following best describes this patient's acid-base disturbance?
options: Metabolic acidosis with appropriate respiratory compensation
Acute respiratory acidosis with renal compensation
Metabolic acidosis with coexisting metabolic alkalosis
Chronic respiratory acidosis with metabolic compensation
items.explanation: The pH of 7.09 shows a severe acidaemia. There are two causes, and each one lowers the pH. First, the pCO2 of 62 mm Hg is high even for a venous sample, so there is a respiratory acidosis. This comes from low cardiac output during the arrest and poor ventilation with the bag-valve-mask. Second, the bicarbonate of 18 mmol/L, base excess of -11 and lactate of 9.2 mmol/L show a lactic metabolic acidosis from 12 minutes of low tissue perfusion. If the lungs were compensating for the metabolic acidosis, Winter's formula (1.5 x 18 + 8 = 35 +/- 2 mm Hg) says the pCO2 should be low. Instead it is high, so a second, respiratory process is present. This matters for his care. ANZCOR post-resuscitation guidance asks for normocapnia, so his ventilation should be increased and adjusted to arterial gases. Do not give bicarbonate routinely. The lactate should clear once perfusion improves with reperfusion and blood pressure support (MAP at least 65 mm Hg). The mild rise in potassium and the high glucose are expected after an arrest.
why: Wrong: if the lungs were compensating, the pCO2 would be about 35 mm Hg, but it is 62 mm Hg, so there is also a respiratory acidosis.
Wrong: renal compensation would raise the bicarbonate, and the kidneys need days to do this, but his bicarbonate is low at 18 mmol/L.
Wrong: he has nothing that causes a metabolic alkalosis, such as vomiting or diuretics, and his low bicarbonate and base excess show only a metabolic acidosis.
Wrong: in chronic respiratory acidosis the bicarbonate is raised and the pH is close to normal, but he has a low bicarbonate and severe acidaemia after an acute event.

items.stem: A 78-year-old woman sees her general practitioner about a painful ulcer on the tip of her left second toe. It has not healed in 2 months. For 3 weeks, pain in her left forefoot has woken her at night, and it eases when she hangs the foot over the side of the bed. She has had type 2 diabetes for 25 years and has chronic kidney disease. She is a former smoker. Her medicines are metformin, insulin glargine and atorvastatin. Blood pressure is 146/80 mmHg, pulse 78/min and regular, and temperature 36.6°C. The left foot is cool and hairless, and the pedal pulses cannot be felt. The ulcer is 0.8 cm across, dry and punched out, with a pale base and no surrounding erythema. Probe to bone is negative. Monofilament sensation is reduced at 2 of 10 sites. eGFR is 41 mL/min/1.73 m2. Handheld Doppler studies show: right brachial systolic 146 mmHg, left brachial systolic 140 mmHg; left dorsalis pedis systolic 178 mmHg and left posterior tibial systolic 184 mmHg (ABI 1.26); left pedal waveforms monophasic; left hallux systolic 22 mmHg (toe-brachial index 0.15; normal above 0.70).
items.ask: Which of the following is the most accurate interpretation of the vascular studies?
options: Normal perfusion, so the ulcer is neuropathic in origin
Isolated digital disease with patent tibial vessels
Normal ankle readings with an artefactual toe reading
Mild disease with perfusion adequate for healing
Severe ischaemia masked by medial arterial calcification
items.explanation: The answer is A. Long-standing diabetes and chronic kidney disease cause medial calcification of the tibial arteries. Calcified arteries are hard to compress with a cuff, so ankle pressures read falsely high, and an ABI that looks normal (0.9 to 1.3) does not rule out peripheral arterial disease. Diabetes Feet Australia guidelines therefore combine the ABI with Doppler waveforms and the toe-brachial index (TBI). Here, monophasic pedal waveforms and a TBI of 0.15 confirm arterial disease. The digital arteries are usually spared from calcification, so the toe pressure shows the true perfusion of the foot. A toe pressure below 30 mmHg means severe ischaemia and a low chance of healing. With rest pain and tissue loss, this is chronic limb-threatening ischaemia, which needs urgent vascular imaging and referral for revascularisation. Why the other options are wrong: B wrongly takes the ABI at face value, and mild neuropathy can coexist with but does not explain the abnormal waveforms and very low TBI. C is wrong because monophasic pedal waveforms show disease at or above the ankle, not only in the toe. D is wrong because the low toe pressure fits the rest pain, cool hairless foot and absent pulses, and photoplethysmography is the recommended method. E is wrong because a toe pressure of 22 mmHg is below the healing threshold of about 30 mmHg.
why: Wrong: an ABI in the normal range does not exclude disease in diabetes, and the monophasic waveforms and very low TBI show poor perfusion; the painful toe-tip ulcer with rest pain is ischaemic.
Wrong: monophasic pedal waveforms show disease at or above the ankle, so the tibial vessels are not patent.
Wrong: the toe pressure is the more reliable reading in calcified vessels, and it fits the rest pain, cool hairless foot and absent pulses.
Wrong: a toe pressure below 30 mmHg predicts poor healing and, with rest pain and tissue loss, means chronic limb-threatening ischaemia that needs urgent vascular referral.

items.stem: A 31-year-old woman, para 2, is on the birth suite 25 minutes after a spontaneous vaginal birth at 38 weeks' gestation. Her labour was induced for pre-eclampsia. She received oxytocin 10 units at the birth, and the placenta and membranes were complete. She is now bleeding heavily with clots, and the measured loss is 1,300 mL. Bimanual compression has been done, a catheter has drained 450 mL of urine, an oxytocin infusion is running, and tranexamic acid 1 g IV was given 10 minutes ago. In labour she took oral labetalol and had a magnesium sulfate infusion. She has no history of asthma. Pulse is 122/min, blood pressure 104/66 mmHg (158/102 mmHg before the birth), respirations 24/min and SpO2 98% on oxygen 15 L/min by mask. The fundus is soft and above the umbilicus. Speculum examination shows no cervical or vaginal tear. Haemoglobin is 95 g/L, platelets 146 x 10^9/L and fibrinogen 3.4 g/L. Crossmatched blood has been requested.
items.ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
items.explanation: This is a major primary postpartum haemorrhage (1,300 mL with tachycardia) caused by uterine atony. The fundus is soft and high, and the other Ts have been checked: no tear (trauma), a complete placenta (tissue) and normal fibrinogen and near-normal platelets (thrombin). First-line measures are already done: uterine compression, an empty bladder, oxytocin IM then by infusion, and tranexamic acid. RANZCOG C-Obs 43 and Queensland Clinical Guidelines say the next step for ongoing atony is a second-line uterotonic. Ergometrine is contraindicated in hypertension and pre-eclampsia because it can cause a hypertensive crisis, stroke or eclampsia, even though her BP has fallen from bleeding. Magnesium sulfate also adds to atony. She has no asthma, so carboprost (15-methyl PGF2-alpha) 250 micrograms IM is the right choice. It can be repeated every 15 minutes up to 8 doses (2 mg). Balloon tamponade and surgery are for bleeding that continues despite uterotonics.
why: Wrong: ergometrine is contraindicated in pre-eclampsia and hypertension because it can cause severe hypertension, stroke or eclampsia, and her current lower BP is from blood loss, not a resolved disease.
Wrong: misoprostol is slower in onset and less effective than other uterotonics, so guidelines keep it for when carboprost or ergometrine are unavailable or contraindicated.
Wrong: balloon tamponade is the next step only once uterotonics have failed, and she has not yet had a second-line uterotonic.
Wrong: laparotomy with a B-Lynch or similar suture is for haemorrhage that continues despite uterotonics and tamponade, so it is premature here.

items.stem:
A 44-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with 30 hours of constant right upper quadrant pain. It began after a fried dinner and radiates to her right shoulder. Over the past 8 months she has had brief, similar episodes after meals. Her temperature is 38.7 °C, pulse 106/min, blood pressure 126/80 mm Hg and SpO2 98% on room air. She is not jaundiced, and Murphy's sign is positive. Investigations show:
White cell count 13.8 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0)
CRP 88 mg/L (<5)
Total bilirubin 24 µmol/L (<20)
ALP 440 U/L (30-110)
GGT 210 U/L (<40)
ALT 31 U/L (<35)
Lipase 30 U/L (<60)
Ultrasound shows a gallbladder wall thickened to 5 mm, pericholecystic fluid and a stone impacted in the gallbladder neck. The common bile duct measures 5 mm, but bowel gas hides its distal end. She is given analgesia, IV fluids and IV antibiotics, and is admitted for laparoscopic cholecystectomy.
items.ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate investigation before surgery?
options: Repeat liver function tests in 6 weeks
items.explanation: The ultrasound and inflammatory markers already show acute calculous cholecystitis. The question is what the liver function tests mean for her. A stone stuck in the cystic duct on its own usually causes only mild LFT changes. Her ALP and GGT are about 4 to 5 times the upper limit, with a normal ALT and a bilirubin that is only slightly raised. This cholestatic pattern suggests a common bile duct stone causing partial or intermittent blockage. A 5 mm duct and a bilirubin of 24 make complete obstruction unlikely, but they do not rule out a stone, especially since the distal duct could not be seen. That puts her at intermediate risk of choledocholithiasis. Guidelines (eTG, ASGE) recommend non-invasive duct imaging before cholecystectomy, either MRCP or endoscopic ultrasound, or else an intraoperative cholangiogram. ERCP is kept for a duct stone that has been confirmed, or for cholangitis that needs urgent drainage.
why: ERCP carries a risk of pancreatitis, bleeding and perforation, so it is used to treat a confirmed duct stone or cholangitis needing drainage rather than to look for a stone in a woman who is not jaundiced and has a non-dilated duct.
A HIDA scan tests whether the cystic duct is patent to diagnose cholecystitis, which the ultrasound has already confirmed, and it does not show stones in the common bile duct well.
CT misses many bile duct stones because cholesterol stones are often isodense with bile, and it adds radiation without answering the question the LFTs raise.
Waiting 6 weeks to repeat the LFTs would leave a possible duct stone unchecked through cholecystectomy during this admission, risking a retained stone, cholangitis or pancreatitis.
