items.stem: A 21-year-old man comes to a suburban general practice with 16 hours of abdominal pain. It started overnight as a vague ache around his umbilicus and has since moved to the right lower abdomen. He has vomited twice, has not eaten since yesterday, and says the walk from the car park jolted the pain. He has no diarrhoea and no urinary symptoms. He has no past medical history and takes no regular medicines. His temperature is 38.1 °C, heart rate 106/min, blood pressure 122/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 18/min, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. He lies still on the couch. He is tender at McBurney's point with guarding, and pressing on the left iliac fossa causes pain on the right. Bowel sounds are present. A urine dipstick shows ketones 1+ and is negative for blood, leucocytes and nitrites. He asks if he can go home and see how he feels tomorrow.
items.ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Arrange an outpatient abdominal ultrasound and review the result tomorrow
Start oral amoxicillin with clavulanate and review him in 24 hours
Withhold all analgesia until a surgeon has examined his abdomen
Give analgesia, keep nil by mouth and arrange same-day hospital referral
Request faecal calprotectin and refer him to a gastroenterologist
items.explanation: This young man most likely has acute appendicitis. He has periumbilical pain that has moved to the right iliac fossa, anorexia, vomiting, fever, tachycardia, pain when jolted, guarding at McBurney's point and a positive Rovsing's sign. A normal urine dipstick does not rule it out. When appendicitis is suspected in general practice, he needs same-day transfer to an emergency department or surgical unit. The GP should phone a handover, keep him nil by mouth in case he needs theatre, give adequate analgesia, record his allergies and arrange safe transport. Giving analgesia does not hide the diagnosis or delay it. If the diagnosis is confirmed, antibiotics are given in hospital under eTG guidance, alongside appendicectomy or, for some patients, supervised non-operative care. Sending him home raises the risk of perforation, peritonitis and abscess.
why: An outpatient scan with review the next day delays surgical assessment in a febrile, tachycardic patient with localised peritonism, and a normal scan would not exclude appendicitis.
Treating suspected appendicitis with oral antibiotics in the community, without imaging or surgical review, can mask a progressing or perforating appendix and does not follow eTG advice.
Withholding pain relief is outdated, because analgesia does not reduce diagnostic accuracy and leaving pain untreated causes avoidable suffering.
Ileocaecal Crohn's disease is unlikely after a 16-hour illness with no diarrhoea, weight loss or bleeding, and an elective gastroenterology referral would miss a surgical emergency.

items.stem: A 71-year-old woman comes to her general practitioner because of 6 weeks of yellow eyes, generalised itch, dark urine and pale stools. She also has a dull epigastric ache that goes through to her back, poor appetite and a 6 kg weight loss. Type 2 diabetes was diagnosed 8 months ago and she takes metformin. She has a 45 pack-year smoking history. Her temperature is 36.8°C, pulse is 82/min and blood pressure is 134/78 mm Hg. She has scleral icterus and excoriations on her forearms. A smooth, non-tender mass is palpable below the right costal margin. Results: total bilirubin 164 µmol/L (reference less than 20), ALP 540 U/L (30–110), GGT 690 U/L (less than 38), ALT 118 U/L (less than 35), INR 1.2, white cell count 7.1 x10^9/L, CA 19-9 860 U/mL (less than 37). A pancreatic-protocol CT shows a 26 mm hypoattenuating mass in the pancreatic head with dilated common bile and pancreatic ducts, no vascular involvement and no liver metastases.
items.ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Urgent referral to a hepatobiliary surgical unit
Endoscopic retrograde cholangiography with stent insertion
Endoscopic ultrasound-guided fine-needle biopsy of the mass
Magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography of the biliary tree
Repeat CA 19-9 and liver function tests in four weeks
items.explanation: This woman has obstructive jaundice. She has a conjugated, cholestatic picture with ALP and GGT raised far more than ALT, pale stools, dark urine and itch. She also has a palpable non-tender gallbladder (Courvoisier's sign), weight loss, back pain, new-onset diabetes, heavy smoking, a CA 19-9 of 860 and a pancreatic head mass with a double duct sign. This is pancreatic head adenocarcinoma until proven otherwise. The CT shows no vascular involvement and no metastases, so the tumour looks resectable, and surgery is the only potential cure. The Australian optimal care pathway for pancreatic cancer says a GP who suspects pancreatic cancer should refer the patient urgently to a specialist centre with a hepatopancreatobiliary multidisciplinary team, to be seen within 2 weeks. That team decides on further staging, tissue sampling, biliary drainage and timing of surgery. She is afebrile with a normal white cell count, so there is no cholangitis needing emergency drainage or antibiotics.
why: Routine biliary stenting before resection raises infective and surgical complications, and it is only needed for cholangitis, long delays to surgery or neoadjuvant therapy, which the specialist team decides.
A tissue diagnosis is not required before resecting a lesion that looks resectable on imaging; biopsy is arranged by the specialist team, for example before neoadjuvant or palliative chemotherapy.
The pancreatic-protocol CT has already shown the cause and the level of obstruction, so MRCP adds delay without changing the need for specialist referral.
Watching and repeating tests delays the only potentially curative treatment, and CA 19-9 trends do not replace imaging and specialist assessment.

items.stem: A 68-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department after vomiting dark, coffee-ground material three times this morning. She has had black, sticky stools for 3 days. She has knee osteoarthritis and has taken naproxen 500 mg twice daily for 2 months. She also takes aspirin 100 mg daily because of a previous transient ischaemic attack. She does not drink alcohol. On arrival, her pulse is 106/min, blood pressure 112/70 mm Hg (usually 145/85 mm Hg), respirations 18/min, SpO2 97% on room air and temperature 36.8 °C. There are no stigmata of chronic liver disease. The abdomen is soft with mild epigastric tenderness and no guarding. Rectal examination shows melaena. Two large-bore cannulas are inserted and 500 mL of crystalloid is given. Her pulse falls to 92/min and her blood pressure rises to 124/74 mm Hg. Haemoglobin is 97 g/L (baseline 131 g/L), platelets 302 x10^9/L, INR 1.0, urea 13.9 mmol/L, creatinine 81 µmol/L, albumin 39 g/L and bilirubin 9 µmol/L. Gastroscopy is booked for the next morning.
items.ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate drug to give now?
items.explanation: This woman has a non-variceal upper GI bleed, most likely from a peptic ulcer caused by naproxen and aspirin together. She has coffee-ground vomiting, melaena, a 34 g/L fall in haemoglobin and a urea raised out of proportion to her creatinine. She has responded to fluids. She drinks no alcohol, has no stigmata of liver disease, and her platelets, INR, albumin and bilirubin are normal, so varices are unlikely. Her Glasgow-Blatchford score is high, so she needs admission and gastroscopy within 24 hours. Her haemoglobin is above the restrictive transfusion threshold (below 70 g/L, or below 80 g/L with cardiovascular disease), so she does not need red cells. eTG and the NSW ACI guidelines recommend an IV proton pump inhibitor (for example, pantoprazole 80 mg IV) while she waits for endoscopy. Before endoscopy it reduces the number of high-risk stigmata seen and the need for endoscopic therapy. After endoscopic haemostasis of a high-risk ulcer, high-dose IV PPI lowers the risk of rebleeding. The naproxen should be stopped for good. The decision on aspirin is made with gastroenterology, and it is usually restarted within days.
why: Terlipressin is used for suspected variceal bleeding, and she has no alcohol use, no liver stigmata and normal liver function and coagulation results.
Tranexamic acid does not reduce death from GI bleeding and increases venous thromboembolism (HALT-IT trial), so guidelines advise against using it.
Prophylactic antibiotics such as ceftriaxone lower infection and mortality rates in variceal bleeding in cirrhosis, not in non-variceal ulcer bleeding.
Vitamin K reverses warfarin or treats a deficiency-related coagulopathy, and her INR is normal and she takes no vitamin K antagonist.

items.stem:
A 64-year-old man presents to the emergency department with a painful, swollen right knee that came on suddenly overnight. Two years ago he had an attack in his left big toe that settled on its own. He has hypertension and stage 4 chronic kidney disease. He takes amlodipine, irbesartan and furosemide, and has no drug allergies. He recalls no injury. His temperature is 37.2 °C, pulse 88/min and blood pressure 148/86 mm Hg. The right knee is hot, red and tensely swollen with a large effusion, and the skin is intact. Investigations show:
Serum creatinine 245 µmol/L (60–110)
eGFR 23 mL/min/1.73 m² (>90)
Serum urate 0.52 mmol/L (0.20–0.42)
CRP 64 mg/L (<5)
Synovial fluid: white cell count 22 000 ×10^6/L with 80% neutrophils; needle-shaped, negatively birefringent intracellular crystals; Gram stain shows no organisms; culture pending.
items.ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment for this attack?
items.explanation: The aspirate shows needle-shaped, negatively birefringent monosodium urate crystals, so this is an acute flare of gout. He is afebrile with a negative Gram stain. An NSAID, low-dose colchicine and a corticosteroid work about equally well for a flare, so the choice depends on comorbidities. This man has severe chronic kidney disease (eGFR 23) and takes an angiotensin receptor blocker and a loop diuretic. That makes an NSAID unsafe, and colchicine can build up to toxic levels. A short course of oral prednisolone (eTG) is the safest effective option. Intra-articular corticosteroid is another option, but only once infection is reasonably excluded, and the culture is still pending. Culture must be followed to its final report, because crystals do not rule out coexisting infection. Allopurinol is not used to treat the attack itself. Antibiotics are not indicated when the patient is afebrile, the Gram stain is negative, the synovial count is below 50 000 and urate crystals are present.
why: Allopurinol is urate-lowering therapy for long-term prevention; it does not treat a flare and is started later, at a low dose for his eGFR, with flare prophylaxis.
Colchicine is cleared by the kidneys and builds up in severe chronic kidney disease, causing toxicity such as diarrhoea, myopathy and bone marrow suppression, so a corticosteroid is the safer choice.
An NSAID given with an angiotensin receptor blocker and a diuretic (the 'triple whammy') in someone with an eGFR of 23 risks acute kidney injury and hyperkalaemia.

Empirical antibiotics for septic arthritis are not needed: he is afebrile, the Gram stain is negative, the synovial white cell count is below 50 000 and urate crystals are present, though the culture should still be followed up.

items.stem: A 63-year-old man is brought to the emergency department with 3 days of right upper quadrant pain, fever with rigors and yellow eyes. Today his wife noticed he was muddled. He has untreated gallstones and type 2 diabetes treated with metformin. On arrival he is jaundiced and disoriented to time. Temperature is 39.2 °C, pulse 122/min, blood pressure 84/50 mm Hg, respiratory rate 24/min and SpO2 95% on room air. The right upper quadrant is tender. Results: total bilirubin 104 µmol/L (reference <20), conjugated bilirubin 82 µmol/L, ALP 438 U/L (30–110), GGT 590 U/L (<50), ALT 112 U/L (<40), lipase 52 U/L (<60), white cell count 19.1 x10^9/L (4.0–11.0), creatinine 139 µmol/L (60–110), INR 1.2 and venous lactate 3.8 mmol/L (<2.0). Ultrasound shows gallbladder calculi with a 3 mm wall and a common bile duct of 12 mm containing a distal shadowing calculus. Blood cultures are taken, and he is given IV amoxicillin, IV gentamicin and 30 mL/kg of crystalloid. His blood pressure is now 98/60 mm Hg.
items.ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
items.explanation: This man has Reynolds' pentad: jaundice, right upper quadrant pain, fever, confusion and hypotension. Under the Tokyo Guidelines 2018 this is severe (grade III) acute cholangitis, because he has neurological and cardiovascular dysfunction. It is caused by a stone in a dilated common bile duct, with a cholestatic liver test pattern, and he also has sepsis with hypoperfusion (lactate 3.8 mmol/L and acute kidney injury). The eTG and the ACSQHC Sepsis Clinical Care Standard say to take blood cultures, give IV antibiotics within 60 minutes (amoxicillin plus gentamicin for biliary sepsis) and give fluids, all of which has been done. Antibiotics alone cannot clear pus from a blocked duct. Once he has been resuscitated, he needs urgent source control by decompressing the bile duct with ERCP (sphincterotomy and stone extraction, or a stent if he is too unstable), and his care should be escalated to ICU. Cholecystectomy should follow once he has recovered, ideally during the same admission. A normal lipase and a thin gallbladder wall make gallstone pancreatitis and acute cholecystitis unlikely.
why: Wrong: cholecystectomy removes the gallbladder but does not clear the stone blocking the common bile duct, and operating on a septic, hypotensive patient is high risk. It is planned after the duct has been cleared and he has recovered.
Wrong: ultrasound has already shown a dilated duct with a stone in it, so MRCP would only delay drainage in a deteriorating septic patient.

Wrong: cholecystostomy drains the gallbladder, not the blocked common bile duct. It is used for acute cholecystitis in unfit patients, whereas percutaneous transhepatic biliary drainage is the fallback if ERCP fails.
Wrong: delaying drainage by 72 hours is acceptable only in mild cholangitis that responds to antibiotics. In severe cholangitis with hypotension and confusion, this delay increases the risk of death.

items.stem: A 67-year-old retired electrician is reviewed on day 3 of admission to the general surgical ward. He came in with 2 days of constant left iliac fossa pain, loose stools and a temperature of 38.4 °C. On admission, CT abdomen and pelvis with intravenous contrast showed multiple sigmoid diverticula and a 5 cm segment of sigmoid wall thickening with pericolic fat stranding. There was no abscess, extraluminal gas, fistula or obstruction. He was treated with intravenous antibiotics, fluids and paracetamol. He is now afebrile, eating normally and has minimal pain, and he has been switched to oral amoxicillin-clavulanate. He has hypertension treated with perindopril. He has never had any lower bowel investigation and did not return his last two national bowel screening kits. There is no family history of bowel disease. Temperature is 36.8 °C, pulse 72/min and blood pressure 130/80 mm Hg. His abdomen is soft, with mild left iliac fossa tenderness and no guarding. Haemoglobin is 141 g/L (130–180), white cell count 9.2 x10^9/L (4.0–11.0) and CRP 34 mg/L (<5). He is to be discharged today.
items.ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate follow-up investigation?
options: CT abdomen and pelvis in 48 hours
items.explanation: This man has CT-confirmed acute uncomplicated sigmoid diverticulitis and is getting better on treatment. CT cannot reliably tell inflamed diverticular wall thickening from a sigmoid carcinoma. He is 67, has never had his colon examined and has not done his bowel screening, so cancer in the thickened segment has to be excluded. Colonoscopy should be done once the inflammation has settled, usually about 6 weeks after recovery. CT colonography or flexible sigmoidoscopy are alternatives if colonoscopy is unsuitable. Scoping during acute inflammation is avoided because inflating the bowel with air and passing the scope through the inflamed segment risks perforation. A repeat CT is only needed if he fails to improve within 48 to 72 hours or gets worse. Tumour markers such as CEA are not used to diagnose or screen for colorectal cancer. A faecal immunochemical test is a screening tool for people without symptoms. It cannot replace looking directly at a segment that CT has already shown to be abnormal.
why: A repeat CT is only indicated if he does not improve within 48 to 72 hours or gets worse, and he is clearly improving.
Colonoscopy during or just after acute diverticulitis risks perforating the inflamed colon and is harder to interpret while the inflammation persists, so it should be delayed.
CEA is not sensitive or specific enough to diagnose or exclude colorectal cancer and is used only to monitor known disease.
A faecal immunochemical test is a screening test for people without symptoms and cannot exclude cancer in a sigmoid segment that CT has already shown to be abnormal.

items.stem:
A 29-year-old woman who is a primary school teacher comes to her general practitioner with a 5-month history of crampy lower abdominal pain and loose stools. She opens her bowels three to four times a day, mostly in the morning, with urgency, and the pain eases after defecation. She is bloated most afternoons. She has had no rectal bleeding or weight loss, and she does not wake at night to open her bowels. She has not travelled overseas. No family members have bowel disease. She takes no regular medicines. Her temperature is 36.7°C, pulse 76/min, blood pressure 114/70 mm Hg and BMI 23 kg/m2. The abdomen is soft, with mild left iliac fossa tenderness and no masses. Rectal examination is normal. Investigations show:
Haemoglobin 131 g/L (115–165)
Ferritin 62 µg/L (30–300)
C-reactive protein 3 mg/L (<5)
Total IgA 2.0 g/L (0.7–4.0)
Tissue transglutaminase IgA 1 U/mL (<7)
Stool microscopy, culture and PCR: no pathogens detected
items.ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate next investigation?
items.explanation: This young woman has symptoms that fit irritable bowel syndrome with diarrhoea. She has recurrent lower abdominal pain that eases after defecation, a change in stool frequency and form, and bloating. She has no red flags: no rectal bleeding, weight loss, nocturnal symptoms, anaemia, fever, mass or family history. Her full blood count, ferritin and CRP are normal. Coeliac serology is negative and valid, because her total IgA is normal. Stool tests show no infection. The main serious condition left to exclude is inflammatory bowel disease, because loose stools with urgency in a young adult can be early Crohn's disease or ulcerative colitis, and a normal CRP does not rule it out. The first-line test before making a positive diagnosis of IBS is faecal calprotectin, as recommended in eTG and Australian gastroenterology practice. It is cheap and non-invasive. A result below 50 µg/g makes IBD unlikely and avoids colonoscopy. A raised result calls for gastroenterology referral and colonoscopy. Colonoscopy is wrong at this stage because it is invasive and kept for red flags or a raised calprotectin. Duodenal biopsy is wrong because a negative tTG-IgA with normal total IgA makes coeliac disease very unlikely. A lactose hydrogen breath test is wrong because it does not exclude IBD, and a trial of cutting out dairy is the preferred first step. A faecal immunochemical test is wrong because in Australia it is a screening test for people aged 45 to 74 without symptoms, not a way to assess a symptomatic young adult.
why: Colonoscopy is invasive and kept for red flags or a raised calprotectin, neither of which she has yet.
Duodenal biopsy is not needed because a negative tTG-IgA with a normal total IgA makes coeliac disease very unlikely.
A lactose hydrogen breath test cannot exclude inflammatory bowel disease, and a trial of avoiding dairy is preferred over formal breath testing.
A faecal immunochemical test is a population screening tool for people aged 45 to 74 without symptoms and is not used to investigate symptomatic young adults in Australia.

items.stem: A 64-year-old woman, a retired pharmacist, sees her general practitioner with 8 days of cough. The cough began after a coryzal illness and is now productive of rust-coloured sputum, with fevers and right-sided pleuritic chest pain. She has hypertension treated with amlodipine. She has never smoked and has no drug allergies. Temperature is 38.4 °C, pulse 102/min, respiratory rate 24/min, blood pressure 112/68 mmHg and SpO2 95% on room air. She is alert and oriented, with an abbreviated mental test score of 10/10. There is dullness, bronchial breathing and crackles at the right base. Urgent blood results are: white cell count 15.1 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), neutrophils 12.4 x10^9/L (2.0-7.5), urea 6.8 mmol/L (2.5-8.0), creatinine 74 µmol/L (45-90), sodium 135 mmol/L (135-145) and C-reactive protein 162 mg/L (less than 5). A chest X-ray shows right lower lobe consolidation.
items.ask: Which of the following is this patient's CURB-65 score?
items.explanation: CURB-65 gives one point for each of five criteria: new confusion; urea above 7 mmol/L; respiratory rate of 30/min or more; systolic BP below 90 mmHg or diastolic BP of 60 mmHg or less; and age 65 years or older. This patient meets none of them. She is alert with an AMTS of 10/10. Her urea of 6.8 mmol/L is below the CURB-65 cut-off of 7, even though it sits near the top of the laboratory range. Her respiratory rate of 24/min is high, but below 30. Her BP of 112/68 mmHg is above both thresholds. At 64, she is just under the age criterion. Her score is 0, which means low-severity pneumonia. In a stable patient with SpO2 of 92% or more, this supports oral treatment at home. eTG recommends amoxicillin 1 g 8-hourly for 5 days, with review at 48 hours and a safety-net plan. Clinical judgement still applies alongside the score. Tachycardia, neutrophilia and a high CRP show a systemic inflammatory response, but they are not CURB-65 criteria.
why: A score of 1 would need one criterion. Students reach it by scoring her respiratory rate of 24/min (the cut-off is 30 or more) or by counting her age of 64 as 65 or older.

A score of 2 would need two criteria. Students reach it by wrongly scoring the urea of 6.8 mmol/L (the cut-off is above 7) and the raised respiratory rate, or by counting the tachycardia, which is not part of CURB-65.
A score of 3 would mean high-severity pneumonia needing hospital admission. This woman is alert, normotensive, younger than 65 and has a urea below 7 mmol/L.
A score of 4 would need four criteria such as confusion and hypotension, and she has none of them. The high white cell count and CRP do not count towards the score.

items.stem: A 46-year-old man comes to his general practitioner with 3 weeks of sharp anal pain. It starts with each bowel motion and lasts about 2 hours afterwards, and there is a small amount of bright red blood on the toilet paper. The pain began after a week of hard stools while he was driving long-haul freight. For the past 2 weeks he has taken psyllium daily, increased his fluid intake, used warm sitz baths and applied lidocaine gel. His stools are now soft, but the pain has improved only slightly. He has hypertension treated with perindopril and erectile dysfunction treated with tadalafil 5 mg daily. Temperature is 36.7 °C, pulse 84/min and blood pressure 134/82 mmHg. With a chaperone present, inspection shows a single linear tear in the posterior midline of the anal margin with clean, soft edges. There is no sentinel tag, induration or swelling. He is too tender for a digital rectal examination, so it is not done.
items.ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Glyceryl trinitrate 0.2% applied to the anal margin
Diltiazem 2% applied to the anal margin
Hydrocortisone with cinchocaine applied to the anal margin
Botulinum toxin injected into the internal sphincter
items.explanation: This man has an acute primary anal fissure. The fissure is in the posterior midline, has soft edges and no sentinel tag, and has been present for less than 6 weeks. The pain causes spasm of the internal anal sphincter, which reduces blood flow to the posterior anoderm and stops the tear healing. His stools are now soft, but he is still in pain after 2 weeks of conservative care, so the eTG recommends adding a topical drug that relaxes the sphincter. The two choices are glyceryl trinitrate 0.2% and diltiazem 2%. GTN is contraindicated in anyone taking a phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitor. He takes tadalafil daily, and its long half-life means simply skipping doses would not make GTN safe. Topical diltiazem 2% twice daily for 6 to 8 weeks heals about as many fissures as GTN and causes fewer headaches. He should keep using fibre, fluids and sitz baths. If the fissure becomes chronic, he should be referred to a surgeon. Any bleeding that continues after the fissure heals needs investigation.
why: GTN with a phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitor such as daily tadalafil can cause severe, possibly fatal hypotension, so it is contraindicated for him.
Codeine causes constipation, and hard stools would reopen the fissure and keep the pain and spasm going, so it should be avoided.
A topical corticosteroid with local anaesthetic does not relax the sphincter and does not speed fissure healing, and long-term use thins the perianal skin.

Botulinum toxin is a specialist second-line treatment for chronic fissures, or for fissures that have not responded to topical sphincter relaxants, so it is not the next step for an acute fissure that has not yet been treated with one.

items.stem: A 70-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department by ambulance 1 hour after sudden, severe, tearing chest pain that radiated between her shoulder blades while she was gardening. She fainted briefly when the pain began. She has hypertension and smokes 20 cigarettes a day. Her medicines are perindopril and amlodipine. On arrival, her blood pressure is 168/94 mmHg in the left arm and 136/80 mmHg in the right arm, pulse is 104/min and SpO2 is 96% on room air. An early diastolic murmur is heard at the right sternal edge. The ECG shows sinus tachycardia with left ventricular hypertrophy and no ST elevation. CT angiography shows an intimal flap that starts just above the aortic valve and extends into the descending thoracic aorta, with a moderate high-attenuation pericardial effusion. Twenty minutes later she becomes pale and confused. Her blood pressure is 82/54 mmHg, pulse is 124/min, jugular venous pressure is raised 6 cm and her heart sounds are muffled. Two large-bore cannulas are in place and crossmatched blood is available.
items.ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Immediate open repair in the operating theatre
items.explanation: This woman has an acute Stanford type A aortic dissection, because the flap starts in the ascending aorta. She now has the complication most likely to kill her: cardiac tamponade from bleeding into the pericardium. The high-attenuation (blood-density) pericardial effusion, low blood pressure, raised JVP, muffled heart sounds and confusion are the Beck triad with shock. Type A dissection is a surgical emergency. When it is complicated by haemopericardium and shock, the 2024 ESC guidelines and the Heart Foundation/CSANZ guidance used in Australia say she should go straight to theatre for open replacement of the ascending aorta, with blood products given while she is moved. Draining the pericardium only fixes the tamponade, and the blood pressure it restores can make the aorta bleed again. Lowering the heart rate or blood pressure is wrong while she is hypotensive. Anticoagulants make the bleeding worse.
why: Metoprolol is the anti-impulse drug used for a dissection with high blood pressure, but in tamponade and shock it removes the compensating tachycardia and can cause cardiac arrest.

Percutaneous pericardiocentesis raises the blood pressure, which can restart bleeding from the aorta into the pericardium, so it is kept for controlled, small-volume drainage only when theatre cannot be reached in time.
Endovascular stent-graft repair is used for complicated type B (descending) dissection and cannot treat a tear in the ascending aorta just above the valve that is bleeding into the pericardium.
Heparin speeds up bleeding into the pericardium and the false lumen; giving antithrombotics because of the low-grade suspicion of a coronary syndrome is a known harmful error in dissection.

items.stem: A 64-year-old man walks into his general practice without an appointment. He has had chest discomfort for 40 minutes. It began while he was gardening and has not eased with rest. He describes a heavy band across his chest that spreads to his neck and both shoulders, and he feels nauseated and clammy. For the past 2 weeks he has had similar but brief tightness when walking uphill, which settled within minutes of stopping. He has type 2 diabetes and hypertension, and takes metformin and perindopril. He smoked for 35 years and stopped 2 years ago. He is pale and sweaty. Temperature is 36.6°C, pulse 92/min and regular, blood pressure 148/86 mmHg in both arms, respiratory rate 20/min and SpO2 97% on room air. The heart sounds are dual with no murmur, and the chest is clear. Both calves are soft and non-tender.
items.ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate next investigation?
items.explanation: This man has ongoing ischaemic-type chest pain at rest. The pain is heavy, spreads to the neck and shoulders, and comes with nausea and sweating. It follows 2 weeks of new exertional angina, and he has several risk factors: diabetes, hypertension and a long smoking history. This is a possible acute coronary syndrome. Australian guidelines (National Heart Foundation/CSANZ ACS guidelines, eTG Cardiovascular, and the ACSQHC Acute Coronary Syndromes Clinical Care Standard) say a 12-lead ECG should be recorded and read within 10 minutes of first medical contact. It is the single test that sorts the patient into the right pathway straight away. New ST elevation in two or more contiguous leads (or LBBB with ongoing symptoms) means STEMI. In that case, call 000 for ambulance transfer for primary PCI or fibrinolysis, and do not wait for any blood result. If the ECG does not show STEMI, the patient still needs urgent transfer for serial troponins. Equal arm pressures, no aortic regurgitation murmur, normal oxygen saturation and normal calves make aortic dissection and PE less likely, so the ECG comes first. Troponin takes time to rise, and a negative early result cannot rule out infarction, so it must not delay reperfusion. A chest radiograph does not diagnose acute coronary syndrome and would hold up transfer. A D-dimer is used for low-risk suspected PE, and this history does not suggest PE. CT coronary angiography is for stable, low-to-intermediate-risk chest pain, not for ongoing pain at rest.
why: Troponin may still be normal early in infarction and must never delay reperfusion, so it comes after the ECG and should not hold up transfer.
A chest radiograph does not diagnose acute coronary syndrome and would delay the test that decides immediate management.
A D-dimer is used for low-risk suspected pulmonary embolism, and this man has ischaemic-type pain with no PE risk factors, normal SpO2 and normal calves.
CT coronary angiography is for stable, low-to-intermediate-risk chest pain and is not appropriate for ongoing ischaemic pain at rest.

items.stem:
A 24-year-old woman presents to her general practitioner with 3 months of tiredness and breathlessness when climbing stairs at the café she manages. Her cycles are regular every 28 days. Over the past year her periods have lengthened to 7 days. On heavy days she changes a super pad every 2 hours, floods overnight and passes large clots. She has no bruising, nosebleeds or change in bowel habit. She and her partner stopped using condoms 2 months ago and hope to conceive within the next year. Her only medicine is folic acid 0.5 mg daily. Her blood pressure is 114/72 mmHg, pulse 98/min and temperature 36.7 °C. She has conjunctival pallor. Abdominal, speculum and bimanual examinations are normal. Investigations show:
Haemoglobin 92 g/L (115–165)
MCV 71 fL (80–100)
Platelets 438 x10^9/L (150–400)
Ferritin 5 µg/L (30–300)
CRP 3 mg/L (<5)
TSH 1.9 mIU/L (0.4–4.0)
Urine β-hCG negative
items.ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
options: Oral iron and a levonorgestrel intrauterine device
Oral iron and the combined oral contraceptive pill
Intravenous iron and tranexamic acid during menses
Oral iron and tranexamic acid during menses
Oral iron and referral for diagnostic hysteroscopy
items.explanation: She has iron deficiency anaemia (Hb 92 g/L, MCV 71 fL, reactive thrombocytosis, ferritin 5 µg/L with a normal CRP) caused by heavy menstrual bleeding. Management must replace the deficit and treat the cause. Under eTG and the National Blood Authority guidance, oral iron is first line in a stable patient who has not yet tried it. Daily or alternate-day dosing works, and alternate-day dosing may improve absorption and tolerance. Recheck the FBC in 2 to 4 weeks (expect a rise of about 20 g/L by 3 to 4 weeks) and continue for about 3 months after the Hb normalises. The levonorgestrel IUD is usually first line for heavy menstrual bleeding (ACSQHC Clinical Care Standard), but it and the combined pill both prevent pregnancy, and she is trying to conceive. Tranexamic acid (1 g orally three to four times daily for up to 5 days during heavy bleeding) is a non-hormonal option. It reduces menstrual loss by about 40 to 50%, is taken only while bleeding and does not affect fertility. She has a normal pelvic examination and no risk factors for endometrial pathology, so invasive investigation is not needed yet. B: the LNG-IUD is contraceptive and does not suit a woman trying to conceive. C: the combined pill prevents ovulation and conception, so it goes against her plan for pregnancy. D: IV iron is for oral intolerance, failure, malabsorption or a need for rapid repletion, and none of these applies. E: hysteroscopy is for women aged 45 or older, those with risk factors for endometrial hyperplasia or cancer, or those whose medical treatment has failed.
why: Wrong: the levonorgestrel IUD is contraceptive, so it conflicts with her wish to conceive, even though it is often first line for heavy menstrual bleeding.
Wrong: the combined oral contraceptive pill suppresses ovulation and prevents the pregnancy she is trying for.
Wrong: intravenous iron is reserved for oral intolerance, failure, malabsorption or a need for rapid repletion, and she is stable and has not tried oral iron.
Wrong: hysteroscopy is not indicated in a 24-year-old with a normal pelvic examination, no endometrial risk factors and no failed medical treatment.

items.stem: A 72-year-old woman comes to a rural emergency department with a racing heart and mild central chest tightness. Both started suddenly 70 minutes ago while she was watching television. She has never had this before. She has hypertension treated with perindopril and type 2 diabetes treated with metformin. Her pulse is 138/min and irregularly irregular, blood pressure 132/84 mm Hg, respiratory rate 18/min, SpO2 97% on room air and temperature 36.7 °C. Her chest is clear and she has no peripheral oedema. A 12-lead ECG shows atrial fibrillation with a ventricular rate of about 140/min, a narrow QRS and no ST-segment or T-wave change. Blood was taken on arrival, 75 minutes after symptom onset: high-sensitivity troponin T 9 ng/L (99th centile 14), creatinine 84 µmol/L (eGFR 66 mL/min/1.73 m^2), potassium 4.4 mmol/L and TSH 2.1 mIU/L (reference 0.4 to 4.0).
items.ask: Which of the following is the most accurate interpretation of her troponin result?
options: Myocardial infarction cannot yet be ruled out at this point
Acute myocardial infarction is excluded by this single value
Rate-related type 2 myocardial infarction is confirmed
Chronic myocardial injury from renal impairment is shown
Unstable angina is excluded by this normal value
items.explanation: Her high-sensitivity troponin T of 9 ng/L is below the 99th centile, but it was taken only 75 minutes after her symptoms began. Troponin takes time to rise after myocardial injury, so one value taken this soon can miss an evolving infarction. The NHFA/CSANZ ACS guideline accepts a single-sample rule-out only when the hs-troponin T is very low (below about 5 ng/L) and symptoms started more than 3 hours before the sample. Otherwise, the test is repeated using an accelerated protocol (usually at 2 hours, or at 1 hour with validated algorithms) and the change between the two values is assessed. Her chest tightness, age, hypertension and diabetes make ACS an important alternative cause and a possible trigger for her AF. So this result does not yet rule out myocardial infarction, and she needs a repeat troponin while her AF is rate-controlled. A: A value below the 99th centile does not rule out infarction when it is taken less than 3 hours after onset and is above the very-low threshold. C: A type 2 infarction needs troponin above the 99th centile with a rise or fall, and her value is normal. D: Chronic myocardial injury means a stable troponin above the 99th centile, and her eGFR of 66 does not explain any rise. E: Troponin is normal in unstable angina by definition, so a normal value cannot exclude it.
why: Correct: a single hs-troponin T below the 99th centile but above the very-low rule-out level, taken under 3 hours after onset, cannot rule out infarction, so a repeat is needed.
Wrong: a type 2 infarction needs troponin above the 99th centile with a rise or fall, and her value is normal.
Wrong: chronic myocardial injury means a stable troponin above the 99th centile, and her near-normal renal function does not explain any rise.
Wrong: troponin is normal in unstable angina by definition, so a normal value cannot exclude it.

items.stem:
A 74-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with 2 days of colicky abdominal pain, distension and repeated vomiting, which is now faeculent. She has passed no flatus for 24 hours. She has known gallstones and has never had abdominal surgery. Her medicines are perindopril, metformin and ibuprofen. Her temperature is 37.2°C, pulse is 108/min, blood pressure is 112/68 mmHg and respiratory rate is 16/min. Her mucous membranes are dry. Her abdomen is distended, with high-pitched bowel sounds and no peritonism. An abdominal X-ray shows dilated small bowel loops with multiple air-fluid levels. Venous blood results:
pH 7.43 (7.32 to 7.42)
pCO2 46 mmHg (41 to 51)
Bicarbonate 30 mmol/L (22 to 28)
Base excess +6 mmol/L (-2 to +2)
Lactate 1.8 mmol/L (less than 2.0)
Sodium 136 mmol/L (135 to 145)
Potassium 2.8 mmol/L (3.5 to 5.2)
Chloride 93 mmol/L (95 to 110)
Creatinine 128 µmol/L (her baseline is 78)
items.ask: Which of the following best describes these blood gas findings?
options: Respiratory acidosis with renal bicarbonate retention
Lactic acidosis from metformin and kidney injury
Normal anion gap acidosis from small bowel losses
Metabolic alkalosis from gastric acid and volume loss
Mixed high anion gap acidosis and alkalosis
items.explanation: The pH is at the alkalaemic end, and bicarbonate (30 mmol/L) and base excess (+6) are both raised. That means the main problem is metabolic alkalosis. The low chloride (93 mmol/L) and low potassium (2.8 mmol/L) show it is hypochloraemic and hypokalaemic, the typical picture with vomiting. Losing gastric hydrochloric acid produces the alkalosis. Losing volume then keeps it going: it causes a prerenal acute kidney injury (creatinine 1.6 times her baseline) and switches on aldosterone, so the kidney holds on to bicarbonate and loses potassium. A venous pCO2 of 46 mmHg is within the normal range and fits mild respiratory compensation, not a primary respiratory problem. The anion gap is normal (136 - (93 + 30) = 13) and lactate is normal, so there is no hidden acidosis, although a normal lactate does not rule out bowel ischaemia. In practice she needs IV 0.9% sodium chloride with potassium chloride, magnesium checked, and her perindopril, metformin and ibuprofen withheld.
why: Wrong: a primary respiratory acidosis needs an acidaemic pH and a raised pCO2, but her pH is high and her venous pCO2 is normal, so the raised bicarbonate is the primary change.
Wrong: metformin and the kidney injury make this a tempting choice, but her lactate (1.8 mmol/L), anion gap (13) and pH are all normal, so there is no lactic acidosis.
Wrong: losing alkaline small bowel fluid can cause a normal anion gap acidosis, but her bicarbonate is raised and her pH is not acidaemic.
Wrong: with a normal anion gap of 13 and a normal lactate, there is no evidence of a second, high anion gap acidosis alongside the alkalosis.

items.stem: A 31-year-old woman comes to the emergency department with 3 days of tingling that started in her feet and has spread up to her waist. Over the same time her legs have become steadily weaker. Since this morning she has been unable to pass urine. She has had no back pain, fever, trauma or weight loss. Eighteen months ago she had 2 weeks of blurred vision and pain on moving her left eye, which got better without treatment. She takes no medicines. Temperature is 36.7 °C, pulse 80 beats/min, blood pressure 118/74 mm Hg and respiratory rate 16 breaths/min. Cranial nerve and upper limb examination is normal. Tone is increased in both legs. Hip flexion and ankle dorsiflexion are 3/5 on the left and 4/5 on the right. Knee and ankle reflexes are brisk, and both plantar responses are extensor. Pinprick sensation is reduced below the umbilicus. A bladder scan shows 900 mL. Full blood count and C-reactive protein are normal.
items.ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate next investigation?
options: Lumbar puncture for CSF oligoclonal bands
Nerve conduction studies of both lower limbs
Urgent MRI of the lumbosacral spine only
Urgent gadolinium-enhanced MRI of the whole spine
items.explanation: Both legs are weak with spastic tone, brisk reflexes and extensor plantars, so this is an upper motor neuron lesion. The arms and cranial nerves are normal, and there is a sensory level at the umbilicus (T10) with urinary retention, so the lesion is in the thoracic spinal cord. An acute myelopathy with a sensory level and loss of bladder control is cord compression until proven otherwise. The next step is an urgent MRI of the whole spine with gadolinium. Imaging the whole spine matters because a sensory level only gives the lowest possible level of the lesion, and there can be lesions at more than one level. The same scan separates a compressive cause (disc, tumour, abscess, haematoma) from an inflammatory myelitis. Her past episode of painful vision loss suggests optic neuritis, so this may be a second demyelinating attack (multiple sclerosis). A brain MRI is usually done at the same time. CSF and antibody tests come after imaging has ruled out compression.
why: CSF oligoclonal bands help confirm multiple sclerosis, but a lumbar puncture should not be done before imaging has ruled out cord compression, and it would delay the time-critical scan.

Nerve conduction studies look for a peripheral process such as Guillain-Barré syndrome, which causes floppy weakness with absent reflexes, not spastic weakness with brisk reflexes, extensor plantars and a truncal sensory level.
A lumbosacral scan only looks at the cauda equina and would miss the thoracic cord lesion suggested by upper motor neuron signs and a T10 sensory level.
Aquaporin-4 antibodies help tell neuromyelitis optica from multiple sclerosis, but the result takes days and does not rule out cord compression, so it is not the next investigation.

items.stem: A 44-year-old man is reviewed on the surgical ward at 08:00. He was admitted overnight with 26 hours of central abdominal pain that moved to the right iliac fossa, with anorexia and nausea. The emergency theatre list was full, so he is booked for laparoscopic appendicectomy this afternoon. He is fasting and receiving maintenance Hartmann's solution, and regular paracetamol is his only charted medicine. He has no past medical history and no allergies. His temperature is 37.6 °C, pulse 90/min, blood pressure 128/80 mm Hg, respiratory rate 16/min and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. He is tender at McBurney's point with localised guarding, and there is no generalised rigidity. White cell count is 14.1 x10^9/L (4.0–11.0), neutrophils 11.6 x10^9/L (2.0–7.5), CRP 52 mg/L (<5) and creatinine 80 µmol/L (60–110). CT of the abdomen with contrast shows a 10 mm appendix with an enhancing wall and periappendiceal fat stranding, with no appendicolith, free gas or collection.
items.ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management while he awaits surgery?
options: Repeat CT scan with oral contrast today
Withhold opioid analgesia until surgical review
items.explanation: This man has acute uncomplicated appendicitis. He has the classic migrating pain, McBurney's point tenderness, neutrophilia and a raised CRP, and his CT shows an inflamed appendix with no appendicolith, free gas or collection. He is stable and booked for appendicectomy, but there has already been a delay of many hours and he has had no antimicrobial cover. eTG (Antibiotic: Intra-abdominal infections, Appendicitis) advises starting empirical intravenous antibiotics when surgery for appendicitis is delayed. This treats the infection and lowers the risk of the appendix progressing to gangrene or perforation before theatre. Surgical prophylaxis is still given within 60 minutes before incision. The delay should also be flagged to the registrar. Percutaneous drainage is only for an appendiceal abscess, and he has none. Repeating the CT adds nothing, because the diagnosis is already confirmed. Treating him with antibiotics alone at home is not the standard for a patient who is booked for and agrees to surgery, and about 3 in 10 such patients need an appendicectomy within a year. Withholding pain relief is outdated: analgesia does not mask the signs of appendicitis or delay the diagnosis.
why: Wrong: percutaneous drainage treats an appendiceal abscess or collection, and his CT shows neither.
Wrong: the contrast CT has already confirmed uncomplicated appendicitis, so another scan delays treatment and adds radiation without changing management.

Wrong: treating with antibiotics alone at home is an alternative only after a shared decision, and about 3 in 10 patients still need an appendicectomy within a year; he is booked for and agreeable to surgery, the standard treatment.
Wrong: giving opioid analgesia does not mask the signs of appendicitis or worsen diagnostic accuracy, so leaving him in pain is not appropriate.

items.stem: A 20-hour-old girl is reviewed on the postnatal ward because the midwife reports that she has stopped feeding and started grunting. She was born vaginally at 39+2 weeks, weighing 3.4 kg, with Apgar scores of 8 and 9. She fed well for the first 12 hours. Her mother carried group B streptococcus and received intravenous benzylpenicillin 90 minutes before the birth. The membranes had ruptured 22 hours before delivery, and the mother's temperature in labour was 38.4 °C. On examination, the baby is lethargic and mottled. Temperature is 38.3 °C, pulse 184/min, respirations 72/min, systolic pressure 55 mmHg and oxygen saturation 92% on room air. Capillary refill time is 4 seconds. She has subcostal recession and grunting. Heart sounds are normal and the femoral pulses are palpable. Capillary glucose is 3.9 mmol/L. Intravenous access has been obtained, and antibiotics are about to be given.
items.ask: Which of the following investigations is most likely to confirm the diagnosis?
items.explanation: This term baby has early-onset neonatal sepsis with shock. She has a fever, tachycardia, tachypnoea, grunting, a capillary refill time of 4 seconds, mottling and lethargy. She also has four risk factors: maternal GBS carriage, intrapartum antibiotics given less than 4 hours before birth, membranes ruptured for 18 hours or more, and maternal fever in labour. A positive blood culture is the reference standard for confirming early-onset sepsis. It identifies the organism (most often GBS or E. coli) and its antibiotic sensitivities. Under the RCH Neonatal antimicrobial guidelines and Queensland Clinical Guidelines, at least 1 mL is taken before the first doses of benzylpenicillin and gentamicin, but antibiotics are not delayed to get it. The culture result and the baby's condition are then used to review antibiotics at 36 hours. CRP and procalcitonin are nonspecific markers that can support the diagnosis but cannot confirm it. Urine culture has little value in early-onset sepsis. A chest X-ray shows lung involvement but does not show what organism is causing it.
why: CRP takes 12 to 24 hours to rise and can be raised by non-infectious causes, so it helps to monitor or rule out infection but cannot confirm sepsis.
Procalcitonin rises normally in the first 48 hours of life, and it is not a confirmatory test in Australian neonatal sepsis guidelines.
Early-onset sepsis comes from maternal flora at birth, not from the urinary tract, so urine culture is not recommended in the first 72 hours and would rarely be positive.
A chest X-ray may show pneumonia, but GBS pneumonia can look the same as surfactant deficiency or transient tachypnoea, and the film cannot identify an organism.

items.stem: A 58-year-old woman who works as a hairdresser sees her general practitioner with 10 weeks of right neck pain. The pain runs down the back of her arm to her middle finger and is worse when she looks up. Eight weeks ago she started regular paracetamol and ibuprofen and a supervised physiotherapy program. The pain has eased only a little, and she still drops her hair dryer. She has no hand clumsiness, change in gait or bladder symptoms. She has hypertension treated with amlodipine. Temperature is 36.7 °C, pulse 74/min and regular, and blood pressure 134/80 mmHg. Right elbow extension and wrist flexion are 4-/5, the same as 8 weeks ago, and the right triceps reflex is reduced. Sensation is reduced over the right middle finger. Tone, coordination and the lower limb examination are normal, and Hoffmann's sign is absent. MRI of the neck shows severe right C6-7 foraminal stenosis compressing the right C7 nerve root, with a normal cord.
items.ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Same-day transfer to an emergency department
Outpatient referral to a spine surgeon
items.explanation: This is a right C7 radiculopathy from cervical spondylosis. The radicular pain runs to the middle finger and gets worse on neck extension. There is weakness of elbow extension and wrist flexion, a reduced triceps reflex and C7 sensory loss, and the MRI shows concordant C6-7 foraminal stenosis. Most cervical radiculopathy settles with analgesia, physiotherapy and modified activity. This patient has had 8 weeks of conservative treatment and still has an objective motor deficit, a matching MRI lesion and pain that limits her work. That combination warrants referral to a spine surgeon to assess her for decompression. Urgent assessment is not needed: there are no myelopathic symptoms, no upper motor neuron signs, her weakness is not getting worse and the cord is normal. She still needs safety netting to seek urgent review if weakness progresses, or if hand clumsiness, gait disturbance or bladder symptoms develop. Continuing physiotherapy alone delays treatment of a persisting motor deficit. Transfer to the emergency department is for myelopathy or rapidly progressive weakness. Carotid imaging investigates a TIA, which this fixed lower motor neuron deficit with radicular pain is not. A rigid collar long term is not recommended and causes stiffness and deconditioning.
why: Continuing physiotherapy alone and waiting 3 more months is wrong because she still has an objective motor deficit with a matching MRI lesion after 8 weeks of conservative care, so she needs a surgical opinion now.

Same-day emergency transfer is for suspected cord compression, myelopathy or rapidly progressive weakness, and she has none of these: there are no upper motor neuron signs, the cord is normal and her deficit is stable.
Carotid duplex ultrasonography is part of the workup for a TIA, but she has a fixed lower motor neuron deficit in one root pattern with radicular pain, not transient episodes of focal weakness.
Immobilising the neck in a rigid collar for weeks has no proven benefit in cervical radiculopathy and causes stiffness and muscle deconditioning.

items.stem: A 45-year-old woman is admitted from the emergency department of a regional hospital. She has had 2 days of colicky periumbilical pain and bilious vomiting, and she has passed no flatus. She has had two caesarean sections and an open appendicectomy. Adhesive small bowel obstruction is diagnosed. She is treated with nil by mouth, nasogastric decompression and intravenous fluids with added potassium. Eight hours later her pain is constant and severe despite intravenous morphine. Temperature is 38.1°C, pulse 126/min, blood pressure 104/66 mm Hg and respirations 22/min. The abdomen is distended, with localised tenderness and guarding in the right lower quadrant, and bowel sounds are reduced. Nasogastric output so far is 1.4 L. Leukocyte count is 16.2 x10^9/L (4.0 to 11.0). Venous lactate is 1.5 mmol/L (less than 2.0). CT of the abdomen with intravenous contrast shows a closed loop of small bowel with reduced wall enhancement and fluid in the mesentery.
items.ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
items.explanation: The most serious risk in adhesive small bowel obstruction is strangulation, where the bowel loses its blood supply and dies. This patient has the warning signs. Her pain has changed from colicky to constant and is not controlled by morphine. She has a fever, a rising heart rate, localised guarding and a raised white cell count. CT shows a closed loop with reduced wall enhancement and fluid in the mesentery. The WSES Bologna guidelines say that strangulation, a closed loop, peritonitis or ischaemia on CT are reasons to stop non-operative management and operate straight away. This lets the surgeon release the bowel and remove any dead segment before it perforates and causes sepsis. Lactate often rises only once bowel has already died, so a normal value does not exclude ischaemia and should not delay the operation. In a regional hospital this means calling the surgeon now and, if no one there can operate, arranging urgent transfer. Resuscitation and antibiotics should continue while this happens.
why: A water-soluble contrast challenge is used to predict which uncomplicated obstructions will settle without an operation, and it is not appropriate when CT shows strangulation.
Lactate rises late in bowel ischaemia, so waiting for a repeat value delays the operation while more bowel dies.
Conservative management for up to 72 hours is only for uncomplicated adhesive obstruction without signs of ischaemia, and continuing it here risks perforation.
Colonoscopic decompression treats large bowel problems such as sigmoid volvulus or pseudo-obstruction and cannot reach or relieve an obstructed small bowel loop.

items.stem: A 52-year-old woman presents to the emergency department 2 days after a day-surgery hysteroscopy and dilatation and curettage for heavy, irregular bleeding. Since yesterday evening she has had worsening lower abdominal pain, nausea and anorexia. The operation record describes a retroverted, bulky uterus and a view partly obscured by blood, and lists the procedure as uneventful. The histology report, released this morning, describes disordered proliferative endometrium with fragments of mature adipose tissue. She has type 2 diabetes treated with metformin, and her body mass index is 42 kg/m2. Her temperature is 38.2°C, pulse 104/min, blood pressure 132/80 mm Hg, respiratory rate 20/min and SpO2 97% on room air. The lower abdomen is tender with voluntary guarding but no rigidity, and bowel sounds are reduced. There is scant brown vaginal loss. White cell count is 15.6 x 10^9/L (4.0 to 11.0), C-reactive protein 148 mg/L (less than 5) and lactate 1.6 mmol/L (less than 2.0). Fluids, analgesia and antibiotics have been started.
items.ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate next investigation?
options: CT of the abdomen and pelvis with intravenous contrast
MRI of the pelvis with gadolinium
items.explanation: There should be no fat inside the uterus. Adipose tissue in the curettings means the curette went through the uterine wall into omentum, mesentery or bowel fat, so this is uterine perforation until proven otherwise. A perforation like this can injure bowel without anyone noticing, and the injury often shows itself days later. That fits this patient: fever, lower abdominal guarding, reduced bowel sounds and high inflammatory markers 2 days after surgery. She is haemodynamically stable, her lactate is normal and she has no generalised peritonitis, so there is time to image her before deciding on surgery. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis is the best test here. It can show free fluid, free gas, a collection or abscess, bowel wall thickening or a leak, and bleeding, and it is not limited by her body habitus. A senior gynaecologist and the general surgeons should be told now. If the CT shows a visceral injury, or if she deteriorates, she needs laparoscopy or laparotomy. Erect chest X-ray: free gas under the diaphragm is not reliable after recent uterine instrumentation, and the film shows nothing about the pelvis, collections or bowel. Transvaginal ultrasound: it may show free fluid or a pelvic collection, but obesity limits the views and it cannot reliably find bowel injury or free gas. MRI of the pelvis: it is slow, less available urgently, covers only the pelvis and is poor at showing free gas and bowel leaks in an acutely unwell patient. CT pulmonary angiography: her tachycardia and fever are explained by an intra-abdominal source, her oxygen saturation is normal and she has no respiratory symptoms.
why: Free gas can enter the peritoneum through a uterine perforation during hysteroscopy, so finding it does not tell you the bowel is injured, and the film cannot show collections or pelvic disease.
With a body mass index of 42 the views are limited, and ultrasound cannot reliably find bowel injury, free gas or collections higher in the abdomen.
MRI is slow and less available as an emergency test, covers only the pelvis and is poor at showing free gas or a bowel leak in a febrile, acutely unwell patient.
She has no chest symptoms and normal oxygen saturation, and her fever, tachycardia and lower abdominal guarding point to an intra-abdominal source rather than pulmonary embolism.

items.stem: A 56-year-old woman comes to a metropolitan emergency department 2 hours after sudden sharp left-sided chest pain began. The pain is worse on deep inspiration, and she is short of breath. Her left calf has been swollen and aching for 3 days. Five days ago she flew from Los Angeles to Sydney. She takes oral oestradiol for menopausal symptoms and smokes. She has no history of bleeding, peptic ulcer or stroke. Temperature is 37.4 °C, pulse 114/min, blood pressure 128/82 mm Hg, respirations 26/min and SpO2 93% on room air. Her left calf is swollen and tender. The ECG shows sinus tachycardia only. hs-troponin I is 4 ng/L (99th percentile for women, 16 ng/L), haemoglobin 138 g/L, platelets 240 x10^9/L and creatinine 70 µmol/L. A CT pulmonary angiogram shows filling defects in the left lower lobe segmental and subsegmental arteries and in a right middle lobe segmental artery. The RV to LV diameter ratio is 0.8, with no septal bowing and no contrast reflux into the hepatic veins.
items.ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Discharge home with apixaban 10 mg orally twice daily
Catheter-directed thrombolysis of the pulmonary arteries
Insertion of an inferior vena cava filter
Admission and apixaban 10 mg orally twice daily
items.explanation: The CT pulmonary angiogram shows emboli in both lungs. However, it shows no right ventricular strain: the RV to LV ratio is below 1, and there is no septal bowing or contrast reflux. She also has a normal blood pressure and a normal hs-troponin. So this is not high-risk (massive) PE, and clots in both lungs alone do not justify thrombolysis. Her pulse of 114/min (at least 110) gives her an sPESI score of 1. She is therefore not low risk. She has intermediate-low risk PE, which needs hospital admission for monitoring, not outpatient care. Her bleeding history, platelets and renal function are reassuring. The THANZ guideline and eTG recommend starting a direct oral anticoagulant, such as apixaban 10 mg twice daily for 7 days and then 5 mg twice daily, for at least 3 months for provoked VTE. Her oestrogen should be stopped.
why: Outpatient treatment is only for low-risk PE with an sPESI of 0, and her pulse of 114/min gives her an sPESI of 1.
Systemic thrombolysis is for high-risk PE with sustained hypotension or shock, and she is normotensive with no RV strain.
Catheter-directed therapy is for high-risk PE when systemic thrombolysis is contraindicated or has failed, or for intermediate-high risk PE that is getting worse, and neither applies to her.
An IVC filter is used only when anticoagulation is contraindicated or has failed, and she has no bleeding risk factors.

items.stem: A 73-year-old man is brought to the emergency department with sudden severe breathlessness that began overnight. For 3 weeks he has needed three pillows to sleep, and his ankles have become swollen. He had an anterior myocardial infarction treated with a stent 9 years ago, and he has hypertension and type 2 diabetes. He has had no cardiac imaging since the infarct. On arrival, pulse is 112/min, blood pressure 178/96 mmHg, respiratory rate 30/min and SpO2 86% on room air. His jugular venous pressure is raised, there is a third heart sound, crackles reach the mid-zones and there is pitting oedema to the shins. ECG shows sinus tachycardia with Q waves in V1 to V4, unchanged from 2 years ago. Chest X-ray shows cardiomegaly, upper lobe diversion, Kerley B lines and small bilateral pleural effusions. NT-proBNP is 5800 ng/L. hs-troponin I is 42 ng/L, and 45 ng/L 3 hours later (99th percentile below 34 ng/L). He improves with non-invasive ventilation, glyceryl trinitrate and IV furosemide.
items.ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate next investigation to establish the underlying diagnosis?
items.explanation: This man has acute cardiogenic pulmonary oedema, which is acute decompensated heart failure. His old anterior infarct points to an ischaemic cardiomyopathy. The 2018 NHFA/CSANZ heart failure guideline recommends transthoracic echocardiography for every patient with suspected heart failure. It confirms the structural or functional cardiac cause. It measures LVEF, which separates HFrEF from HFpEF and decides which disease-modifying drugs to use. It also shows regional wall motion abnormalities, valve disease, filling pressures and pulmonary pressures. It is non-invasive and can be done at the bedside once he is stable. The troponin is raised but nearly flat (42 then 45 ng/L) with an unchanged ECG. That pattern fits myocardial injury from heart failure, not an acute MI. Bilateral effusions with pulmonary oedema are expected transudates that settle with diuresis.

Diagnostic pleural aspiration is not needed: small bilateral effusions with pulmonary oedema in heart failure are presumed transudates and are managed with diuresis, with aspiration kept for atypical, unilateral or non-resolving effusions.
Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging is a second-line test, used when echocardiography images are inadequate or a specific cardiomyopathy needs characterising, and it is not the first investigation.

items.stem: A 34-year-old woman comes to a rural emergency department with 18 hours of fevers and shaking chills and 6 hours of constant right upper quadrant pain. This morning her partner noticed that her eyes had turned yellow. She reports dark urine and pale stools. She takes the combined oral contraceptive pill and has no other medical history. Her temperature is 39.4 °C, pulse 112/min, blood pressure 118/72 mm Hg, respiratory rate 20/min and oxygen saturation 97% on room air. She is alert and oriented. She is jaundiced and tender in the right upper quadrant. Investigations show: white cell count 16.4 x10^9/L (4.0–11.0); platelets 240 x10^9/L (150–400); total bilirubin 61 µmol/L (<20); ALP 310 U/L (30–110); GGT 402 U/L (<40); ALT 160 U/L (<35); albumin 37 g/L (35–50); creatinine 68 µmol/L (45–90); INR 1.0; venous lactate 2.4 mmol/L (<2.0). Ultrasound shows a 10 mm common bile duct with a calculus in its distal end.
items.ask: Which of the following best describes the severity of this patient's condition according to the Tokyo Guidelines 2018?
options: Mild (Grade I), as organ dysfunction is absent
Moderate (Grade II), owing to the serum bilirubin level
Moderate (Grade II), owing to leucocytosis and pyrexia
Severe (Grade III), owing to the raised venous lactate
Severe (Grade III), owing to tachycardia and tachypnoea

Severity is graded from the results. Grade III (severe) needs dysfunction of at least one organ system: hypotension needing vasopressors, a reduced level of consciousness, PaO2/FiO2 below 300, oliguria or creatinine above 176 µmol/L, INR above 1.5, or platelets below 100 x10^9/L. She has none of these, because her blood pressure, mental state, oxygenation, creatinine, INR and platelets are all normal. Grade II (moderate) needs any two of: white cell count above 12 or below 4 x10^9/L, temperature of 39 °C or more, age 75 or more, bilirubin of 85 µmol/L or more, or low albumin. She meets two (white cell count 16.4 and temperature 39.4 °C), so she has Grade II cholangitis. For her, this means she is at risk of getting worse. Along with the sepsis pathway (blood cultures and IV antibiotics within 60 minutes, as eTG recommends, plus fluids and a repeat lactate), she needs early biliary drainage by ERCP. In a rural hospital, that means early referral and transfer to a centre that can do ERCP.

Wrong: a bilirubin of 61 µmol/L is below the 85 µmol/L TG18 threshold, so it does not count towards Grade II.
Wrong: lactate is not one of the TG18 organ dysfunction criteria; a mildly raised lactate supports sepsis escalation but does not make her Grade III.
Wrong: tachycardia and tachypnoea are not TG18 organ dysfunction criteria, and her blood pressure and oxygenation are normal.

items.stem: A 23-year-old woman sees her general practitioner because of a throbbing right-sided headache that began 4 hours ago. This is her sixth similar episode in 4 months. Her only medicine is a combined oral contraceptive pill. She is sexually active with one male partner. Her temperature is 36.8 °C, pulse 74/min, blood pressure 128/80 mm Hg and respiratory rate 14/min. She has no neck stiffness. Neurological examination, including fundoscopy, is normal. A point-of-care urine beta-hCG test done by the practice nurse is negative, and the control line is present.

A serum test is needed before any analgesic is given
A triptan is unsafe until her next menstrual period
Aspirin plus metoclopramide can be used for her acute attacks

A triptan can be added if this is not enough, or used first for severe attacks. Pregnancy would have restricted these choices, especially aspirin and NSAIDs. A negative test does not make the combined pill safe: migraine with aura is UKMEC category 4 whatever her pregnancy status. She also remains a woman who could become pregnant, which affects which preventive medicines are suitable.

Wrong: valproate is strongly teratogenic and should be avoided in women who could become pregnant; one negative test does not make it suitable, and propranolol or amitriptyline would be preferred.
Wrong: a point-of-care urine beta-hCG test with a valid control line is reliable enough to guide acute treatment, so a serum test is not needed first.
Wrong: she is not pregnant, so nothing about her menstrual cycle makes a triptan unsafe; it can be taken at the start of the headache phase if first-line treatment fails.

items.stem: A 20-month-old girl is brought to the emergency department by her father 70 minutes after an episode at day care. Staff saw her go stiff and unresponsive with her eyes rolled back, then she had rhythmic jerking of all four limbs for about 2 minutes. She was sleepy for about 30 minutes afterwards. She has had a runny nose and cough for 2 days. She has never had a seizure before. She is fully immunised, her development is normal, and she takes no medicines. Her mother had a febrile convulsion as a child. Temperature is 39.0 °C, pulse 145/min, respirations 32/min, blood pressure 92/56 mmHg, SpO2 98% in room air and capillary refill 2 seconds. She is now alert, playing and interacting normally. She has clear rhinorrhoea and an injected pharynx. Her tympanic membranes are normal and her chest is clear. There is no rash and no neck stiffness. Neurological examination is normal. Capillary blood glucose is 5.1 mmol/L. She has been given oral paracetamol.
items.ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Discharge with parental education and safety-netting advice
Admission to the ward for overnight observation
Lumbar puncture for cerebrospinal fluid analysis
Regular alternating paracetamol and ibuprofen for 3 days
items.explanation: This is a simple febrile seizure. The RCH Febrile seizure guideline defines this as a single generalised tonic-clonic seizure lasting under 15 minutes, with full recovery within 1 hour and no repeat seizure in the same illness, in a child aged 6 months to 6 years. She has a clear viral upper respiratory source, a normal blood glucose, no signs of meningitis and a normal neurological examination now that she is back to baseline. Once she is back to normal and the source is found, she can go home. Her father needs to hear that the outlook is good: there is no brain damage, the chance of later epilepsy is about 1 to 2 in 100, and the chance of another febrile seizure is about 1 in 3 (higher here because of the family history). He also needs to be taught seizure first aid: time the seizure, put her in the recovery position, put nothing in her mouth, and call an ambulance if it lasts 5 minutes. He should bring her back if she becomes drowsy, gets a rash or neck stiffness, has another seizure, or he is worried. Admission is not needed because she has recovered fully and the source is benign. Lumbar puncture is only for meningism, ongoing drowsiness or a very young or unwell child. EEG is not indicated after a simple febrile seizure. Antipyretics make her more comfortable but do not prevent febrile seizures.
why: Wrong: admission is for complex seizures, slow recovery, a worrying source or concern about how the family will cope, and she has none of these.
Wrong: she has no meningism, no rash and no ongoing drowsiness, and she is not very young or unwell, so lumbar puncture is not indicated.
Wrong: EEG does not predict recurrence or later epilepsy after a simple febrile seizure and is not recommended.
Wrong: antipyretics are given for comfort only, do not prevent febrile seizures, and an alternating schedule raises the risk of dosing errors.

items.stem: A 34-year-old woman, gravida 3, para 2, at 38 weeks' gestation is in spontaneous labour on the birth suite. An ultrasound at 34 weeks showed polyhydramnios (amniotic fluid index 27 cm), normal fetal growth and a fundal placenta. Ten minutes after spontaneous rupture of the membranes, with a gush of clear liquor, the CTG shows a sudden fall in the fetal heart rate from a baseline of 135/min to 75/min, which has lasted 4 minutes. She has no epidural, and no oxytocin is running. Her pulse is 88/min, blood pressure 118/72 mm Hg, respirations 16/min and temperature 36.9 °C. The abdomen is soft and non-tender between contractions, which come 3 times in 10 minutes. On vaginal examination the cervix is 6 cm dilated, the vertex is at station -3, and a pulsating loop of umbilical cord is felt in the vagina. Help has been called and theatre is being prepared for a category 1 caesarean.
items.ask: While she waits for transfer to theatre, which of the following is the most appropriate immediate action?
options: Manual replacement of the loop back into the uterus
Digital elevation of the head with knee–chest posture
Fetal scalp blood sampling for lactate measurement
Forceps-assisted vaginal birth in lithotomy position
Left lateral tilt with intravenous crystalloid bolus
items.explanation: This is umbilical cord prolapse. Her risk factors are polyhydramnios, a high vertex and recent rupture of the membranes, and the fetal heart rate has dropped and stayed down. The cord is being squeezed between the fetal head and the pelvis. The aim while waiting for a category 1 caesarean is to take that pressure off. The RCOG Green-top Guideline 50, used with RANZCOG guidance in Australian units, advises pushing the presenting part up off the cord by hand through the vagina. The woman is placed knee–chest, or head-down in the left lateral position, so gravity helps. An alternative is filling the bladder with 500 to 750 mL of saline through a urinary catheter. The cord should be handled as little as possible to avoid spasm of its vessels, and tocolysis such as terbutaline can be considered. Elevation continues until the baby is delivered. Delivery should not be delayed for any other test or procedure.
why: Pushing the cord back into the uterus (funic reduction) is not recommended, because handling the cord causes its vessels to spasm, and it delays the definitive caesarean.
Fetal blood sampling is not appropriate for a prolonged deceleration or bradycardia that is not recovering, and it would delay a birth that is already known to be needed.
Forceps need a fully dilated cervix and an engaged head, but here the cervix is 6 cm and the vertex is at station -3.
Left lateral tilt and fluids treat maternal hypotension, but her blood pressure is normal, and neither measure relieves the mechanical squeezing of the cord.

items.stem: A 26-year-old woman sees her general practitioner with 2 days of constant left calf pain and swelling. She has worked at a desk from home for the past 4 months and rarely goes out. She has taken a combined oral contraceptive pill for 6 years and takes no other medicines. Before she started the pill, her periods were heavy and lasted 8 days. She has no personal or family history of venous thromboembolism. Her BMI is 31 kg/m2. Temperature is 36.9 °C, pulse 84/min, blood pressure 118/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min and SpO2 99% on room air. Her left calf measures 3.5 cm more than the right and has pitting oedema. Compression ultrasound shows a non-compressible left popliteal vein, with thrombus extending into the posterior tibial and peroneal veins. Platelets are 268 x10^9/L (150 to 400), INR 1.0 and eGFR over 90 mL/min/1.73 m2. Serum beta-hCG is under 5 IU/L. Rivaroxaban is started for 3 months. She wants to avoid pregnancy for at least 2 years.
items.ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate contraception for this patient?
options: Her current combined oral contraceptive pill
A combined pill with 20 micrograms ethinylestradiol
An etonogestrel and ethinylestradiol vaginal ring
items.explanation: She has an acute proximal DVT provoked by the combined oral contraceptive pill, with prolonged sitting and obesity adding to the risk. After an oestrogen-related VTE, the key prevention and counselling step is to stop all oestrogen-containing contraception and switch straight away to a reliable non-oestrogen method. This prevents recurrence, and it also prevents pregnancy while she takes rivaroxaban, which can harm a fetus. Under UKMEC, which Australian practice uses, any combined hormonal method with current or past VTE is category 4 (unacceptable risk). Progestogen-only methods such as the levonorgestrel intrauterine device are category 2, meaning the benefits outweigh the risks. The levonorgestrel device is the best choice here for three reasons. It is long-acting and highly effective, it needs nothing from her day to day, and it reduces menstrual bleeding. That matters because she had heavy periods before the pill, and heavy menstrual bleeding is a common, troublesome side effect of rivaroxaban in women.

Lowering the oestrogen dose still leaves a combined hormonal method, which remains UKMEC category 4 after VTE because any dose of ethinylestradiol raises clotting risk.
The vaginal ring delivers ethinylestradiol, and its VTE risk is at least as high as the combined pill, so it is also category 4.
Fertility awareness-based methods fail often with typical use, which is unacceptable during DOAC treatment, and cycle tracking is unreliable just after stopping hormonal contraception.
