items.stem: A 5-month-old girl is brought to the emergency department by her father. She has had a runny nose for 4 days, and cough with fast breathing for the last 2 days. Her bottles have been getting shorter, and she has had 3 wet nappies in the past 24 hours. She was born at term, has been well, and her immunisations are up to date. She weighs 7.0 kg. Temperature is 37.6 °C, heart rate 165/min, respiratory rate 60/min, blood pressure 88/52 mm Hg, and SpO2 86% in room air. She is alert, with nasal flaring, moderate subcostal and intercostal recession, and fine crackles and expiratory wheeze on both sides. Capillary refill time is 2 seconds. On 1 L/min oxygen by nasal prongs her SpO2 rises to 94%. An hour later she is offered 180 mL of her usual milk. She takes 45 mL over 25 minutes, stopping often to breathe, with a heart rate of 178/min, then refuses the rest. She has had no wet nappy in the 2.5 hours since arrival.
items.ask: Based on this assessment of her oral intake, which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: IV 0.9% sodium chloride with 5% glucose at 28 mL/h
IV 0.9% sodium chloride 140 mL over 20 minutes
Oral bottle every 2 hours with review at 4 hours
items.explanation: This infant has bronchiolitis, and the oral trial shows she cannot feed safely or adequately by mouth. She took 45 of 180 mL (about a quarter of a usual bottle), stopped to breathe, became more tachycardic during the feed, and has passed less urine (3 wet nappies in 24 hours and none since arrival). So the result means she needs hydration support, not that she is in shock. Her capillary refill time, blood pressure and alertness are normal. In bronchiolitis, the RCH guideline prefers nasogastric feeds over IV fluids when oral intake is inadequate. Fluids are limited to two-thirds of maintenance because increased ADH secretion can cause fluid overload and hyponatraemia. By Holliday-Segar, maintenance for 7 kg is 4 mL/kg/h, or 28 mL/h, so two-thirds is about 19 mL/h. If nasogastric feeds fail or are unsafe, the next step is isotonic IV fluid with glucose, also at two-thirds maintenance.

IV fluid is second-line, used only when nasogastric feeds fail or are unsafe, and even then it should run at two-thirds maintenance rather than full maintenance.
A 20 mL/kg bolus treats shock, and this infant is alert with a capillary refill time of 2 seconds and a normal blood pressure, so she needs ongoing hydration, not resuscitation.
Continuing bottles ignores what the trial showed: she takes only a quarter of a feed, tires and becomes more tachycardic, and her urine output is falling, so oral feeding alone is not enough.

items.stem: A 47-year-old woman sees her general practitioner because of a red, painful lump in her right breast for 12 days. She has taken flucloxacillin for 6 days and it has not improved. She last breastfed 9 years ago, her periods are regular, and she has smoked 20 cigarettes a day for 28 years. Her temperature is 37.9 °C, pulse 96/min and blood pressure 124/78 mm Hg. There is a 3 cm tender, fluctuant swelling beside the right areola with overlying redness. Deep to it is a firm, ill-defined area, and the right nipple is newly retracted. White cell count is 12.9 x 10^9/L (reference 4.0–11.0) and CRP is 46 mg/L (reference under 5). Ultrasound shows a 25 x 15 mm thick-walled collection with mobile internal echoes and a hyperaemic wall. Deep to it is a separate 16 mm hypoechoic solid lesion. The lesion is irregular in shape, with angular margins, posterior acoustic shadowing and internal Doppler flow, and its shape does not change with probe compression. A right axillary node has a 4 mm cortex with a preserved fatty hilum.
items.ask: Which of the following is the most accurate interpretation of the deeper solid lesion?
options: Organising phlegmon that is expected to resolve with antibiotics
Inspissated pus that is expected to clear after aspiration
Ectatic duct from periductal mastitis that needs smoking cessation
Reactive glandular oedema that is expected to settle after drainage
Probable malignancy that needs tissue sampling before any reassurance

The thick-walled collection with mobile debris and a hyperaemic wall is the abscess, and it can be aspirated under ultrasound. The deeper lesion is solid, irregular, with angular margins, posterior shadowing and internal vascularity, and it keeps its shape under compression. These are features of malignancy (BI-RADS category 4 or higher). An abscess does not explain them, and they need an image-guided core biopsy. Cancer Australia guidance says triple assessment (clinical, imaging and non-operative biopsy) must be concordant before a lump is called benign. Non-lactational mastitis that fails to settle, new nipple retraction and a residual mass are all red flags for an underlying or inflammatory carcinoma. Aspiration of the abscess, pus culture, antibiotics as per eTG and the planned biopsy should go ahead together, not one after the other.

Inspissated pus lies within the collection, has no internal Doppler flow and changes shape with compression, whereas this lesion is solid, vascular and separate from the abscess.
Periductal mastitis fits her smoking and retroareolar site, but an ectatic duct is a tubular, fluid-filled structure, not an irregular vascular solid lesion with shadowing.
Inflammatory oedema increases echogenicity and blurs tissue planes without forming a discrete, non-compressible, shadowing solid lesion with internal vascularity.

items.stem: A 27-year-old woman comes to a general practice 5 weeks before a 7-week trip through rural Vietnam, Cambodia and Laos for travel advice. Her Australian Immunisation Register statement shows a complete childhood schedule, including one measles-mumps-rubella dose at 12 months, a 3-dose school hepatitis B course and dTpa at age 15. Today the doctor plans to give a second measles-mumps-rubella dose, live attenuated Japanese encephalitis vaccine, combined hepatitis A-typhoid vaccine and dTpa, and to prescribe doxycycline for malaria prophylaxis.

Testing hepatitis B antibodies after a completed adolescent course is not routinely recommended in an immunocompetent traveller, and the result would not affect today's vaccines.

items.stem: A 63-year-old man presents to his general practitioner with 6 days of worsening breathlessness and a cough that now brings up more green sputum than usual. He now has to stop and rest when walking to his letterbox. His grandson had a cold last week. He has severe COPD, uses home oxygen at 2 L/min and has paroxysmal atrial fibrillation. His medicines are inhaled tiotropium–olodaterol, salbutamol as needed, and apixaban. His temperature is 38.3 °C, pulse 112/min and regular, blood pressure 128/78 mm Hg, respiratory rate 24/min, and SpO2 87% on 2 L/min. He has widespread expiratory wheeze without focal crackles. His JVP is not raised and he has no ankle oedema. A 12-lead ECG shows a regular rhythm at 112/min, with an upright P wave of the same shape before every QRS complex in lead II. The PR interval is 160 ms, QRS 90 ms and axis +60°. There are no ST-segment or T-wave changes, and V1 has a dominant S wave. His ECG from 8 months ago showed an irregularly irregular rhythm at 92/min with no P waves.

options: Sinus tachycardia driven by the exacerbation

Multifocal atrial tachycardia from chronic hypoxia

Wrong because there is no right axis deviation, RBBB, right precordial T-wave inversion or S1Q3T3 pattern, and he is already taking apixaban.
Wrong because the axis is normal at +60°, V1 has a dominant S wave rather than a dominant R wave, and there is no P pulmonale, raised JVP or oedema.

items.stem: A 69-year-old woman comes to the emergency department with 24 hours of crampy, diffuse abdominal pain, profuse watery diarrhoea without blood, and repeated vomiting. Two days ago she looked after her grandson, who goes to childcare and had diarrhoea. Her husband started vomiting this morning. She has not travelled, taken antibiotics or been in hospital recently. She has type 2 diabetes and hypertension, and she is an ex-smoker. Her medicines are metformin, ramipril and omeprazole. Temperature is 37.8 °C, pulse 118/min, blood pressure 98/60 mm Hg lying, respiratory rate 18/min and SpO2 97% on room air. Her abdomen is soft with mild diffuse tenderness, no guarding and hyperactive bowel sounds. ECG shows sinus tachycardia. Creatinine is 131 µmol/L (baseline 72), potassium 3.4 mmol/L, venous lactate 1.5 mmol/L (reference below 2.0) and CRP 28 mg/L. She is given an intravenous crystalloid bolus, her metformin and ramipril are withheld, and she is to be admitted under contact precautions.
items.ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate next investigation?
options: Faecal microscopy for ova and parasites
items.explanation: This woman has acute infectious diarrhoea. The likely cause is norovirus: she had sudden vomiting and watery diarrhoea two days after contact with a child who had diarrhoea, and another person in her household is now ill. She also has hypovolaemia and a prerenal acute kidney injury. Most people with acute gastroenteritis do not need a stool test. Therapeutic Guidelines (eTG) recommends one in specific situations: severe illness, admission to hospital, bloody diarrhoea, immunocompromise, recent antibiotic use, symptoms lasting more than 7 days, or a suspected outbreak. She is being admitted with significant dehydration and an AKI, and her household cluster fits an outbreak. A faecal multiplex PCR is the most useful test. It detects norovirus and the common bacterial causes (Campylobacter, Salmonella, Shigella) in one sample. The result confirms the cause, guides contact precautions and bed placement on the ward, and shows whether antibiotics are needed. CT mesenteric angiography is not indicated. Her pain is not out of proportion to the examination, her abdomen is soft, she is in sinus rhythm and her lactate is normal, and intravenous contrast carries extra risk while she has an AKI. A C. difficile toxin assay on its own is too narrow: she has had no recent antibiotics or hospital stay, and the household cluster points to a transmissible virus. Faecal microscopy for ova and parasites is for travellers, people with diarrhoea for more than 7 days and immunocompromised people, so it is unlikely to help with a 24-hour illness. Blood cultures are for high fever (38.5 °C or more), sepsis or immunocompromise, and they would not detect norovirus.

Her abdomen is soft, mildly distended and nontender. Investigations show:

MCV 75 fL (80–100)
Ferritin 5 µg/L (30–300)
Serum folate 4.8 nmol/L (>7)
Vitamin B12 310 pmol/L (150–700)
CRP 3 mg/L (<5)
TSH 2.1 mIU/L (0.5–4.0)
Tissue transglutaminase IgA 180 U/mL (<20)
Endomysial antibody IgA: positive
Total IgA 2.0 g/L (0.7–4.0)

The test is gastroscopy with multiple duodenal biopsies: at least four from the second part of the duodenum and one or two from the bulb. These are taken while she is still eating gluten, and the aim is to show villous atrophy, crypt hyperplasia and intraepithelial lymphocytosis. The no-biopsy approach used in some children is not used for Australian adults. A biopsy also gives a baseline and checks for other pathology. HLA-DQ2 and HLA-DQ8 genotyping is mainly useful for ruling the disease out: about a third of the population carries these alleles, so a positive result cannot confirm coeliac disease. Colonoscopy with ileal biopsies looks for Crohn's disease or microscopic colitis. Her CRP is normal, she has no bleeding or pain, and colonoscopy does not sample the duodenum, where coeliac disease shows. Colonoscopy with ileal biopsies looks for Crohn's disease or microscopic colitis, and it does not sample the duodenum, where coeliac disease shows.
A gluten challenge is only needed for patients who have already stopped gluten, and she is eating a normal gluten-containing diet.

items.stem: A 29-year-old woman comes to the emergency department with 2 days of sharp central chest pain. The pain is worse when she lies flat or breathes in, and it eases when she sits forward. She had a sore throat and runny nose a week ago. She has no medical history, takes no regular medicines and weighs 62 kg. Her temperature is 37.6 °C, pulse 96/min, blood pressure 122/74 mm Hg, respiratory rate 16/min and SpO2 99% on room air. A scratchy friction rub is heard at the left sternal edge while she holds her breath. An ECG shows widespread concave ST elevation with PR depression. High-sensitivity troponin I is 4 ng/L at 0 hours and 4 ng/L at 2 hours (women's 99th percentile, under 16). CRP is 38 mg/L (under 5). A chest X-ray is normal, and a bedside echocardiogram shows no pericardial effusion. She is to be discharged on ibuprofen 600 mg orally 8-hourly.
items.ask: Along with the ibuprofen, which of the following is most likely to lower her risk of the most common complication of this condition?
options: Prednisolone 50 mg orally once daily for 5 days
Colchicine 500 micrograms orally once daily for 3 months
Esomeprazole 20 mg orally once daily while on ibuprofen
Colchicine 500 micrograms orally once daily for 1 week
Metoprolol 25 mg orally twice daily for 3 months
items.explanation: This woman has low-risk acute viral or idiopathic pericarditis. She has typical pain, a friction rub and typical ECG changes. Her troponin is normal, she has no effusion, her temperature is below 38 °C and the onset was acute, so she can be treated as an outpatient. The most common complication is recurrence, which happens after about 15 to 30% of first episodes. Tamponade and constriction are rare after idiopathic pericarditis. Adding colchicine to an NSAID speeds symptom relief and roughly halves recurrence (ICAP trial). eTG and the 2025 ESC guidelines recommend a 3-month course, dosed by weight: 500 micrograms once daily under 70 kg and twice daily from 70 kg. At 62 kg, she needs the once-daily dose. Ibuprofen is tapered once pain and CRP settle, and she should have gastroprotection. She should also be told to avoid strenuous exercise until symptoms resolve and CRP returns to normal.

A proton pump inhibitor is appropriate gastroprotection with high-dose NSAIDs, but it prevents drug-induced gastrointestinal injury and has no effect on recurrent pericarditis.
One week of colchicine is too short to reduce recurrence, because the evidence-based course for a first episode is 3 months.
Beta-blockers have no role in preventing recurrent pericarditis, and her mild tachycardia reflects inflammation and pain rather than a rhythm or ischaemic problem needing rate control.

items.stem: A 41-year-old man is admitted to the rheumatology ward with 3 weeks of painful, swollen hands and 2 hours of morning stiffness each day. Both wrists and the second to fourth MCP and PIP joints are warm and boggy, and the DIP joints are spared. He has fixed ulnar deviation, swan neck deformities and firm nodules over both elbows. Haemoglobin is 118 g/L (130 to 180), CRP 46 mg/L (less than 5), ALT 24 U/L (less than 40), and creatinine 82 µmol/L (60 to 110). Rheumatoid factor and anti-CCP antibodies are strongly positive. A chest X-ray taken in the emergency department overnight is clear. The team plans a short course of prednisolone and to restart methotrexate.

items.explanation: This man has a flare of established seropositive, erosive rheumatoid arthritis after 5 months off methotrexate. The diagnosis is already settled: he has symmetrical synovitis that spares the DIP joints, fixed deformities, rheumatoid nodules, raised CRP, and strongly positive RF and anti-CCP. The question to answer now is whether it is safe to restart treatment. Australian guidance (eTG Rheumatology and the Australian Rheumatology Association's methotrexate information) says that before starting methotrexate you need a FBC, LFT, UEC, a baseline chest X-ray, and serology for hepatitis B and C. Methotrexate can cause liver injury, and immunosuppression (especially with prednisolone added) can reactivate hepatitis B. His FBC, LFT, creatinine and chest X-ray have already been done. His earlier screening cannot be found and he smokes, so hepatitis B and C serology is the one essential test still missing. It also tells you whether he needs hepatitis B vaccination or antiviral prophylaxis.

Wrist aspiration is for suspected septic arthritis, and this man is afebrile with a symmetrical polyarthritis and no single joint out of proportion to the others.
Serum urate does not help here: the nodules are firm and rubbery, he has never had an acute attack, and strongly positive anti-CCP already confirms rheumatoid arthritis.
An ANA titre looks for lupus, but fixed erosive deformities with strongly positive anti-CCP point to rheumatoid arthritis, not the reversible Jaccoud's arthropathy of SLE.

Haemoglobin 106 g/L (115–160)
MCV 75 fL (80–100)
Ferritin 7 microgram/L (30–300)
Serum folate 5.0 nmol/L (above 7.0)
TSH 2.1 mU/L (0.5–4.0)
CRP 3 mg/L (below 5)
Tissue transglutaminase IgA 96 U/mL (below 20)
Total IgA 2.1 g/L (0.7–4.0)
Faecal elastase 380 microgram/g (above 200)
Stool microscopy, culture and multiplex PCR: no pathogens detected
items.ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Strict gluten-free diet, then repeat serology in 3 months
Pancreatic enzyme replacement taken with meals
Gastroscopy with duodenal biopsies while on her current diet
items.explanation: She has malabsorption (steatorrhoea, weight loss, iron and folate deficiency). She also has autoimmune risk factors and a strongly positive tTG-IgA with a normal total IgA, so the serology result can be trusted. This picture is highly likely to be coeliac disease. Coeliac Australia, GESA and eTG advise that adults have the diagnosis confirmed by gastroscopy with multiple duodenal biopsies (including the duodenal bulb) while still eating gluten, to show villous atrophy and intraepithelial lymphocytosis. A biopsy-confirmed diagnosis supports a lifelong gluten-free diet with a dietitian, replacement of iron, folate and vitamin D, bone health assessment, and screening of first-degree relatives. Starting a gluten-free diet before the biopsy can heal the mucosa and make the serology and histology falsely normal. HLA typing is useful only for ruling coeliac disease out. A normal faecal elastase and CRP make pancreatic insufficiency and Crohn disease unlikely.

HLA-DQ2/DQ8 typing has a high negative predictive value but is present in about a third of the population, so a positive result cannot confirm coeliac disease.
Her normal CRP, lack of blood in the stool and strongly positive tTG-IgA point to coeliac disease rather than ileal Crohn disease, so ileocolonoscopy is not the first investigation.
A normal faecal elastase of 380 microgram/g rules against exocrine pancreatic insufficiency, so enzyme replacement would not treat the cause of her steatorrhoea.

items.stem: A 51-year-old man comes to his general practitioner for a cardiovascular risk assessment. He feels well and says his blood pressure "always jumps" at the doctor's. He takes no regular medicines, vapes nicotine daily and drinks four coffees a day. He is seated and has rested for 5 minutes, and a correctly sized cuff is used. His blood pressure is 152/94 mmHg and then 148/92 mmHg in the right arm, and 150/92 mmHg in the left arm. His pulse is 74/min. His BMI is 29 kg/m2. His fundi, heart sounds and peripheral pulses are normal. He brings a list of 9 home readings from the past 12 days. He took them on a wrist monitor he bought online, one reading each evening after dinner and coffee. They average 126/79 mmHg. A 12-lead ECG is normal. Serum potassium is 4.2 mmol/L (3.5 to 5.2), eGFR is above 90 mL/min/1.73 m2 and the urine albumin to creatinine ratio is 1.0 mg/mmol (below 2.5).
items.ask: Which of the following best describes the significance of his home readings?
options: They demonstrate a normal nocturnal dipping pattern
They are inadequate to confirm or exclude hypertension
items.explanation: His repeated clinic readings of 148 to 152/92 to 94 mmHg are in the grade 1 range. He has no end-organ damage (normal fundi, ECG, eGFR and urine albumin), so the Heart Foundation guideline says to confirm the diagnosis with out-of-office measurement before labelling or treating him. A home average below 135/85 mmHg would usually point to white coat hypertension, but only if it comes from a valid protocol. That protocol is a validated upper-arm device with a correctly sized cuff, two seated readings one minute apart every morning and evening for 7 days, discarding day 1 and averaging the rest. His readings fail it. The wrist device is not validated, he took single evening readings only, he took them after caffeine, and he has too few readings. They can neither confirm nor exclude hypertension. The next step is 24-hour ambulatory monitoring or a correctly done home protocol. A diagnosis of white coat hypertension cannot rest on invalid home data. Sustained hypertension is not confirmed because the out-of-office data are unreliable and, as recorded, normal. Masked hypertension is the reverse pattern: normal in the clinic and raised outside it. Nocturnal dipping can only be judged from ambulatory readings taken during sleep.
why: White coat hypertension can only be diagnosed from a valid out-of-office measurement, and these single, post-caffeine evening readings on an unvalidated wrist device are not one.
Sustained hypertension needs a valid out-of-office average of at least 135/85 mmHg, and his recorded average is normal, though unreliable.
Masked hypertension means normal clinic but raised out-of-office readings, which is the opposite of his pattern.
Nocturnal dipping can only be judged from ambulatory readings taken during sleep, not from evening home readings taken while awake.

items.stem:
A 47-year-old man sees his general practitioner because he woke 2 days ago with muffled hearing and constant ringing in his right ear. He had a cold with a blocked nose 10 days ago and says the ear feels full. He has hypertension treated with perindopril and takes no other medicines. His temperature is 36.7°C, pulse 76/min and blood pressure 138/84 mm Hg. Otoscopy shows normal tympanic membranes on both sides. A 512 Hz tuning fork placed on the vertex is heard louder in the left ear. The rest of the cranial nerve examination is normal. Tympanometry shows a type A trace in both ears. Pure-tone audiometry thresholds (dB HL; normal 20 or less) are:
Right air conduction: 250 Hz 35, 500 Hz 40, 1 kHz 45, 2 kHz 55, 4 kHz 60
Right bone conduction (masked): 250 Hz 30, 500 Hz 40, 1 kHz 45, 2 kHz 50, 4 kHz 60
Left air and bone conduction: 10 to 15 at every frequency
items.ask: Which of the following best describes this audiogram?
items.explanation: The right ear's air conduction thresholds are 35 to 60 dB HL and fall away in the high frequencies. The masked bone conduction thresholds are raised by the same amount, never more than 5 dB from air conduction. That means there is no meaningful air-bone gap (a gap of 10 dB or less is within test variability), so the loss is sensorineural. The type A tympanograms (normal canal volume, pressure and compliance) rule out a middle ear effusion or Eustachian tube dysfunction after his cold, and the normal otoscopy rules out wax or a perforation. The Weber test lateralising to the left, the better ear, fits a right sensorineural loss. The right ear is more than 30 dB worse than the left over at least three contiguous frequencies, and the loss came on within 72 hours, so this meets the definition of sudden sensorineural hearing loss. He needs same-day ENT contact, prompt corticosteroids and MRI of the internal auditory canals to exclude a retrocochlear lesion such as a vestibular schwannoma. The feeling of fullness is a common symptom of the sensorineural loss itself, not a sign of a middle ear cause.
why: A conductive loss would show normal bone conduction with a gap of more than 10 dB to air conduction, usually an abnormal tympanogram, and a Weber lateralising to the affected right ear, and none of these are present.
A mixed loss needs raised bone conduction thresholds plus an air-bone gap of more than 10 dB, but the largest gap here is 5 dB, which is within test variability.
Left air and bone conduction thresholds are normal (10 to 15 dB HL); the Weber is louder on the left because that is the better-hearing cochlea, not the affected one.
Bilateral loss would need raised thresholds in both ears, but every left threshold is within the normal range of 20 dB HL or less, so the loss is one-sided.

items.stem: A 46-year-old woman presents to her general practitioner with 3 weeks of intermittent bright red blood on the toilet paper after opening her bowels. The blood is not mixed with the stool, and she has no pain when passing stool. She has had hard stools and has strained for years. She has had no change in bowel habit, weight loss or abdominal pain. She has no family history of bowel disease and takes no regular medicines. Her temperature is 36.7°C, pulse is 76/min and blood pressure is 124/78 mm Hg. The abdomen is soft and nontender. Perianal inspection and digital rectal examination are normal. Proctoscopy shows enlarged vascular cushions above the dentate line at the 3, 7 and 11 o'clock positions, with no prolapse on straining and normal lower rectal mucosa. Laboratory studies show haemoglobin 134 g/L (115–165), MCV 88 fL (80–100), ferritin 64 µg/L (30–300) and CRP 3 mg/L (less than 5). She is started on dietary fibre and a bulk-forming laxative.

items.explanation: She has painless bright red blood on the toilet paper, chronic constipation with straining, and non-prolapsing internal cushions at the classic positions on proctoscopy. This fits grade I internal haemorrhoids. Finding haemorrhoids does not rule out a lesion higher in the bowel. Cancer Council Australia guidelines and the optimal care pathway for colorectal cancer recommend colonoscopy for adults with new rectal bleeding, including those under 50. Colonoscopy looks at the whole colon and allows biopsy or removal of polyps. A normal haemoglobin and ferritin make significant hidden blood loss less likely, but they do not exclude a polyp or early cancer. Conservative treatment with fibre, fluids and a bulk-forming laxative can start while she waits for colonoscopy, and bleeding that persists despite treatment also needs investigation.
why: The iFOBT is a screening test for people without symptoms, and it will almost certainly be positive in someone with visible bleeding, so it adds nothing and only delays definitive investigation.
CT colonography is kept for patients who cannot have or cannot complete colonoscopy, because it cannot take biopsies or remove polyps and misses small flat lesions.
CEA is too insensitive and nonspecific to diagnose or exclude colorectal cancer and is used for monitoring after treatment, not for working up symptoms.

Faecal calprotectin helps tell inflammatory bowel disease from functional disorders in patients with diarrhoea, but she has no diarrhoea, urgency or mucus, a normal CRP and normal rectal mucosa, and the test does not look for neoplasia.

items.stem: A 24-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with 30 minutes of sudden, fast, regular palpitations that began while she was sitting at rest. Her first ECG showed a regular narrow complex tachycardia at 150/min. A modified Valsalva manoeuvre reverted it to sinus rhythm. On further questioning, she reports 4 months of 5 kg weight loss, heat intolerance, loose stools and feeling on edge. She has no past medical history and takes no medicines. After reversion, her pulse is 98/min and regular, blood pressure is 116/72 mm Hg, respiratory rate is 16/min, oxygen saturation is 98% on room air and temperature is 37.3 °C. She has a fine tremor of the outstretched hands and a diffuse, smooth, non-tender goitre with no palpable nodules. There is no proptosis. A repeat 12-lead ECG shows sinus rhythm with a normal PR interval and no delta waves. Blood results: TSH <0.01 mIU/L (0.4–4.0), free T4 32 pmol/L (10–25), free T3 11.5 pmol/L (3.5–6.5), beta-hCG negative.
items.ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate investigation to confirm the cause of her hyperthyroidism?
items.explanation: She had an SVT (probably AVNRT) set off by thyrotoxicosis. A suppressed TSH with raised free T4 and free T3 means primary hyperthyroidism. In a young woman with 4 months of symptoms and a diffuse, smooth, non-tender goitre with no nodules, Graves' disease is the most likely cause. Therapeutic Guidelines (Endocrinology) recommend TSH receptor antibodies (TRAb) as the first test to confirm Graves' disease. The test is highly sensitive and specific, cheap, carries no radiation, and the level helps predict relapse after antithyroid drugs. A positive TRAb confirms the diagnosis, so no imaging is needed and an antithyroid drug can be started with endocrinology input. Thyroid scintigraphy is kept for when TRAb is negative or the cause is unclear, for example a nodular gland or possible thyroiditis. Thyroid peroxidase antibodies are not specific, ultrasound does not tell the causes apart, and fine-needle aspiration is only for suspicious nodules.

Scintigraphy is a second-line test, used when TRAb is negative or a nodular gland or thyroiditis is suspected, and it means a radiation dose that this diffuse goitre does not need.
Ultrasound shows the size and structure of the gland but does not reliably tell Graves' disease from other causes, and it is mainly used when nodules are felt, which she does not have.
Fine-needle aspiration checks thyroid nodules for cancer, so it has no role in finding the cause of hyperthyroidism in a smooth goitre with no nodules.

Serum sodium is 137 mmol/L (135–145), potassium 4.8 mmol/L (3.5–5.2) and creatinine 104 µmol/L (60–110).
items.ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate advice to give him before discharge?
options: Weigh himself each morning and book a GP review if he gains more than 2 kg in 2 days
Limit his fluid intake to 1 litre per day whatever his thirst or sodium level

Use a potassium-based salt substitute to cut the sodium in his cooking
Stop his bisoprolol if he feels more tired during the next few weeks

The Heart Foundation/CSANZ guidelines and eTG recommend that he weighs himself every morning, on the same scales, after voiding and before breakfast. A strict 1 L fluid limit is not routine; restriction to about 1.5 L/day is kept for severe congestion or hyponatraemia, and his sodium is normal. Supervised exercise and cardiac rehabilitation are recommended in stable HFrEF, so bed rest is wrong. Regular exercise and cardiac rehabilitation improve symptoms and lower hospitalisation in stable HFrEF, so avoiding walking is harmful.
Potassium chloride salt substitutes can cause dangerous hyperkalaemia in a patient on sacubitril/valsartan and spironolactone whose potassium is already high-normal.
Fatigue early in beta-blocker treatment is common and usually short-lived, and stopping it removes a proven mortality benefit and can bring on ischaemia or arrhythmia.

items.stem: A 20-year-old man comes to the emergency department 90 minutes after sudden onset of sharp right-sided pain and breathlessness. Both started while he was sitting at his desk at work. The pain is worse with deep breaths and has not eased with rest. He has no cough, fever, haemoptysis, leg swelling, recent travel or trauma. He smokes 10 cigarettes a day and takes no medicines. He is 191 cm tall and weighs 68 kg. His temperature is 36.9 °C, pulse 104/min, respiratory rate 22/min, blood pressure 126/80 mm Hg and oxygen saturation 95% on room air. He speaks in full sentences. The trachea is central and the jugular venous pressure is not raised. Over the right hemithorax, expansion is reduced, the percussion note is hyper-resonant and breath sounds are reduced. A 12-lead ECG shows sinus tachycardia at 104/min with no ST-segment or T-wave changes.
items.ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate next investigation?
items.explanation: This tall, thin young man who smokes has sudden one-sided pleuritic pain and breathlessness. He has reduced expansion, a hyper-resonant percussion note and reduced breath sounds on the right, so the most likely diagnosis is a primary spontaneous pneumothorax. Tension pneumothorax is a clinical diagnosis and needs decompression straight away, before any imaging. Here there are no features of tension: his blood pressure is normal, the trachea is central and the JVP is not raised. That means there is time to confirm the diagnosis. The first-line test is a standard erect posteroanterior chest radiograph taken in inspiration (BTS 2023, used in Australian EDs). It shows the visceral pleural line with no lung markings beyond it, lets you measure the size of the pneumothorax (2 cm or more at the hilum is large) and shows any mediastinal shift. Together with his symptoms, this guides the choice between observation, needle aspiration, an ambulatory device or a drain. CT is kept for unclear or complex cases.
why: An arterial blood gas does not confirm or size a pneumothorax, and with an oxygen saturation of 95% on room air it is not needed to assess his oxygenation.
CT pulmonary angiography involves radiation and contrast and looks for pulmonary embolism, which is unlikely here with no risk factors and clear one-sided signs of air in the pleural space.
Expiratory films are no longer recommended because they add little to detection over a standard inspiratory film and can make the size of the pneumothorax harder to judge.
A D-dimer is non-specific, does not confirm a pneumothorax, and should not come before imaging when the examination already points strongly to another diagnosis.

items.stem: A 24-year-old man sees his general practitioner because of 10 weeks of crampy right lower abdominal pain and four to six loose stools a day. Some stools are streaked by blood, and they wake him from sleep. He has lost 4 kg without trying and has had occasional night sweats. He smokes 10 cigarettes a day and has taken ibuprofen most days for the pain. He has not travelled and has had no antibiotics in the past 3 months. His temperature is 37.8°C, pulse 92/min and blood pressure 118/74 mm Hg. He is tender in the right iliac fossa, where there is vague fullness but no guarding. A soft perianal skin tag is present. Haemoglobin is 112 g/L (130–180), CRP 42 mg/L (<5) and albumin 31 g/L (35–50). Faecal calprotectin is 640 µg/g (<50). Stool bacterial and parasite PCR, culture and Clostridioides difficile toxin are negative.
items.ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate investigation to confirm the diagnosis?
items.explanation: This young man most likely has ileocolonic Crohn's disease. The clues are a chronic history (over 6 weeks) of right iliac fossa pain, nocturnal diarrhoea with blood, weight loss, low-grade fever, a perianal skin tag, smoking, raised inflammatory markers, low albumin and a very high faecal calprotectin, with negative stool tests for infection. Under GESA and eTG guidance, diagnosis needs ileocolonoscopy, meaning colonoscopy that passes into the terminal ileum, with biopsies from the ileum and from each colonic segment, including normal-looking areas. This shows how far the disease extends and whether there are skip lesions or rectal sparing. Histology can show patchy transmural-type inflammation and non-caseating granulomas, and it can exclude intestinal tuberculosis, infection and malignancy. Small-bowel imaging is added after the diagnosis to stage the disease, not to make it. He should also stop ibuprofen and get urgent referral to gastroenterology.
why: Flexible sigmoidoscopy only reaches the distal colon, so it would miss ileocaecal disease, and the rectum and sigmoid are often spared in Crohn's disease.
MR enterography is useful for staging small-bowel extent, strictures and fistulae once the diagnosis is made, but it gives no tissue and cannot confirm the diagnosis.
Capsule endoscopy takes no biopsies and is not a first-line test, and an ileocaecal mass or stricture puts him at risk of the capsule getting stuck.
ASCA and ANCA serology has low sensitivity and specificity, so it cannot confirm or exclude Crohn's disease, and guidelines do not recommend it for diagnosis.

items.stem: A 21-day-old girl is brought to the emergency department by her parents on the advice of their general practitioner because of jaundice. Her skin has been yellow since day 4, her stools have been pale grey for the past 9 days, and her urine stains the nappy dark. The GP took a capillary blood sample this morning, and the heel site oozed for 20 minutes. She was born at term at home after an uncomplicated pregnancy. Her parents declined all newborn injections. She is exclusively breastfed and has regained her birth weight. Temperature is 36.8°C, pulse 148/min and respirations 38/min. She is alert and jaundiced, with a soft, flat fontanelle. The liver is firm, 3 cm below the right costal margin. There is no bruising and no petechiae. Results: total bilirubin 186 µmol/L, conjugated bilirubin 121 µmol/L (less than 25), INR 3.6 (0.9 to 1.2), APTT 66 s (25 to 38), platelets 305 x 10^9/L and haemoglobin 131 g/L. Cranial ultrasound shows no haemorrhage.
items.ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Phytomenadione 1 mg by slow intravenous injection
items.explanation: This infant has conjugated (cholestatic) jaundice with pale stools, dark urine and a firm liver, which should be treated as biliary atresia until it is ruled out. She also has late vitamin K deficiency bleeding. She never had prophylaxis, she is exclusively breastfed, and cholestasis stops her absorbing fat-soluble vitamins. Her INR and APTT are prolonged, her platelets are normal, and the heel site oozed. This may be a warning bleed before an intracranial haemorrhage. Australian guidance (NHMRC, RCH jaundice in early infancy) says to give vitamin K 1 mg straight away, without waiting for further results. In hospital it is given by slow IV injection, which works within hours and avoids a haematoma from an IM injection while clotting is deranged. Repeat the INR afterwards. The urgent cholestasis work-up and referral to the liver service go ahead at the same time. Plasma products are kept for active serious bleeding, and the cranial ultrasound shows no haemorrhage.
why: Oral vitamin K is poorly and unpredictably absorbed when there is cholestasis and fat malabsorption, so it is not acceptable for treating a deficiency.
Fresh frozen plasma is kept for active life-threatening bleeding or intracranial haemorrhage, and neither is present here, so vitamin K alone is the right treatment.
Phototherapy treats unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia and does nothing for conjugated jaundice or the coagulopathy, which is the immediate danger.
Ursodeoxycholic acid may be used later in some cholestatic conditions, but it does not correct the prolonged INR and it does not treat the bleeding risk.

items.stem: A 27-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department with breathlessness and wheeze that began 6 hours ago, two days into a head cold. She has had asthma since childhood and uses only a salbutamol reliever. When she arrived 70 minutes ago, she could speak only in phrases and was using her accessory muscles. Since then she has had salbutamol 12 puffs and ipratropium 8 puffs via spacer every 20 minutes for three doses, prednisolone 50 mg orally, and oxygen by nasal prongs. She is alert but still speaks in phrases and uses her accessory muscles. Temperature is 37.4 °C, pulse 118/min, respirations 28/min, blood pressure 124/76 mm Hg and SpO2 94% on 2 L/min oxygen. There is widespread expiratory wheeze with equal air entry on both sides, and no rash or lip swelling. Venous blood gas: pH 7.44, pCO2 36 mmHg (reference 41–51), lactate 2.1 mmol/L. Chest X-ray shows hyperinflation, with no pneumothorax or consolidation. Salbutamol is being continued.
items.ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
items.explanation: This is severe acute asthma (she speaks only in phrases and uses her accessory muscles) that has not responded well to an hour of standard treatment. She has had repeated salbutamol and ipratropium by spacer, oral prednisolone within the first hour, and oxygen titrated to an SpO2 of 92–96%. The Australian Asthma Handbook and eTG advise adding IV magnesium sulfate (10 mmol over 20 minutes in adults) for severe or life-threatening asthma that responds poorly to the first bronchodilators. Salbutamol continues alongside it. She has no life-threatening features: she is alert, her SpO2 is 90% or above, her pCO2 is low rather than normal or rising, and her chest is not silent. So she does not yet need intubation, but she needs senior review and close monitoring. Aminophylline is not recommended in Australian guidelines because it adds little to standard treatment and causes arrhythmias, vomiting and seizures. IM adrenaline is for anaphylaxis or impending arrest, and she has no urticaria, angioedema or hypotension. IV hydrocortisone adds nothing when oral prednisolone has been given and can be swallowed. Antibiotics are not indicated, because the trigger is viral and there is no consolidation.
why: Aminophylline is not recommended in Australian guidelines: it gives little extra bronchodilation and has a narrow therapeutic index, with a risk of arrhythmias and seizures.
IM adrenaline is for anaphylaxis or near-arrest, and she has no urticaria, angioedema, stridor or hypotension.
She has already had oral prednisolone and can swallow; IV corticosteroid is no more effective and is only needed when oral intake is not possible.
A viral cold triggered this attack, and with no fever, purulent sputum or consolidation there is no indication for antibiotics.

items.stem: A 41-year-old woman sees her general practitioner because she has not opened her bowels for 6 days. Nine days ago she had an uncomplicated laparoscopic appendicectomy. She went home on oxycodone 5 mg up to four times daily, which she still takes three times a day. She was given no bowel medicine. Her last stools were small and hard. She had to strain, passing them caused sharp anal pain, and there was bright red blood on the toilet paper. She is passing flatus and has no vomiting or abdominal pain. She takes ferrous sulfate for iron deficiency. Temperature is 36.8 °C, pulse 78/min and blood pressure 120/78 mm Hg. Her abdomen is soft and non-tender, and bowel sounds are normal. Anal inspection shows a posterior midline fissure. Digital rectal examination finds hard stool and no mass. Haemoglobin is 124 g/L (115–165), ferritin 20 µg/L (30–300), corrected calcium 2.38 mmol/L (2.10–2.60) and TSH 1.4 mIU/L (0.5–4.0). The opioid will be weaned and simple analgesia started.
items.ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate laxative treatment?
items.explanation: This woman has opioid-induced constipation, made worse by oral iron and less activity after surgery. Passing hard stool has caused an acute anal fissure. Postoperative ileus and obstruction are unlikely: she is passing flatus, has no pain or vomiting, and her abdomen is soft with normal bowel sounds. Opioids slow gut transit and make stools dry and hard. eTG recommends a regular stimulant laxative (such as senna) combined with an osmotic laxative (such as macrogol) for opioid-induced constipation, continued while she takes the opioid. Treatment should then be stepped down. Softening the stool is also the main treatment for the fissure: it stops the repeated tearing that keeps the fissure from healing and that would push it toward becoming chronic. Fibre, warm baths and simple analgesia help as well, and topical glyceryl trinitrate or diltiazem can be added if the fissure does not heal. Bulk-forming agents add volume without improving the slowed transit, and can make symptoms worse. Peripherally acting opioid antagonists are used only when standard laxatives have failed. Softeners alone and as-needed rectal treatment are not enough for ongoing opioid use.
why: Bulk-forming laxatives are not recommended in opioid-induced constipation because they add bulk to slowed bowel and can worsen bloating and impaction.
Peripherally acting opioid antagonists are kept for constipation that has not responded to standard laxatives, which she has not yet tried.
A stool softener on its own does not overcome the slowed transit caused by opioids and is not effective enough as the only treatment.
As-needed suppositories are a rescue measure, not maintenance therapy, and inserting them through a painful acute fissure is poorly tolerated.

items.stem: A 34-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department by ambulance 40 minutes after her horse fell on her during a trail ride, crushing the right side of her chest. She had right-sided pleuritic pain straight away and has become steadily more breathless during transport. She has no past medical history and takes only a combined oral contraceptive pill. On arrival she is agitated and can speak only in single words. Temperature is 36.4 °C, pulse 138/min, blood pressure 82/50 mmHg, respiratory rate 34/min, and oxygen saturation 85% on 15 L/min via a non-rebreather mask. Her trachea is deviated to the left and her neck veins are distended. There is bruising and tenderness over the right lateral ribs. The right hemithorax is hyper-resonant to percussion, and breath sounds are absent on the right. Heart sounds are clearly audible. Two large-bore cannulae are in place and blood has been sent for group and hold. A mobile chest X-ray has been requested, and the radiographer will arrive in 10 minutes.
items.ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Portable chest X-ray to confirm the diagnosis before any chest procedure
Subxiphoid pericardiocentesis guided by bedside ultrasound
Rapid sequence intubation followed by positive-pressure ventilation
Needle decompression at the fifth intercostal space just anterior to the mid-axillary line
Intravenous bolus of 1 L warmed crystalloid over 15 minutes
items.explanation: This woman has a right tension pneumothorax after blunt chest trauma, with obstructive shock. She has hypoxia, tachycardia, hypotension, distended neck veins, tracheal deviation away from the injured side, and a hyper-resonant hemithorax with absent breath sounds. Tension pneumothorax is a clinical diagnosis. ATLS (11th edition) and eTG advise treating it as soon as it is recognised, without waiting for imaging. In adults, the preferred site for needle decompression is the 4th or 5th intercostal space just anterior to the mid-axillary line, because the chest wall is thinner there and the catheter is more likely to reach the pleura than at the 2nd intercostal space in the mid-clavicular line. Finger thoracostomy at the same site is an acceptable alternative. After decompression, an intercostal catheter is placed in the safe triangle and connected to an underwater seal. A chest X-ray should be done only after that.
why: Wrong: tension pneumothorax is diagnosed clinically, and waiting 10 minutes for a film in a hypotensive, hypoxic patient risks cardiac arrest.

Wrong: tamponade is unlikely because her trachea is deviated, one side of her chest is hyper-resonant with absent breath sounds, and her heart sounds are clear, so the chest needs decompressing rather than the pericardium.
Wrong: positive-pressure ventilation forces more air into the pleural space and can quickly worsen a tension pneumothorax and cause arrest if the chest has not been decompressed first.
Wrong: her shock is obstructive, not caused by blood loss, so fluid will not restore venous return while the tension pneumothorax is untreated, and giving it delays the treatment that saves her life.

items.stem: A 68-year-old woman is reviewed on the medical ward on day 3 of treatment for herpes simplex virus type 1 encephalitis, confirmed by CSF PCR. She has rheumatoid arthritis, and her weekly methotrexate has been withheld since admission. She weighs 70 kg and is receiving aciclovir 10 mg/kg IV every 8 hours. She is still drowsy and has been drinking little. Her maintenance drip was taken down yesterday when the cannula tissued, and it was not restarted. Her urine output over the past 12 hours is 250 mL. Temperature is 37.6 °C, pulse 98/min, blood pressure 112/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min and SpO2 97% on room air. Her mucous membranes are dry, and there is no new focal neurological deficit. Serum creatinine is 164 µmol/L (72 µmol/L on admission; reference 45–90), urea 11.8 mmol/L, sodium 140 mmol/L and potassium 4.6 mmol/L. Urine microscopy shows needle-shaped birefringent crystals.
items.ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Stop the antiviral and start oral valaciclovir 1 g three times daily
Stop the antiviral and start intravenous foscarnet
Continue the current regimen and add intravenous furosemide 40 mg
Arrange urgent haemodialysis through a temporary vascular catheter
Start isotonic crystalloid and reduce antiviral dosing to match renal function
items.explanation: This patient has acute kidney injury from aciclovir crystal nephropathy. Aciclovir is cleared by the kidneys and is poorly soluble in urine, so high-dose IV therapy in a dehydrated patient lets crystals form in the renal tubules. This is the main complication to prevent during treatment of HSV encephalitis, and it is why eTG advises keeping the patient well hydrated and monitoring renal function throughout. Her intake is poor, her drip has been stopped, she is oliguric with dry mucous membranes, her creatinine has more than doubled and her urine shows needle-shaped birefringent crystals. The right step is to restart isotonic IV fluids and adjust the aciclovir dose to her estimated creatinine clearance. Her Cockcroft-Gault clearance is about 30 mL/min, which calls for 10 mg/kg every 12 hours. IV therapy should continue for the full course, at least 14 to 21 days in an immunosuppressed patient, because stopping or under-treating HSV encephalitis carries high mortality and neurological morbidity. The injury usually reverses with hydration and dose adjustment. Methotrexate should stay withheld, because it is also cleared by the kidneys and would add toxicity.
why: Wrong: oral valaciclovir is not recommended for acute HSV encephalitis while the patient is drowsy and still in the IV phase, and it is converted to aciclovir, so it would not prevent crystal formation.
Wrong: foscarnet is reserved for aciclovir-resistant HSV and is more nephrotoxic, so it would make her kidney injury worse.
Wrong: furosemide would deepen her volume depletion and does nothing to clear crystals, and keeping full-dose aciclovir at this clearance would cause further accumulation and toxicity.
Wrong: she has no indication for urgent dialysis (no hyperkalaemia, acidosis, fluid overload or uraemic complications), and this injury usually reverses with hydration and dose adjustment.

items.stem: A newborn boy is assessed in the birth suite 10 minutes after a spontaneous vaginal birth at 39 weeks' gestation. He weighs 3.6 kg. In the final 8 minutes of the second stage, the cardiotocograph showed a fetal heart rate of about 70/min. At birth he was floppy and apnoeic with a heart rate of 70/min. Mask ventilation in air gave no chest rise until his head was repositioned. Once his chest was rising, his heart rate reached 140/min by 3 minutes. Apgar scores were 1 at 1 minute and 7 at 5 minutes. His mother used nitrous oxide only. Her group B streptococcus screen was negative, membranes ruptured 4 hours before birth and the liquor was clear. He is now breathing on his own and crying. Temperature is 36.8 °C, heart rate is 145/min, respirations are 50/min and preductal SpO2 is 88% in room air. He lies in a flexed posture with normal tone and a strong suck. The placenta was delivered 5 minutes ago and is still in the room.
items.ask: Which of the following investigations is the most appropriate next step to confirm the suspected cause of his condition at birth?
options: Blood culture and serum C-reactive protein
Paired umbilical arterial and venous blood gas
Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain
items.explanation:
This term baby had a sudden, long fetal bradycardia, was floppy and apnoeic at birth, and recovered quickly once ventilation worked. This points to respiratory depression from acute perinatal hypoxia. The test that confirms this and measures how severe it is: paired cord blood gases from a double-clamped segment of cord, taken as soon as possible after birth. A valid pair has the artery showing a lower pH and a higher pCO2 than the vein. The arterial pH, base excess and lactate measure the acidaemia. They also show whether the baby meets the hypoxia criterion for therapeutic hypothermia (pH 7.0 or less, or a base deficit of 12 mmol/L or more, in the first hour). That matters because cooling works best if started within 6 hours. The placenta is still in the room, so the cord can be sampled now.

Blood culture and CRP: sepsis is unlikely here. GBS was negative, membranes ruptured only 4 hours before birth, there was no maternal fever and the liquor was clear. CRP is also unreliable this early after birth.

aEEG: this monitors babies who already have encephalopathy. This baby has normal tone, cries and sucks well.

MRI brain: this assesses the extent of HIE injury, usually around days 4 to 7. It does not confirm perinatal hypoxia at birth.

Cranial ultrasound: this is mainly a screen for intraventricular haemorrhage in preterm babies. It is insensitive for early hypoxic injury at term.
why: Sepsis is unlikely with a negative GBS screen, membranes ruptured only 4 hours before birth and clear liquor, and CRP is unreliable in the first hours of life.
aEEG is for monitoring a baby who already shows moderate to severe encephalopathy, and this baby has normal tone, a strong suck and cries.
MRI shows the pattern of HIE injury days after birth but cannot confirm the hypoxic event in the first hour.
Cranial ultrasound mainly screens preterm babies for intraventricular haemorrhage and is insensitive for early hypoxic injury in a term baby.

items.stem: A 2-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department at 11 pm by his mother with noisy breathing. He has had a runny nose and fever for 2 days, and this evening developed a barking cough and a hoarse cry. He is fully immunised and has no medical history. He weighs 12 kg. On arrival he was agitated, with stridor at rest, marked sternal and subcostal recession, and SpO2 91% in room air. He was given nebulised adrenaline 1:1000 (5 mL undiluted) and oral dexamethasone 7.2 mg (0.6 mg/kg), with oxygen held near his face. Sixty minutes later he is sitting on his mother's lap and playing. Temperature is 37.6 °C, pulse 132/min, respiratory rate 28/min, and SpO2 97% in room air. He has an occasional barking cough, no stridor at rest and no chest wall recession. His mother would like to take him home now because his older sister is home alone with a neighbour.
items.ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Discharge home now with written advice on when to return
Obtain a lateral neck X-ray before deciding on discharge
Give a second nebulised adrenaline treatment before discharge
Observe for at least 3 hours after the last adrenaline treatment
Arrange admission to intensive care for elective intubation
items.explanation: This child had severe croup: stridor at rest, a marked increase in work of breathing, agitation and hypoxaemia. Nebulised adrenaline works within minutes but wears off within about 2 hours. Dexamethasone takes several hours to reach full effect, so the obstruction can come back once the adrenaline wears off. The RCH Croup CPG says to observe for at least 3 hours after the last adrenaline dose. Discharge is appropriate only if there is still no stridor at rest at that point, with clear safety-netting advice. The improvement at 60 minutes is likely the adrenaline effect and is not proof that the illness is settling. A mild tachycardia is expected after adrenaline. Discharging now risks the obstruction returning at home in the middle of the night. A lateral neck X-ray is not needed in typical croup, would not change management and could upset the child. Giving more adrenaline to a child with no stridor at rest has no benefit, and it would only restart the observation period. Intubation is for impending airway failure, such as exhaustion, ongoing hypoxaemia or repeated adrenaline needs, and this child has responded well.
why: Correct: the adrenaline effect lasts only about 2 hours, before the steroid has fully taken effect, so the RCH advises observing for at least 3 hours after the last dose and discharging only if there is still no stridor at rest.
Wrong: croup is a clinical diagnosis and this course is typical, so imaging would not change management and upsetting the child can worsen obstruction.
Wrong: adrenaline is given for severe obstruction such as stridor at rest with marked work of breathing, and has no preventive role in a child who has none.
Wrong: intubation is kept for a tiring child, ongoing hypoxaemia or repeated adrenaline needs, none of which this improving child has.

items.stem:
A 19-year-old man is brought to the emergency department by ambulance from a general practice. He has had 14 hours of worsening generalised headache, fever and photophobia. Five days ago he came back from a week in a crowded backpacker hostel. The general practitioner gave benzylpenicillin 2.4 g intramuscularly 4 hours ago, before transfer. He takes no medicines, and his vaccination history is unknown. His temperature is 38.8 °C, pulse 116/min, respirations 22/min, blood pressure 118/72 mm Hg and SpO2 98% on room air. He is alert and oriented (GCS 15). He has neck stiffness, with no focal neurological signs, papilloedema or rash. Two sets of blood cultures were taken on arrival. Lumbar puncture fluid analysis shows:
Appearance: turbid
Neutrophils: 2900 x10^6/L (reference 0)
Lymphocytes: 40 x10^6/L (reference less than 5)
Protein: 1.3 g/L (reference 0.15 to 0.45)
Glucose: 1.1 mmol/L (paired serum glucose 5.6 mmol/L)
Gram stain: neutrophils seen, no organisms seen
items.ask: Which of the following investigations is most likely to identify the causative organism?
options: Bacterial culture of the CSF sample
Bacterial PCR on the CSF sample
Repeat blood cultures from two sites
Viral PCR panel on the CSF sample
items.explanation: This young adult has fever, headache, photophobia and neck stiffness after crowded living. His lumbar puncture fluid shows a marked neutrophil-predominant pleocytosis, high protein and a CSF-to-serum glucose ratio of about 0.2 (below 0.4). These findings mean bacterial meningitis, most likely meningococcal. He correctly had parenteral benzylpenicillin in general practice before transfer. However, that dose sterilises the CSF and blood within hours, which explains why the Gram stain shows no organisms and why culture yield will be low. Nucleic acid testing (PCR) for Neisseria meningitidis, Streptococcus pneumoniae and Haemophilus influenzae on the CSF does not need live bacteria. It stays positive for days after antibiotics have started. eTG and the CDNA invasive meningococcal disease guidelines recommend it, and it is the test most likely to confirm the organism (and give the serogroup for public health) in a pretreated patient. Culture of the CSF should still be sent, because it gives antibiotic susceptibilities, but it is less likely to grow anything. Repeat blood cultures taken even later after antibiotics will give an even lower yield. A throat swab shows only nasopharyngeal carriage, so it cannot confirm invasive disease. A viral PCR panel does not fit the bacterial CSF picture.
why: Correct: PCR detects bacterial DNA even after antibiotics have killed the organisms, so it is the most sensitive way to confirm N. meningitidis (and its serogroup) in pretreated meningitis.
Blood cultures taken even longer after the antibiotic dose are less likely to grow anything than the sets already taken on arrival.
A positive throat culture shows only nasopharyngeal carriage, which is common in young adults, so it supports the diagnosis but cannot confirm invasive disease.
A neutrophilic CSF with high protein and a glucose ratio below 0.4 points to a bacterial cause, not a viral one, so a viral panel will not identify this organism.

items.stem: A 29-year-old woman comes back to her general practitioner 6 weeks after she was diagnosed with ulcerative colitis. Before the diagnosis she had 10 weeks of bloody, mucousy diarrhoea and left-sided abdominal cramps. Stool pathogen tests were negative. Ileocolonoscopy found continuous mucosal inflammation from the rectum to 30 cm and a normal proximal colon and terminal ileum. Biopsies showed crypt distortion with no granulomas and no dysplasia. She now takes oral mesalazine and mesalazine enemas. She has 1 to 2 formed stools a day with no blood. She has never smoked. Her mother was diagnosed with bowel cancer at age 62. No other relatives have had bowel cancer. Temperature is 36.7°C, blood pressure 116/72 mmHg and pulse 72/min. Her abdomen is soft and not tender. Haemoglobin is 129 g/L (115–165), CRP 3 mg/L (<5), ALP 74 U/L (30–110) and GGT 18 U/L (<40). She asks how her bowel cancer risk will be checked.
items.ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate surveillance plan for this patient?
options: Colonoscopy from 8 years after disease onset
Faecal immunochemical test every 2 years from age 45
CT colonography every 5 years starting now
items.explanation: Ulcerative colitis that reaches beyond the rectum raises the risk of colorectal cancer. Her colitis runs from the rectum to 30 cm, so it is left-sided (Montreal E2) and not proctitis alone. The risk depends on how long she has had colitis, how much colon is involved and how much inflammation there is. Cancer Council Australia and GESA recommend a first colonoscopy about 8 years after symptoms began. This colonoscopy restages the disease and uses chromoendoscopy or multiple biopsies to look for dysplasia. After that, the interval (1, 3 or 5 years) is set by risk factors such as ongoing inflammation, strictures, past dysplasia, PSC and family history. Her mother's cancer at 62 may shorten later intervals, but it does not change the start point. Population or family-history screening does not apply to her, because her colitis is the bigger risk and needs colonoscopy with targeted biopsies. Annual colonoscopy straight away is only for coexisting primary sclerosing cholangitis, and her normal ALP and GGT make this unlikely.
why: Colonoscopy every 5 years from 45 is family-history screening for a first-degree relative diagnosed under 55, which does not fit her history and starts too late for her colitis risk.
Two-yearly faecal immunochemical tests are average-risk population screening, and they cannot detect flat colitis-associated dysplasia or tell it apart from inflammatory bleeding.
Annual colonoscopy from diagnosis is for patients who also have primary sclerosing cholangitis, and her normal ALP and GGT make this unlikely.
CT colonography cannot take biopsies or show flat dysplasia, so it is not used for surveillance in inflammatory bowel disease.

items.stem:
A 24-year-old man is brought to the emergency department by ambulance with a headache that has got steadily worse over 6 hours. The headache is generalised and throbbing, and he has fever, rigors, vomiting and pain when looking at lights. He has no history of headaches, head injury or seizures, and he takes no medicines. His temperature is 39.3 °C, pulse 118/min, blood pressure 110/70 mm Hg, respiratory rate 22/min and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. He is alert and oriented, with a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 15. Neck flexion is painful and restricted. Fundoscopy shows sharp optic disc margins. Cranial nerve and limb examinations are normal, and there is no rash. Blood cultures are taken, and he is given dexamethasone 10 mg IV and ceftriaxone 2 g IV. Laboratory studies show:
White cell count 19.6 x10^9/L (4.0 to 11.0)
Platelets 245 x10^9/L (150 to 400)
INR 1.0 (0.9 to 1.2)
C-reactive protein 210 mg/L (less than 5)
items.ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate next investigation?
items.explanation: This man has fever, a headache that built up over hours, photophobia and neck stiffness, so he has bacterial meningitis until proven otherwise. The right first steps have been taken: blood cultures, then dexamethasone and ceftriaxone without waiting for any test. Lumbar puncture is the next investigation. CSF cell count, protein, glucose ratio, Gram stain, culture with susceptibilities and PCR confirm the diagnosis, identify the organism and guide how antibiotics are narrowed and how long they are given. Under eTG, CT before LP is needed only if there is a contraindication: reduced or falling GCS, focal neurological signs, a recent seizure, papilloedema or immunocompromise. He has none of these. His platelets and INR are normal, so it is safe to go straight to LP. Organisms can often still be found in CSF in the first hours after antibiotics, and cell count, protein and glucose changes last longer, so LP should be done promptly and not put off.
why: Correct: with GCS 15, no focal signs, no seizure, no papilloedema and normal platelets and coagulation, LP is safe without imaging, and CSF analysis is the test that confirms bacterial meningitis and identifies the organism.
MRI with contrast can show meningeal enhancement or complications, but it is slow, hard to get in the ED and does not identify the organism or confirm bacterial meningitis.
CT angiography looks for an aneurysm in subarachnoid haemorrhage, which is unlikely here because the headache built up over 6 hours with high fever and was not a thunderclap onset.
Blood meningococcal PCR is a useful extra test, especially after antibiotics, but it detects only one organism and does not replace CSF analysis as the test that confirms meningitis.

items.stem: A 71-year-old woman presents to her general practitioner with 3 days of cough productive of green sputum, fevers, and left-sided chest pain that is worse on inspiration. Six days ago she was discharged from hospital after a 4-day admission to investigate syncope. On the ward she walked daily and received prophylactic enoxaparin. She has hypertension treated with amlodipine and has never smoked. She has no haemoptysis and no history of venous thromboembolism or cancer. Her temperature is 38.5 °C, pulse 106/min, respirations 24/min, blood pressure 132/78 mm Hg, and SpO2 93% on room air. There is dullness and bronchial breathing at the left base. Both calves are soft and nontender, and there is no leg swelling. A chest X-ray shows new consolidation in the left lower lobe. Results: white cell count 15.2 x10^9/L (4.0 to 11.0), CRP 151 mg/L (less than 5), urea 7.9 mmol/L (2.5 to 7.5), D-dimer 0.63 mg/L FEU (less than 0.50).
items.ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in evaluating her for pulmonary embolism?
items.explanation: Start by working out her pre-test probability. Her Wells score is 1.5: she gets 1.5 for a heart rate over 100/min and nothing else. She was not immobilised, because she walked daily on the ward and had prophylactic enoxaparin. She had no surgery, her calves are normal, she has no haemoptysis, no past VTE and no cancer, and pneumonia explains her illness better than PE does. A Wells score of 4 or less means PE is unlikely, so a D-dimer is the right test to rule it out. In patients over 50, the D-dimer cut-off is age-adjusted: age x 0.01 mg/L FEU, which is 0.71 mg/L for a 71-year-old. Her D-dimer of 0.63 mg/L is above the standard laboratory limit of 0.50 but below her age-adjusted cut-off. This is a negative result, and with low pre-test probability it excludes PE (eTG Cardiovascular; ADJUST-PE). She needs no further tests for PE. The next step is to manage the left lower lobe pneumonia, which began soon after a hospital stay. CT pulmonary angiography is wrong because it is only needed if PE is likely (Wells over 4) or the D-dimer is above the age-adjusted cut-off. A V/Q scan is wrong because it is another imaging test for PE, used instead of CTPA when contrast is unsafe, and it is not needed once PE has been excluded. Compression ultrasound of the legs is wrong because her legs are normal on examination and PE has already been excluded. Repeating the D-dimer is wrong because the first result is already negative using the correct cut-off, and repeating it only delays treatment.
why: CT pulmonary angiography is wrong because it is only needed when PE is likely (Wells over 4) or the D-dimer is above the age-adjusted cut-off of 0.71 mg/L, and neither applies to her.

A V/Q scan is wrong because it is an alternative to CTPA for patients who cannot have contrast, and with a low Wells score and a D-dimer below the age-adjusted cut-off she does not need imaging for PE.
Compression ultrasound of both legs is wrong because her calves are normal with no swelling, and a negative D-dimer with low pre-test probability has already excluded thromboembolism.
Repeating the D-dimer is wrong because the first result is already negative using the correct cut-off, so a repeat adds nothing and delays treatment of her pneumonia.

items.stem: A 27-year-old man comes to the emergency department 2 hours after he was punched in the face outside a hotel. He says both sides of his nose are blocked and his nose is painful. He had a nosebleed that stopped on its own after 10 minutes. He has no clear fluid running from his nose, no double vision and no headache. He takes no regular medicines and has no allergies. His temperature is 36.8 °C, pulse 88/min, blood pressure 128/78 mm Hg, respiratory rate 16/min and oxygen saturation 99% on room air. The nasal bridge is swollen and bent to the left. After phenylephrine–lidocaine spray, anterior rhinoscopy shows a smooth, red-purple swelling on both sides of the septum that blocks both nostrils. The swelling has not shrunk and feels soft and fluctuant when pressed with a cotton bud. Eye movements are full, cheek sensation is normal and his bite is normal.
items.ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Same-day incision and drainage with bilateral nasal packing
Closed reduction of the nasal bones in 7 days
Oral amoxicillin–clavulanate with review in 48 hours
Silver nitrate cautery to the anterior septum
CT of the facial bones before specialist review
items.explanation: This man has a bilateral nasal septal haematoma. After a blow to the nose he has blockage on both sides, and on both sides of the septum there is a smooth, red-purple, fluctuant swelling that does not shrink with a decongestant. Septal cartilage has no blood supply of its own and gets its nutrients from the overlying mucoperichondrium. Blood collecting under the perichondrium lifts it off the cartilage. Within about 24 to 72 hours this can cause cartilage necrosis and infection. The results are a septal abscess, which can spread to the cavernous sinus or the meninges, a septal perforation and a saddle nose deformity. Bilateral haematomas carry the highest risk. The aim is to prevent these complications, so the haematoma must be drained the same day, by ENT or by a trained emergency doctor: incise and drain each side, then use bilateral packing or septal splints to stop it filling again. He should also have antibiotics that cover Staphylococcus aureus (as advised in Therapeutic Guidelines) and early ENT follow-up. The displaced nasal fractures can be reduced later, once the swelling settles. Safety-net advice: return straight away if the blockage comes back, or if he develops fever, more pain or a change in the shape of his nose.
why: Delayed closed reduction is right for the displaced nasal bone fracture on its own, but a 7-day wait would let the septal cartilage die and become infected.
Antibiotics are added after drainage, but on their own they cannot remove the blood starving the cartilage, so the necrosis and abscess risk stays.
Cautery treats bleeding from vessels in Little's area; it does nothing for a blood collection under the perichondrium, and his nosebleed has already stopped.
This is a clinical diagnosis, he has no features of a naso-orbito-ethmoid, orbital or other facial fracture, and waiting for imaging delays drainage that should not be delayed.

items.stem: A 38-year-old woman comes to a general practice in July because of a dry cough that started suddenly 3 days ago. She also has fevers, muscle aches, fatigue, a sore throat and a blocked nose. Two colleagues at the café where she works have had similar symptoms this week. She has no breathlessness or chest pain. She has no history of serious illness, takes no medicines, is not pregnant and did not have an influenza vaccine this year. She smokes 10 cigarettes daily. Her temperature is 38.2 °C, pulse 96/min, respiratory rate 16/min, blood pressure 122/76 mm Hg and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. She is alert and talking in full sentences. The pharynx is mildly red without exudate. The chest is clear to auscultation. A multiplex nasopharyngeal PCR swab shows: influenza A RNA detected; influenza B RNA not detected; SARS-CoV-2 RNA not detected; respiratory syncytial virus RNA not detected; Bordetella pertussis DNA not detected.
items.ask: Based on these results, which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Oral oseltamivir 75 mg twice daily for 5 days
Oral amoxicillin 1 g three times daily for 5 days
Paracetamol, fluids and rest, avoiding contact with others until well
Chest X-ray within the next 24 hours
Repeat SARS-CoV-2 rapid antigen test in 48 hours
items.explanation: The PCR confirms influenza A and rules out SARS-CoV-2, RSV and pertussis. Her observations show fever and a high-normal heart rate, but her respiratory rate, oxygen saturation and blood pressure are normal, she is alert and her chest is clear. Together these results mean uncomplicated influenza in a healthy adult. She has no complications and no risk factors for severe disease (she is not pregnant, not immunocompromised and has no chronic heart or lung disease). The right management is symptom relief with paracetamol, fluids and rest. She should stay away from work and other people until she is well, and use cough etiquette and hand hygiene. She should also be offered next season's influenza vaccine and brief smoking cessation advice, and told to seek urgent care if she becomes breathless at rest, gets chest pain or confusion, or gets worse again after improving. eTG keeps oseltamivir for severe illness or people at higher risk. In healthy adults it only modestly shortens symptoms, and only when started within 48 hours of onset. She is at day 3. Antibiotics do not help a viral infection when there is no sign of bacterial pneumonia. A chest X-ray is not needed when the chest is clear and saturation is normal. A negative multiplex PCR is more sensitive than a rapid antigen test, and another cause has already been found.
why: Wrong: oseltamivir is for severe illness or higher-risk patients, and she is a healthy, non-pregnant adult at day 3, past the 48-hour window where it helps a little.
Wrong: the illness is confirmed viral, with a clear chest and normal saturation, so there is no sign of bacterial pneumonia that would justify antibiotics.
Wrong: a clear chest, normal respiratory rate and 98% saturation on room air give no sign of pneumonia, so imaging would not change management.
Wrong: a negative SARS-CoV-2 PCR is more sensitive than a rapid antigen test, and influenza A already explains her illness, so retesting adds nothing.

items.stem: A 47-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with 8 hours of constant, severe epigastric pain that radiates to her back, with repeated vomiting. The pain began 2 hours after a large evening meal. She drinks 2 standard drinks on weekends and does not smoke. She has type 2 diabetes treated with metformin. Her BMI is 34 kg/m2. Temperature is 37.6 °C, pulse 104/min, blood pressure 128/80 mmHg, respiratory rate 18/min and SpO2 97% on room air. She has epigastric tenderness with voluntary guarding, no rigidity and no jaundice. ECG shows sinus tachycardia with no ST changes. Results: lipase 2400 U/L (reference <60), white cell count 13.2 x10^9/L, CRP 40 mg/L, total bilirubin 22 µmol/L (<20), ALT 186 U/L (<35), ALP 140 U/L (30–110), corrected calcium 2.35 mmol/L, triglycerides 1.8 mmol/L and creatinine 78 µmol/L. IV fluids and titrated opioid analgesia have been started.
items.ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate next investigation?
options: Contrast-enhanced computed tomography of the pancreas
items.explanation: She already meets 2 of the 3 criteria for acute pancreatitis: typical epigastric pain going through to the back, and a lipase more than 3 times the upper limit. The diagnosis is made, so the next step is to find the cause. Gallstones cause about half of all cases. An early ALT above about 150 U/L strongly suggests a biliary cause, and her obesity and diabetes add to the risk. Her calcium and triglycerides are normal and she drinks little alcohol. Australian guidance (eTG) and international guidance say every patient with acute pancreatitis should have a transabdominal ultrasound on admission to look for gallstones and a dilated bile duct. This is because a gallstone cause changes management: ERCP if there is cholangitis or a persisting duct stone, and cholecystectomy in the same admission for mild gallstone pancreatitis. The test is quick, cheap, uses no radiation and can be done at the bedside. Early contrast CT does not help when the diagnosis is already clear. ERCP is for cholangitis or a proven obstruction that persists. MRCP and endoscopic ultrasound are second-line tests for when the ultrasound is unclear or no cause is found. Amylase adds nothing once the lipase is raised.
why: Contrast CT is for when the diagnosis is uncertain, or for looking for necrosis if she deteriorates after 72 hours; the diagnosis is already made, and CT in the first days underestimates necrosis and is poor at showing gallstones.
ERCP is invasive, carries a risk of making pancreatitis worse, and in the early phase is only for cholangitis or a proven persisting bile duct obstruction, neither of which has been shown here.
MRCP is a second-line test for suspected duct stones when the ultrasound is unclear or the liver tests stay abnormal; it should not come before the first-line ultrasound.
Amylase is less specific than lipase and clears sooner, so it adds nothing to a lipase already more than 30 times the upper limit and does not show the cause.
