items.stem: A 33-year-old man who works as a mechanic sees his general practitioner because of tiredness for 4 months. He drinks about 4 L of water a day. He gets up three times a night to pass urine, even when he avoids drinks in the evening. He has gained 15 kg over 2 years and has not lost weight recently. He has hypertension treated with perindopril and takes no other medicines. He smokes 15 cigarettes a day. His father has type 2 diabetes. His temperature is 36.7 °C, pulse 82/min, blood pressure 138/86 mm Hg and respiratory rate 14/min. His BMI is 36 kg/m². He has velvety, darkened skin in both axillae and looks well hydrated. Urine dipstick shows glucose 3+, ketones negative, protein negative and specific gravity 1.025. A random fingerprick reading on the practice meter is 15.2 mmol/L.
items.ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate next investigation to confirm the diagnosis?
items.explanation: This man has the typical symptoms of hyperglycaemia: thirst, polyuria and nocturia that continues when he drinks less in the evening. He also has metabolic risk factors: obesity, acanthosis nigricans, hypertension, smoking and a family history of type 2 diabetes. His urine is concentrated and full of glucose, and he has no ketones, which points to type 2 diabetes. A fingerprick meter reading is not enough to diagnose diabetes, so the RACGP handbook and eTG require a laboratory test. HbA1c is the most appropriate test. A level of 6.5% (48 mmol/mol) or more diagnoses diabetes, he does not need to fast for it, and Medicare funds it for diagnosis. Because he has symptoms, one abnormal laboratory result is enough and no repeat test on another day is needed. A fasting or random venous plasma glucose would also be acceptable, but neither is among the options. An oral glucose tolerance test is kept for equivocal results or pregnancy. The water deprivation test, GAD antibodies and C-peptide do not confirm that he has diabetes.
why: An oral glucose tolerance test is kept for equivocal fasting (5.5 to 6.9 mmol/L) or random (5.5 to 11.0 mmol/L) glucose results or for pregnancy, and it is unnecessary and burdensome in a patient with symptoms and marked hyperglycaemia.

A water deprivation test looks for diabetes insipidus, but his urine is concentrated (specific gravity 1.025) and full of glucose, which shows an osmotic diuresis, and fluid restriction could make his dehydration worse.

GAD antibodies help classify suspected type 1 diabetes or latent autoimmune diabetes in adults (for example in a lean patient with weight loss or ketosis), but they do not confirm that diabetes is present.
C-peptide measures how much insulin the pancreas can still make and helps classify the type of diabetes, but it does not diagnose diabetes and can be misleadingly low during hyperglycaemia.

items.stem: A 29-year-old woman comes to a general practice because of recurrent headaches over the past 3 months. She has had four attacks. Each begins with shimmering zigzag lights in one half of her vision that spread slowly over 20 minutes and then clear completely. Within 30 minutes, a throbbing one-sided headache follows, with nausea and sensitivity to light and noise, and lasts about 18 hours. The side varies between attacks, and she is well in between. Her mother has a similar history. She uses a copper intrauterine device, takes ibuprofen during attacks and takes no regular medicines. She is worried that she has a brain tumour. Her temperature is 36.7 °C, pulse 76/min and blood pressure 118/74 mm Hg. There is no neck stiffness. A full neurological examination is normal, including fundoscopy, which shows sharp discs and spontaneous venous pulsations.
items.ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate next investigation?
options: MRI of the brain with gadolinium
items.explanation: This woman has recurrent, stereotyped attacks that meet ICHD-3 criteria for migraine with aura. The aura is a positive visual disturbance that spreads gradually over more than 5 minutes, lasts under 60 minutes, resolves fully and is followed within an hour by a throbbing, unilateral headache with nausea, photophobia and phonophobia. The side varies, she is well between attacks, she has a family history, and her neurological examination and fundi are normal. Migraine is a clinical diagnosis. eTG (Neurology) states that a typical history with a normal examination and no red flags needs no neuroimaging. The most useful next investigation is a diary she keeps from now on, recording when each attack happens, the aura, how long it lasts, triggers, acute medicine days and menstrual timing. The diary confirms the stereotyped pattern and flags any change that would point to a secondary cause. It also counts medicine days to detect medication overuse and gives the attack frequency needed to decide on preventive treatment. Reassure her and explain why she does not need a scan, rather than ordering imaging to ease her worry.
why: MRI is kept for red flags such as an atypical or prolonged aura, a changed pattern, abnormal examination findings or papilloedema, none of which she has, so a scan would not change management.

Non-contrast CT is used for suspected subarachnoid haemorrhage or acute intracranial pathology, but her headaches build up gradually after an aura in a recurrent pattern, and she would receive radiation for no diagnostic benefit.

CT venography is used when cerebral venous sinus thrombosis is suspected, for example with a persistent progressive headache, papilloedema or a prothrombotic risk such as oestrogen use, but she has discrete attacks, normal fundi and a non-hormonal contraceptive.

Electroencephalography is used to investigate seizures, and occipital seizures cause brief coloured circular images lasting seconds to a few minutes, not the slowly spreading zigzag aura followed by migraine headache that she describes.

items.stem: A 63-year-old woman comes to her general practitioner for her annual diabetes review. She has had type 2 diabetes for 14 years. Over the past 4 months, small print has become harder to read with her right eye, even with new reading glasses. She also has hypertension and dyslipidaemia. Her medicines are metformin 1 g twice daily, modified-release gliclazide 60 mg daily, perindopril 5 mg daily and atorvastatin 20 mg daily. Her last eye examination was 2 years ago. Blood pressure is 144/86 mmHg and pulse is 76/min. Visual acuity is 6/18 in the right eye and 6/9 in the left, and the right eye does not improve with a pinhole. Both lenses are clear. Good-quality non-mydriatic retinal photographs show microaneurysms and dot and blot haemorrhages in both eyes, and a ring of hard exudates within one disc diameter of the right fovea. There are no new vessels and no venous beading. HbA1c is 8.8% (73 mmol/mol).
items.ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate investigation to confirm the cause of the reduced vision in her right eye?
items.explanation: She has non-proliferative diabetic retinopathy in both eyes. In the right eye she has hard exudates near the fovea and slowly worsening central vision that a pinhole does not correct, so a refractive error is not the cause. This pattern points to diabetic macular oedema, which causes most vision loss in diabetes and can occur at any stage of retinopathy. Retinal photographs are two-dimensional and cannot show retinal thickening, so they cannot confirm or exclude macular oedema. The NHMRC diabetic retinopathy guideline and the RACGP handbook advise referral to an ophthalmologist. Optical coherence tomography (OCT) is the non-invasive test that confirms the diagnosis. It measures central retinal thickness, shows intraretinal and subretinal fluid, and is used to decide on and monitor anti-VEGF treatment. Fluorescein angiography is an invasive second-line test. Ultrasound is only needed when the fundus cannot be seen. Visual field testing and repeat photographs cannot assess retinal thickness.
why: Fluorescein angiography is invasive, carries a risk of dye reactions, and is kept for assessing ischaemia or new vessels or for planning laser, so it is not the first test to confirm macular oedema.
B-scan ultrasound is used when the view of the retina is blocked, for example by vitreous haemorrhage or dense cataract, but her lenses are clear and the fundus can be seen.
Automated perimetry tests peripheral visual fields for glaucoma or neurological disease, and it cannot show the structural macular changes behind her central blur.
Repeat photographs after dilation give a better view but are still two-dimensional, so they cannot measure retinal thickness or reliably exclude macular oedema.

items.stem: A 36-year-old woman, para 3, is in the birth suite 40 minutes after a spontaneous vaginal birth of twins at 37 weeks' gestation. The placenta is complete and there are no genital tract tears. She keeps bleeding despite intramuscular oxytocin, an oxytocin infusion, intramuscular ergometrine, intramuscular carboprost, an indwelling urinary catheter and bimanual compression. She has been given intravenous tranexamic acid 1 g. The weighed blood loss is 2,000 mL and the blood contains clots. She has no history of a bleeding disorder and takes no regular medicines. Her temperature is 36.3 °C, pulse is 130/min, blood pressure is 86/48 mm Hg, respirations are 26/min and SpO2 is 96% on 6 L/min of oxygen. The fundus is intermittently soft. Two 16-gauge cannulas are in place, the massive transfusion protocol has been activated, O-negative red cells are running and theatre is being prepared. Point-of-care haemoglobin is 82 g/L (reference 115–160 g/L).
items.ask: Which of the following investigations is most appropriate to guide further blood component replacement?
items.explanation: This woman has a major primary postpartum haemorrhage (2,000 mL and still bleeding) from uterine atony. Her risk factors are twins, which overdistend the uterus, and multiparity. Large blood loss leads to dilutional and consumptive coagulopathy, which makes the bleeding worse. In obstetric haemorrhage, fibrinogen is the first clotting factor to fall to a critical level. It falls well before the platelet count or the clotting times change. A fibrinogen level below 2 g/L is the best early lab predictor of progression to severe PPH. RANZCOG, the Queensland Clinical Guidelines and the National Blood Authority Patient Blood Management Module 5 all advise measuring it (Clauss fibrinogen, or FIBTEM on viscoelastic testing where available) and repeating it often. Cryoprecipitate or fibrinogen concentrate is given to keep fibrinogen above 2 g/L. The fact that she is forming clots does not rule out a falling fibrinogen. D-dimer is normally raised in pregnancy and after birth, so it does not help guide replacement. APTT and PT stay normal until late in obstetric haemorrhage, so they are poor early guides. Platelets fall late, usually only after very large losses, so the count is not the best early guide. Haemoglobin lags behind acute blood loss, and red cells are already being given on clinical grounds, so a repeat level does not guide clotting factor replacement.
why: D-dimer is normally raised in pregnancy and the puerperium, so it cannot reliably detect coagulopathy or guide what to give.
The APTT stays normal until late in obstetric haemorrhage, so it misses the early fall in fibrinogen that drives ongoing bleeding.
The platelet count usually falls only after very large losses or with abruption or HELLP, so it is a late and poor guide here.
Haemoglobin lags behind acute blood loss and only measures red cells, so it cannot guide replacement of clotting factors.

items.stem: A 2-year-old girl is brought to a metropolitan emergency department by her father at 03:00 with noisy, fast breathing that started during the evening. She has had a runny nose and cough for 3 days, and several children at her child care centre have colds. Six months ago she had a similar episode during a cold, and it settled within 2 days. She has no cough or wheeze between colds, no choking episode, no new foods and no rash. She has eczema and her immunisations are up to date. Her father smokes outdoors. Her weight is 13 kg. Temperature is 37.9 °C, heart rate 150/min, respiratory rate 42/min, blood pressure 96/60 mm Hg and SpO2 94% on room air. She is alert and talking in short phrases. She has mild subcostal recession and widespread expiratory wheeze, with equal air entry on both sides and no crackles. Inhaled salbutamol is about to be given.
items.ask: In addition to treatment, which of the following is the most appropriate next step in evaluation?
options: Repeated bedside review of response to bronchodilator
Full blood count and C-reactive protein
items.explanation: This toddler has a moderate episode of viral-induced (preschool) wheeze. She has a 3-day coryzal illness, then acute bilateral expiratory wheeze with recession, a similar episode with a previous cold, no symptoms between colds, and risk factors including eczema, child care and smoke exposure. There are no features of anaphylaxis or an inhaled foreign body. The diagnosis is clinical. The RCH acute asthma guideline and the Queensland preschool wheeze guideline grade severity, and confirm the diagnosis, by repeated bedside assessment. This covers mental state, work of breathing, ability to talk, air entry, respiratory rate and SpO2, checked after each salbutamol dose by spacer and mask and again at the end of the first hour. Improvement with a bronchodilator supports the diagnosis and guides the decision to admit or discharge. Routine chest X-ray, blood tests and blood gases are not recommended because they do not change management. Antibiotics are not indicated.
why: Correct: viral-induced wheeze is diagnosed and graded clinically, and serial review of work of breathing, talking, air entry and SpO2 after salbutamol both confirms the diagnosis and directs further management.

A chest X-ray is not routine in preschool wheeze because it seldom changes management; with equal air entry, no crackles and no choking episode, there is no suspicion of pneumonia, pneumothorax or a foreign body.
A blood gas is reserved for severe or life-threatening episodes not responding to treatment, and it is not needed in an alert child with moderate distress and SpO2 of 94%.
Children under about 6 years cannot reliably perform spirometry, and it has no place in assessing an acute episode.

items.stem:
A 25-year-old man attends a hospital pre-admission clinic before a planned colonoscopy. He has had 2 years of intermittent loose stools, crampy right iliac fossa pain, recurrent mouth ulcers and an unintentional 6 kg weight loss. He sometimes wakes at night to open his bowels. His GP started ferrous sulfate tablets 3 weeks ago. He eats a normal diet that includes bread and pasta and takes no other medicines. His temperature is 37.2 °C, pulse 88/min, blood pressure 118/72 mm Hg and respiratory rate 14/min. His conjunctivae are pale, and he has mild right iliac fossa tenderness with no palpable mass. Investigations show:
Haemoglobin 118 g/L (135–175)
MCV 76 fL (80–100)
Platelets 448 x10^9/L (150–400)
Ferritin 16 µg/L (30–500)
Transferrin saturation 8% (20–50)
CRP 28 mg/L (less than 5)
Albumin 31 g/L (35–50)
Vitamin B12 380 pmol/L (150–700)
Faecal calprotectin 520 µg/g (less than 50)
items.ask: Which of the following best explains this patient's blood count findings?
options: Anaemia of inflammation with replete iron stores
Vitamin B12 deficiency from terminal ileal disease
Absolute iron deficiency with coexisting inflammation
Folate deficiency from small bowel malabsorption
items.explanation: This man probably has ileocolonic Crohn's disease. His raised CRP, platelets and calprotectin and his low albumin show active inflammation, and he has a microcytic anaemia (Hb 118 g/L, MCV 76 fL). Ferritin is an acute phase reactant, so inflammation pushes it up. A ferritin of 16 µg/L despite a CRP of 28 mg/L, and despite 3 weeks of oral iron, therefore confirms that his iron stores are truly empty. In active IBD, a ferritin below 100 µg/L already suggests iron deficiency, and below 30 µg/L confirms it. A transferrin saturation of 8% supports this. The likely causes are blood loss from ulcerated mucosa and poor absorption. What this means for him: he needs his iron replaced, and IV iron (for example ferric carboxymaltose) is preferred because oral iron is poorly absorbed and poorly tolerated in active IBD. He should also stop the oral iron 5 to 7 days before colonoscopy. Anaemia of inflammation alone would give a normal or high ferritin. B12 deficiency and folate deficiency both cause a large-cell (macrocytic) anaemia, and his B12 is normal. Thalassaemia trait does not cause a low ferritin or a low transferrin saturation.
why: Wrong: anaemia of inflammation alone gives a normal or raised ferritin, but his ferritin of 16 µg/L is low even though inflammation should be pushing it up.
Wrong: terminal ileal disease can cause B12 deficiency, but that gives a macrocytic anaemia, and his B12 of 380 pmol/L is normal.
Wrong: thalassaemia trait causes microcytosis with normal or high iron stores, so it would not explain a ferritin of 16 µg/L and a transferrin saturation of 8%.
Wrong: folate deficiency causes a macrocytic anaemia, not a microcytic one with an MCV of 76 fL and low iron studies.

items.stem: A 68-year-old man sees his general practitioner because of difficulty swallowing for 10 weeks. Bread and meat feel as if they stick behind his lower sternum a few seconds after he swallows. He now cuts food into small pieces but drinks fluids easily. He has no choking, coughing, nasal regurgitation or hoarseness. He has lost 6 kg without trying and feels tired. He has had heartburn for about 20 years and treats it on and off using over-the-counter antacids. He smoked 30 pack-years until 5 years ago. He takes no regular medicines. His temperature is 36.7 °C, pulse 84/min, blood pressure 136/82 mm Hg and BMI 34 kg/m². He has conjunctival pallor. The abdomen is soft and non-tender, and there is no cervical or supraclavicular lymphadenopathy. Haemoglobin is 116 g/L (reference 130–180), mean corpuscular volume 76 fL (80–100) and ferritin 10 µg/L (30–500).
items.ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate next investigation?
items.explanation: He has progressive dysphagia to solids only, with food sticking after the swallow. This suggests a mechanical oesophageal obstruction. He also has alarm features: weight loss, fatigue and iron deficiency anaemia. His risk factors for distal oesophageal adenocarcinoma are long-standing untreated reflux (a possible Barrett's oesophagus), obesity and a smoking history. The Australian optimal care pathway for oesophagogastric cancer recommends urgent gastroscopy, ideally within 2 weeks, for dysphagia with alarm features. Gastroscopy shows the mucosa directly and allows biopsies, which give the tissue diagnosis needed to confirm cancer, and it can also find Barrett's mucosa or a benign peptic stricture. A barium swallow cannot provide tissue and would delay the endoscopy he needs anyway. CT is used for staging once a cancer is proven by biopsy. Manometry is for suspected motility disorders, and only after endoscopy has ruled out an obstruction. Testing for Helicobacter pylori does not investigate dysphagia and is not appropriate when there are alarm features.
why: A barium swallow cannot take tissue for diagnosis, and any abnormality would still need endoscopy, so it delays the diagnosis.
CT is used to stage an oesophageal cancer after biopsy has confirmed it, and it cannot provide tissue for diagnosis.
Manometry assesses motility disorders such as achalasia, which cause dysphagia to solids and liquids, and should only be done after endoscopy rules out a mechanical cause.
A urea breath test looks for Helicobacter pylori in uncomplicated dyspepsia and does not investigate dysphagia with alarm features.

items.stem: A 68-year-old man comes to his general practitioner because of episodes of a racing, irregular heartbeat. Over the past 6 weeks he has had four episodes. items.stem:

He takes no medicines and is not sure which vaccines he had as a child. His temperature is 37.2°C, pulse is 78/min and blood pressure is 122/76 mm Hg. He has scleral icterus and mild right upper quadrant tenderness. There are no stigmata of chronic liver disease and no asterixis. Investigations show:

AST 720 U/L (less than 40)
ALP 150 U/L (30 to 110)
Total bilirubin 52 µmol/L (less than 20), conjugated 38 µmol/L

Hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg): not detected

Hepatitis C antibody: not detected
items.ask: Which of the following best describes his hepatitis B status?

An anti-HBs of 2 mIU/mL is below the protective level of 10 mIU/mL, so he has no serological immunity. He is therefore susceptible and not infected. Wrong: immunity from vaccination needs an anti-HBs of 10 mIU/mL or more with a negative anti-HBc, and his anti-HBs is only 2 mIU/mL.

items.stem:
A 59-year-old man sees his general practitioner with 4 months of tiredness and 3 kg of weight loss. Several times he has had a non-itchy rash on both shins that fades within a week. He moved to Australia from the Philippines at age 20 and injected heroin for 3 years in his 30s. He has never been tested for blood-borne viruses. No childhood health records are available. He has never had jaundice before and has never received blood products. He takes no regular medicines. Temperature is 36.8 °C, pulse 78/min and blood pressure 128/76 mmHg. His sclerae are icteric, there are spider naevi on his chest, the spleen tip is palpable, and there is palpable purpura on both lower legs. Investigations show:
Platelets 118 x10^9/L (150–400)
Bilirubin (total) 58 micromol/L (<20)
Albumin 30 g/L (35–50)
INR 1.4 (0.9–1.2)
HBsAg: not detected
Anti-HBs: 90 mIU/mL (protective ≥10)
Anti-HBc (total): not detected
Anti-HCV: detected
HCV RNA: 2.1 x 10^6 IU/mL
items.ask: Which of the following is the most likely interpretation of his hepatitis B serology?
items.explanation: To read hepatitis B serology, look at three markers. HBsAg shows current infection. Anti-HBc (core antibody) shows exposure to the virus at any time, because only natural infection makes antibody to the core protein. Anti-HBs (surface antibody) shows immunity. In this man, HBsAg and total anti-HBc are not detected, and anti-HBs is 90 mIU/mL, above the protective level of 10 mIU/mL in the Australian Immunisation Handbook. Surface antibody without core antibody is the pattern after hepatitis B vaccination. He has never received blood products, so passive antibody from hepatitis B immunoglobulin is unlikely. For him, this means hepatitis B is not causing his liver disease and he does not need hepatitis B vaccination. With cirrhosis, he still needs his hepatitis A status checked. The cause of his liver disease is chronic hepatitis C: a positive anti-HCV with detectable HCV RNA confirms current infection. His low albumin, raised INR, low platelets and splenomegaly suggest cirrhosis, and the palpable purpura suggests cryoglobulinaemic vasculitis (ASHM; GESA hepatitis C consensus statement).
why: Resolved past infection would show a positive total anti-HBc along with anti-HBs, but his core antibody is not detected.
Inactive chronic infection needs HBsAg to be present for more than 6 months, usually with anti-HBc and anti-HBe, and his HBsAg is not detected.
In the window period of acute infection, HBsAg has cleared but anti-HBs has not yet appeared, and anti-HBc IgM is positive; he has the opposite pattern, with anti-HBs present and no core antibody.
Occult infection means HBV DNA is detectable without HBsAg, and anti-HBc is usually present; his negative core antibody and protective surface antibody do not suggest it.

items.stem: A 29-year-old man comes to a sexual health clinic in Melbourne with his regular male partner, aged 32, to discuss results. Last week the patient was diagnosed with HIV-1 infection after a reactive screening immunoassay was confirmed on Western blot. He has no other illness and takes no medicines. He starts daily antiretroviral therapy today. The couple have had condomless anal sex about weekly for 2 years, most recently 5 days ago. The partner says he dislikes condoms and will not use them reliably. The partner is well, has had no fever, rash or sore throat, and has a temperature of 36.7 °C and a normal examination. The patient's CD4 count is 480 cells/µL (reference 500–1500) and his HIV-1 viral load is 64,000 copies/mL. The partner's results today: HIV-1/2 antigen and antibody immunoassay non-reactive; hepatitis B surface antigen negative; hepatitis B surface antibody 120 mIU/mL; creatinine 79 µmol/L; eGFR >90 mL/min/1.73 m².
items.ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate measure to prevent HIV transmission to the partner?
options: Daily oral tenofovir disoproxil–emtricitabine for the partner until viral suppression is sustained
A 28-day course of three-drug post-exposure prophylaxis for the partner
Condomless sex resumed once the patient's first follow-up viral load is undetectable
Suppressive valaciclovir for the patient to reduce genital mucosal viral shedding
Three-monthly HIV testing of the partner with no antiretroviral medicine
items.explanation: The partner is HIV negative, will not use condoms reliably, and is having regular condomless anal sex with a man whose viral load is high (64,000 copies/mL) and who only starts ART today. He is at high ongoing risk and meets ASHM criteria for PrEP. Australia's PBS subsidises PrEP. His kidney function is normal and he is immune to hepatitis B, so he can start daily tenofovir disoproxil–emtricitabine today. He needs a repeat HIV test at about 4 weeks because his last exposure was 5 days ago, which is still inside the window period of the fourth-generation test. Under U=U, sexual transmission is prevented only once the patient's viral load has been undetectable for at least 6 months. PrEP should continue until then and can be reviewed after that. Post-exposure prophylaxis is not appropriate because the last exposure was more than 72 hours ago. Stopping protection at the first undetectable result is too early. Valaciclovir does not lower HIV transmission. Testing alone gives no protection.
why: Wrong: PEP must start within 72 hours of exposure and his last exposure was 5 days ago; it also does not cover ongoing exposures, which is what PrEP is for.
Wrong: U=U applies only after the viral load has stayed undetectable for at least 6 months, so a single first undetectable result is not enough to prevent sexual transmission.
Wrong: trials of herpes suppression with aciclovir or valaciclovir did not reduce HIV transmission to partners, and there is no evidence that this patient has HSV.
Wrong: regular testing picks up infection after it has happened but does nothing to stop it during high-risk ongoing exposure.

items.stem: A 63-year-old woman is on the orthopaedic ward 6 days after an elective left total knee replacement. This afternoon she suddenly became short of breath and developed sharp left-sided chest pain that is worse on inspiration. Her left calf has been aching and swollen since yesterday. She has hypertension treated with perindopril. Since surgery she has had subcutaneous low-molecular-weight heparin 40 mg each evening, and the last dose was 18 hours ago. She weighs 74 kg. Her temperature is 37.6 °C, pulse 114/min, blood pressure 136/80 mm Hg, respiratory rate 24/min and oxygen saturation 92% on room air. Her left calf measures 3 cm more around than the right. An ECG shows sinus tachycardia. Haemoglobin is 115 g/L, platelets 245 x10^9/L, creatinine 72 µmol/L (eGFR >90 mL/min/1.73 m2) and high-sensitivity troponin T 8 ng/L (reference <14). CT pulmonary angiography shows segmental filling defects in both lower lobes. The right-to-left ventricular diameter ratio is 0.8.
items.ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Switch to enoxaparin 1 mg/kg twice daily
Inferior vena cava filter insertion today
Enoxaparin 1 mg/kg twice daily added to current prophylaxis
Warfarin 5 mg orally daily without heparin cover
items.explanation: This woman has an acute pulmonary embolism caused by surgery, with a left calf DVT as the likely source. She is haemodynamically stable: her blood pressure is normal, her troponin is normal and her right ventricle is not dilated (RV:LV ratio below 1.0). That makes her non-high-risk. eTG recommends immediate therapeutic anticoagulation for stable PE. In a patient 6 days after surgery, a short-acting injectable drug is the sensible choice. Stop the prophylactic low-molecular-weight heparin and replace it with therapeutic enoxaparin, 1 mg/kg (about 75 mg) subcutaneously every 12 hours. Give the first dose now, because the last prophylactic dose was 18 hours ago. Do not give both. Her eGFR is normal, so she needs no renal dose change. Agree the bleeding risk with the surgical team. Later she can move to a DOAC or warfarin, and a provoked PE is treated for 3 months. Prophylaxis lowers the risk of VTE but does not remove it, so PE can still occur while she is on it. Thrombolysis is for PE with shock. A filter is only for patients who cannot be anticoagulated. Warfarin started alone is unsafe.

An inferior vena cava filter is only for patients with acute VTE who cannot be anticoagulated, and this patient has no contraindication to anticoagulation.
Giving a therapeutic dose on top of the prophylactic dose doubles up the heparin and raises the risk of bleeding with no extra benefit, so the prophylactic dose must be stopped.
Warfarin takes several days to work and can cause a temporary prothrombotic state at the start, so it must overlap with a parenteral anticoagulant until the INR is in range.

items.stem:

She was born in China and moved to Australia at the age of 20. Her vaccination history is unknown. She uses a levonorgestrel intrauterine device. Temperature is 36.9°C, pulse is 88/min and blood pressure is 118/72 mm Hg. Her abdomen is soft and mildly tender in the left iliac fossa. She has no jaundice, no hepatomegaly and no stigmata of chronic liver disease. Results:
HBsAg: positive
Anti-HBs: 2 mIU/mL (immune 10 or more)
Anti-HBc total: positive; anti-HBc IgM: negative
HBeAg: negative; anti-HBe: positive
HBV DNA: 420 IU/mL
ALT: 24 U/L (reference less than 35)
Bilirubin, INR and platelet count: normal
Hepatitis C antibody and HIV: negative
QuantiFERON-TB Gold Plus: negative, with a valid mitogen control
Liver elastography: 5.1 kPa (normal less than 7)

options: Begin infusions and monitor HBV DNA and ALT every 3 months
Complete a hepatitis B vaccine course, then begin infusions
Begin infusions and treat only if ALT rises above twice normal
Oral tenofovir now, with infusions deferred until antiviral cover is in place
Give hepatitis B immunoglobulin with each infliximab infusion

Vaccination prevents infection in people who are not infected and does nothing for an established chronic infection.
The ALT threshold guides treatment in people who are not immunosuppressed, and waiting for an ALT rise on anti-TNF therapy risks severe or fulminant reactivation.
Hepatitis B immunoglobulin gives passive protection after exposure or at birth and does not prevent reactivation of a chronic infection.

items.stem: A 24-year-old man sees his general practitioner on the afternoon after his first half marathon (21 km). His longest previous run was 10 km, three weeks ago. Over the final 6 km he became gradually more short of breath, slowed to a walk, and felt back to normal within 15 minutes of finishing. Transthoracic echocardiogram to look for cardiomyopathy
Reassurance, a slower mileage build-up and return precautions

Wrong: he has a low pretest probability and meets every PERC criterion, so a D-dimer is not indicated and could give a false positive that leads to unnecessary CTPA.
Wrong: he has no exertional chest pain, syncope, palpitations, murmur, family history of sudden death or ECG abnormality, so echocardiography is not indicated.

items.stem: A 63-year-old man sees his general practitioner because of 6 months of numbness and intermittent shooting pain in both feet. He feels unsteady when he walks to the bathroom at night. He has no back pain and no bladder or bowel symptoms. He has had type 2 diabetes for 8 years and has taken metformin 1 g twice daily the whole time, along with ramipril. He drinks two standard drinks a week and eats a mixed diet. His blood pressure is 134/82 mm Hg and pulse is 76/min. Pinprick and 10 g monofilament sensation are reduced symmetrically to the mid-shins. Vibration sense is absent at both great toes. Ankle reflexes are absent, knee reflexes are normal and plantar responses are flexor. Power and tone are normal. Romberg test is positive. Pedal pulses are palpable. Investigations: HbA1c 8.4% (target 7.0% or less), haemoglobin 141 g/L, MCV 92 fL (80 to 100), eGFR 74 mL/min/1.73 m2 and TSH 2.1 mIU/L (0.5 to 4.0).

options: Nerve conduction studies of the legs

Wrong: he has no back pain, sphincter symptoms, saddle anaesthesia, upper motor neuron signs or dermatomal pattern, so imaging the spine is not indicated.

Wrong: CSF protein is used when chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy is suspected, which presents with proximal and distal weakness and loss of all reflexes, not a purely distal sensory picture.

items.stem: A 71-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department by her daughter with 3 days of worsening breathlessness and green sputum. She has COPD and smokes 30 cigarettes a day (about 55 pack-years). Her medicines are tiotropium and budesonide-formoterol inhalers. At triage her SpO2 was 84% on room air. She was put on 15 L/min oxygen through a reservoir bag device and given nebulised salbutamol driven by 8 L/min wall oxygen. Forty minutes later she is drowsy but opens her eyes to voice and obeys commands. She has a flapping tremor. Temperature 37.9 °C, pulse 112/min, blood pressure 150/88 mmHg, respiratory rate 12/min, SpO2 99%. There is widespread expiratory wheeze. Arterial blood gas on her current oxygen: pH 7.27 (7.35 to 7.45), PaCO2 78 mmHg (35 to 45), PaO2 165 mmHg, bicarbonate 34 mmol/L (22 to 26). A gas taken at a clinic visit 4 months ago showed PaCO2 54 mmHg with a normal pH.
items.ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

Remove all supplemental oxygen at once
Start bilevel non-invasive ventilation at the current oxygen flow rate
Arrange rapid sequence intubation and mechanical ventilation

Wrong: NIV is for hypercapnic acidosis that persists despite optimal treatment, and running it at the same excessive oxygen flow would leave the cause of the acidosis in place.
Wrong: she obeys commands and has a reversible, iatrogenic cause, so intubation is not yet needed and should be kept for failure of controlled oxygen and NIV.
Wrong: this is a respiratory acidosis, and bicarbonate does not treat the cause and can increase CO2 production, so it has no role here.

She has constant right upper quadrant pain for more than a few hours, fever, a positive Murphy's sign, a raised white cell count and CRP, and an ultrasound showing gallstones, a thickened wall and pericholecystic fluid. Her ALP, GGT and ALT are all less than 1.5 times the upper limit of normal. Her bilirubin is normal and her common bile duct is not dilated (4 mm) with no duct stone seen. With a normal bilirubin, a normal duct calibre and no stone seen, her risk of a common bile duct stone is low. She does not need a preoperative MRCP or ERCP and can go to early laparoscopic cholecystectomy, with IV antibiotics as eTG recommends. A raised bilirubin, a dilated duct or a duct stone would change this. With fever, they would point to cholangitis. Option A is wrong because a blocked duct would normally raise the bilirubin and widen the duct, and she has neither. Option B is wrong because the transaminases are barely raised and the pattern is mildly cholestatic, not the large ALT rise of acute hepatitis. Option D is wrong because cholangitis needs signs of a blocked duct (jaundice or a raised bilirubin, a dilated duct) as well as fever, and she has none. Option E is wrong because a small GGT rise alongside a raised ALP fits reactive cholestasis, and she rarely drinks.
why: A blocked common bile duct would normally raise the bilirubin and dilate the duct, but her bilirubin is 15 µmol/L and her duct is 4 mm, so ERCP is not indicated.
Acute viral hepatitis causes a large ALT rise, often in the hundreds or thousands, but her ALT is only 44 U/L with a mildly cholestatic pattern, and the ultrasound explains her symptoms.
Cholangitis needs fever plus evidence of a blocked duct, such as jaundice, a raised bilirubin or a dilated duct, and she has none of these, so urgent decompression is not needed.
A small GGT rise alongside a raised ALP fits reactive cholestasis, and she rarely drinks, so alcohol does not explain these results.

items.stem: A 31-year-old woman, a primary school teacher, comes to the rheumatology outpatient clinic to discuss treatment of rheumatoid arthritis diagnosed 2 weeks ago. She has had 4 months of pain and swelling in both hands, wrists and forefeet, with 2 hours of morning stiffness. She has a 3-year-old daughter. She stopped her combined oral contraceptive pill 2 months ago, is trying to conceive and does not want to use contraception or delay pregnancy. Her only medicine is naproxen 500 mg twice daily. Temperature is 36.8 °C, pulse 78/min and blood pressure 116/72 mm Hg. She has soft synovial swelling of both wrists and the 2nd to 4th MCP and PIP joints, and the DIP joints are spared. CRP is 31 mg/L (reference below 5), rheumatoid factor 88 IU/mL (below 20) and anti-CCP 240 U/mL (below 7). Hepatitis B and C serology is negative, ALT is 22 U/L, eGFR is above 90 mL/min/1.73 m² and urine beta-hCG is negative. A hand X-ray shows periarticular osteopenia and a marginal erosion at the right 2nd MCP joint.
items.ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate disease-modifying drug to start?
items.explanation: She has early, seropositive, erosive rheumatoid arthritis with poor prognostic features, so she needs a DMARD started now to prevent more joint damage. The most important risk in her case is the drug harming a pregnancy, because she is trying to conceive and will not use contraception. Under eTG and Australian Rheumatology Association guidance, sulfasalazine and hydroxychloroquine are the conventional synthetic DMARDs that can be used before conception and through pregnancy. Sulfasalazine is started at a low dose and increased to 1 g twice daily. It is a folate antagonist, so she should also take high-dose folic acid (5 mg daily) before conception. It can be combined with hydroxychloroquine and short-term low-dose prednisolone if needed. She should plan her pregnancy with the rheumatologist and stop naproxen while trying to conceive. Leflunomide and methotrexate are teratogenic and need reliable contraception. Mycophenolate and tofacitinib are also unsuitable.
why: Leflunomide is teratogenic and its active metabolite stays in the body for up to 2 years, so a woman trying to conceive would need a washout with cholestyramine; it is contraindicated for her.

Methotrexate is usually the first-line DMARD, but it is teratogenic and abortifacient, so it needs reliable contraception and must be stopped before conception; it is contraindicated while she is actively trying to conceive.
Mycophenolate is a strong teratogen that causes miscarriage and malformations, and it is not a standard DMARD for rheumatoid arthritis.
Tofacitinib is a JAK inhibitor that should be avoided around conception and in pregnancy, and in Australia it is reserved for disease that has not responded to conventional synthetic DMARDs.

items.stem: A 32-year-old woman sees her general practitioner with 3 months of palpitations, heat intolerance and 6 kg of unintentional weight loss. She is not breathless and has no chest pain. She has no past medical history, takes no medicines or supplements, and has a contraceptive implant. Temperature is 37.0 °C, pulse 110/min and irregularly irregular, blood pressure 126/78 mm Hg, respiratory rate 16/min and oxygen saturation 99% on room air. She is alert and has a fine tremor, warm moist hands, and bilateral lid retraction and mild proptosis, with normal visual acuity, colour vision and eye movements. There is a diffuse, smooth, non-tender goitre with a bruit. There are no signs of heart failure. ECG shows atrial fibrillation at 110/min with narrow QRS complexes. TSH is <0.01 mIU/L (0.4–4.0), free T4 48 pmol/L (10–20), free T3 18.5 pmol/L (3.5–6.5) and TSH receptor antibodies 12.4 IU/L (<1.8). Full blood count, liver function tests and serum beta-hCG are normal.
items.ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
items.explanation: She has Graves' disease, shown by suppressed TSH, high free T4 and T3, strongly positive TRAb, a diffuse goitre with a bruit and orbitopathy. It is complicated by thyrotoxic atrial fibrillation. She is haemodynamically stable, afebrile and alert, with no heart failure, so she does not have thyroid storm and can be managed as an outpatient. eTG recommends a non-selective beta blocker such as propranolol to control the heart rate and adrenergic symptoms. It also recommends a thionamide, with carbimazole first-line outside the first trimester, to make her euthyroid. Baseline FBC and LFTs are normal and she is not pregnant. Thyrotoxic AF usually reverts to sinus rhythm once she is euthyroid. Her CHA2DS2-VA score is 0, so anticoagulation is not indicated. She must be told to stop carbimazole and have a same-day FBC if she gets a sore throat, fever or mouth ulcers. Amiodarone is wrong because its iodine load worsens thyrotoxicosis, and she does not need anticoagulation. Digoxin works poorly in a hyperadrenergic state, and propylthiouracil is kept for the first trimester or thyroid storm because it can damage the liver. Radioiodine is not first-line here and can worsen her active orbitopathy. Cardioversion while she is still thyrotoxic usually fails, so it is deferred until she is euthyroid.
why: Amiodarone's iodine load can worsen thyrotoxicosis, and with a CHA2DS2-VA score of 0 she does not need anticoagulation.
Digoxin controls the rate poorly in a hyperadrenergic thyrotoxic state, and propylthiouracil is kept for the first trimester of pregnancy or thyroid storm because it can cause severe liver injury.
Radioiodine is not first-line treatment for a new, uncontrolled presentation and can worsen her active Graves' orbitopathy, especially before she is euthyroid.
Cardioversion in a patient who is still thyrotoxic often fails and the AF tends to come back, so it is deferred until she is euthyroid, by which time the AF usually reverts on its own.

items.stem: A 70-year-old woman presents to a metropolitan emergency department with 10 days of worsening breathlessness. It has been severe since overnight, and she has orthopnoea and paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea. Six weeks ago she had an anterior myocardial infarction treated with a stent. Since then she has been taking over-the-counter naproxen for knee pain. Her pulse is 110/min and regular, blood pressure 194/102 mm Hg, respiratory rate 30/min and SpO2 87% on room air. She has a raised jugular venous pressure, a third heart sound and bilateral basal crackles. Her ECG shows sinus tachycardia with anterior Q waves, unchanged from her discharge ECG. Her chest X-ray shows bilateral perihilar opacification and small effusions. NT-proBNP is 7900 ng/L (age-adjusted rule-in level above 900 ng/L). High-sensitivity troponin I is 38 ng/L, then 37 ng/L at 3 hours (female 99th percentile 16 ng/L). Creatinine is 142 µmol/L. After CPAP, glyceryl trinitrate and intravenous furosemide, she is comfortable on 2 L/min of oxygen by nasal prongs.
items.ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate next investigation?
items.explanation: This woman has acute cardiogenic pulmonary oedema. She has orthopnoea, PND, a raised JVP, an S3, crackles, alveolar oedema with effusions on X-ray and a very high NT-proBNP. The likely cause is ischaemic left ventricular dysfunction after her recent anterior MI, made worse by NSAID-related fluid retention and hypertension. Her two troponin values are stable and barely raised, and her ECG has not changed, so this is chronic myocardial injury rather than a new infarct. The 2018 National Heart Foundation and CSANZ heart failure guideline recommends transthoracic echocardiography for every patient with suspected heart failure. Echo confirms the diagnosis and measures the LVEF, which decides between HFrEF and HFpEF and therefore which survival-improving treatments she should get. Echo also looks for mechanical complications of the recent MI (mitral regurgitation, ventricular septal defect, aneurysm, left ventricular thrombus), regional wall motion problems and valve disease. It is quick, done at the bedside and needs no contrast or radiation.
why: Incorrect: orthopnoea, PND, an S3, alveolar oedema and an NT-proBNP of 7900 explain her hypoxia, so pulmonary embolism is unlikely and iodinated contrast with a creatinine of 142 µmol/L brings risk for no gain.
Incorrect: her troponin is flat with no new ECG change, so there is no acute coronary syndrome needing urgent angiography, and the contrast load would add to her kidney injury.
Incorrect: cardiac MRI is a second-line test for when echo images are poor or the cause is unclear, not the first test for ventricular function in an acutely unwell patient.
Incorrect: a V/Q scan tests for pulmonary embolism, which the clinical picture does not suggest, and alveolar oedema and effusions make the scan hard to interpret.
